Candor is frank, open speech about difficult matters; artlessness is a more general lack of calculation or affectation in one's manner.

examples.everyday: Her artlessness is part of her charm; she says exactly what she thinks and never tries to look cool.
examples.professional: His artlessness in the meeting made it hard to tell whether he was being strategic or just honest.
examples.analytical: The poet's artlessness is itself a rhetorical achievement, since its plain diction conceals considerable craft.

nuance.analogy: Like a child's drawing that looks effortless and honest because nothing in it is trying to impress you.
nuance.etymology: From artless plus -ness; artless is from art (skill) plus -less, originally meaning 'without skill' and later 'without guile'.
common_mistakes: Confusing artlessness with artistry, which means skill in art.
Pronouncing -less as /lɛs/ instead of /lɪs/.

senses.definition: Something or someone that is assessed.

core.definition: A person or thing that is being assessed, such as a property owner whose property is being valued for tax purposes.

pronunciation.tip: The primary stress falls on the final long ee sound, SEE, which is the -ee suffix. Avoid stressing the first syllable, and do not say the ss as a z.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in official contexts, but it can feel impersonal, since it reduces a person to their role in a process.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'assessee' mainly in tax, insurance and education policy, and it appears in official notices and legal documents. In everyday conversation, people say 'the person being assessed' or refer to themselves as 'the homeowner' or 'the student'. You are unlikely to need this word outside professional or administrative settings.

distinctions.note: An assessor makes the judgment, while an assessee is the one being judged or valued.
An examinee takes a test, while an assessee can be a property owner, taxpayer or any person or thing under evaluation.
Taxpayer is a general word for anyone who pays tax, while assessee specifically refers to the party whose value or liability is being assessed.

examples.everyday: The county sent me a new valuation letter for my house, so I guess I'm the assessee this year.
examples.professional: The assessee must submit supporting documents within thirty days of the notice, or the audit proceeds without them.
examples.analytical: The assessee's perspective is often absent from policy debates, which treat the process as a neutral measurement rather than a negotiated judgment.

nuance.analogy: Like a patient at a checkup: the doctor evaluates, but the patient is the one being measured.
nuance.etymology: From assess, plus the suffix -ee, which denotes the person who is the object of an action.
common_mistakes: Reversing the roles, so 'assessee' is used for the person who does the assessing; the assessor is the evaluator.
Stressing the first syllable instead of the final -ee.

senses.definition: A person or thing which assimilates.
In algae, a filament of cells involved with photosynthesis, usually full of chloroplasts.
senses.example: Under the microscope, each assimilator in the alga glowed green with chloroplasts.

core.definition: A person or thing that takes in new ideas, customs or material and makes them part of itself.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on SIM, and the final -or is a reduced er sound, not the oar sound. Say the last syllable lightly, as ter.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it describes a capacity without judging it.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use assimilator in everyday talk. It appears in academic writing on culture, learning and biology, including the algae sense. In casual speech people say a quick study or someone who fits right in. Use it when you need a precise word for a person or system that absorbs and adapts new material.

distinctions.note: An absorber takes in liquid, energy or shock physically; an assimilator takes in material and makes it part of itself.
An adapter changes to fit new conditions; an assimilator takes new material in and makes it its own.

examples.everyday: My cousin is a quick assimilator; within a month she knew everyone at the office.
examples.professional: Our best hire was a fast assimilator who picked up our codebase in two weeks.
examples.analytical: Many educators treat the student as an assimilator who connects new facts to existing knowledge rather than memorizing them.

nuance.analogy: Like a sponge that holds water and becomes part of its structure, the assimilator takes in new ideas and makes them its own.
nuance.etymology: From Latin assimilare, 'to make similar', from ad- 'to' and similis 'like'.
common_mistakes: Confusing the noun assimilator with the verb assimilate; the noun names the person or thing that does the absorbing.
Saying it as uh-SIM-uh-LAY-tor; the main stress stays on SIM and the ending is a reduced er.

senses.definition: A person or an animal that exhibits no symptoms of disease.
senses.example: After a 10-day observation period, group 1 was divided into subgroup 1A (symptomatics) and subgroup 1B (asymptomatics).

senses.definition: Preceded by the: people or animals that exhibit no symptoms of disease regarded collectively.
senses.example: At the end of the observation period, those who are still symptomatic require second-line treatment, whereas the asymptomatic are discharged.

senses.definition: Not exhibiting any symptoms of disease, as for example in a case which is subclinical (“without signs detectable by physical examination or laboratory test”).
senses.example: The patient was asymptomatic, so the screening test was the only reason we found the infection.

core.definition: Showing no symptoms of illness, even though a disease may be present.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on MAT, with weaker stress on ay. Pronounce the mp and pt clusters clearly, since the p in symptom is heard, and end with a short -ik, not -ick.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and clinical; in public health it can carry worry because asymptomatic people can still spread disease.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use asymptomatic mostly in medical and public health news, such as asymptomatic cases or asymptomatic carriers. In everyday talk, people say they feel fine or have no symptoms. It is a formal word and can sound stiff at a dinner table.

distinctions.note: Subclinical describes disease too mild to be detected by standard clinical tests; asymptomatic means no symptoms are noticed, though tests may still show disease.
Presymptomatic describes someone who will develop symptoms later; asymptomatic means no symptoms now, with no implication about the future.

examples.everyday: My sister had the virus but was asymptomatic, so she never knew.
examples.professional: About a third of the enrolled patients remained asymptomatic through the twelve-week follow-up.
examples.analytical: The study distinguishes between symptomatic and asymptomatic disease, since treatment thresholds differ.

nuance.analogy: Like a slow leak under the floorboards that you cannot see until the damage shows.
nuance.etymology: From Greek a- not plus symptōma, occurrence or symptom.
common_mistakes: Dropping the p in symptom and saying asymtomatic
Confusing it with asymptote, a math term with a similar spelling

senses.definition: Of or pertaining to ataraxia or ataraxy.
Ataractic; tranquilizing.
An ataractic or tranquilizing agent.
senses.example: The doctor prescribed a mild ataraxic to help her sleep through the anxious weeks.

core.definition: Calm and free from anxiety or disturbance; tranquilizing, or relating to ataraxia.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on RAK, and the ending -ic is short, like 'ick'. Keep the first syllable light and unstressed.

nuance.connotation: Positive or neutral. It describes a calming quality or effect, and it is a technical word used mostly in philosophy or pharmacology.
nuance.usage_note: Most Americans would never use this word in everyday speech. You will see it in philosophy papers or in technical writing about calming drugs. For ordinary talk, say 'calming' or 'soothing' instead.

distinctions.note: Calming is common and everyday; ataraxic is technical and is mostly used for states of mind or agents that produce tranquility in a formal sense.
A sedative is a drug that makes you drowsy; ataraxic describes a tranquilizing effect that does not necessarily cause sleep.

examples.professional: The medication has an ataraxic effect, so the pharmacy team recommends against driving after the first dose.
examples.analytical: The Stoic ideal is ataraxic in character, since it seeks a mind unmoved by external events.

nuance.analogy: Like a heavy blanket on a restless mind: it does not remove the worry, but it quiets the motion underneath.
nuance.etymology: From ataraxia, from Greek ataraxia 'freedom from disturbance', from a- 'not' and tarassein 'to disturb'.
common_mistakes: Using ataraxic as a noun for a calming person; it is mainly an adjective.
Confusing it with ataxic, which describes uncoordinated movement.

core.definition: The queen of Judah in the Hebrew Bible, who seized the throne after her son's death and tried to destroy the royal family.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the third syllable, LY. The th is voiceless, as in 'thin,' and the final -ah is a soft American 'uh,' not a separate 'ah' vowel.

nuance.connotation: Negative. She is a villain in the biblical narrative, remembered for violence and usurpation.
nuance.usage_note: Americans know Athaliah from Bible study, Sunday school, and church history. She is not a common word, but it is a recognized name, and people usually introduce her with 'the wicked queen' or 'the queen of Judah.'

examples.everyday: Did you know Athaliah was a queen who tried to wipe out her own family to keep the throne?
examples.professional: In the Sunday school curriculum, Athaliah appears in the story of Joash, who was hidden and saved from her violence.
examples.analytical: Athaliah's seizure of power after Ahaziah's death shows how the line of David was almost broken by an act of violence within the royal house.

nuance.analogy: Like a ruler who burns down the palace to keep the crown, leaving only one hidden heir alive.
nuance.etymology: From a Hebrew personal name, often rendered 'Yahweh is exalted,' though the derivation is debated.
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable, as in 'ATH-uh-LY-uh.'
Pronouncing the final -ah as a full 'ah' vowel instead of a soft 'uh.'
nuance.biblical_note: Athaliah was the daughter of Ahab and Jezebel's house, and the wife of Jehoram king of Judah. After her son Ahaziah died, she destroyed the royal family, but her grandson Joash was hidden by Jehosheba and survived (2 Kings 11:1-3). The priest Jehoiada later had her put to death (2 Kings 11:16 and 2 Kings 11:20). 2 Chronicles 22:10-12 gives a parallel account of her reign and the hidden child.

senses.definition: Of or relating to atheism; atheistic.

core.definition: Relating to atheism or atheists; a rare older variant of atheistic.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the -IS- syllable. The ending '-ical' is usually reduced to 'ih-kul', so do not pronounce it as a full 'eye-kal'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral, but it sounds old-fashioned and literary compared with atheistic.
nuance.usage_note: Atheistical is an older, rarer variant of atheistic and sounds dated in modern American English. You may see it in older books or historical writing, but in your own speech or writing, use atheistic instead. Americans rarely use it in conversation.

distinctions.note: Atheistic is the standard modern adjective, while atheistical is rare and archaic in tone, so choose atheistic for nearly all modern writing.

examples.professional: The editor flagged the word atheistical in our draft and asked us to use atheistic instead.
examples.analytical: Eighteenth-century critics often described Hume's writings as atheistical, though his position was more complicated than the label suggests.

nuance.analogy: Atheistical is like an old coat in a closet: it still fits, but few people wear it outside.
nuance.etymology: From atheist with the adjectival suffix -ical, a variant of -ic.
common_mistakes: Choosing atheistical in modern writing when atheistic is the normal form.
Confusing the rare adjective with the noun atheist.

senses.definition: To try.
senses.example: to attempt an escape from prison

senses.definition: To make a substantial but unsuccessful effort (to commit a crime).
senses.example: The man was arrested after he attempted to rob a bank downtown.

senses.definition: The action of trying at something.
senses.example: We made an attempt to cross the stream, but didn’t manage.

senses.definition: An assault or attack, especially an assassination attempt.
senses.example: Police investigated the attempt on the senator's life during the rally.

senses.definition: An act of trying to commit suicide.
senses.example: Her attempt was not successful, and resulted in her being hospitalized.

senses.definition: A substantial but unsuccessful effort (to commit a crime).
senses.example: After their first attempt failed, the climbers tried again before the storm arrived.

core.definition: To try to do something, especially something difficult, uncertain, or important.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the second syllable, TEMPT. The mpt cluster is pronounced smoothly with no extra vowel between the m and the p and t, and the first syllable is a weak 'uh'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it often suggests the effort may not succeed, and in crime reports it is a serious legal term.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say 'try' in everyday talk, as in 'I'll try to call you,' and 'attempt' sounds more serious or formal in conversation. It is common in news and legal writing, as in 'attempted robbery' or 'an attempt on his life.' The informal phrase 'an attempt at' means a try at something, as in 'my first attempt at baking bread,' and a natural reply is 'It turned out great!'

distinctions.note: Try is the everyday word; attempt is more formal and often suggests a serious effort, especially one that might fail.
An endeavor is a sustained, serious effort toward a larger goal; an attempt can be a single try at something specific.
Effort is the work or energy you put in; attempt is the act of trying, often one specific instance.

examples.everyday: I'll make one more attempt to fix the Wi-Fi before I call the company.
examples.professional: We will attempt a rollout to the western region next week and review the results before going wider.
examples.analytical: Kant's attempt to ground morality in pure reason has been criticized for underestimating the role of human feeling.

nuance.analogy: Like reaching for a shelf that may be just out of reach: the attempt is the reaching, whether or not your hand gets there.
nuance.etymology: From Latin attemptare, 'to try, test', from ad- 'toward' and temptare 'to test, try'.
common_mistakes: Using attempt for everyday trying, which sounds stiff: say 'I tried to call' rather than 'I attempted to call'.
Writing 'attempt doing' instead of 'attempt to do'; 'attempt to' is the standard form, while 'attempt at' is used only with nouns.
Adding an extra vowel to the mpt cluster, saying 'uh-TEMP-it' instead of 'uh-TEMPT'.

attempt.etymology: Late 14th century, as Middle English *attempten*, from Old French *atempter*, from Latin *attemptō* (“to try, solicit”), from *ad-* (“to”) + *temptō*; see *tempt*.

senses.definition: Gold.
A sweet, orange-flavored Italian liqueur.
senses.example: After dinner, our host poured small glasses of aurum and we toasted the trip.

core.definition: Latin word for gold, seen mostly in chemistry and Latin phrases such as aurum potabile, or drinkable gold.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, with the vowel of 'or' and a weak final 'um.' Classical Latin said AW-room, but English speakers say AW-rum.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; a technical or historical term.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use aurum in ordinary English; you will see it in the chemical symbol Au, in Latin phrases or in historical writing. The Italian orange liqueur called Aurum is a brand name, so do not read it as an everyday word for gold.

distinctions.note: Gold is the everyday English word for the metal, while aurum is a Latin term used in science and scholarship.
Au is the chemical symbol for gold, and it comes from aurum.

examples.everyday: The bottle says Aurum on the label, but it is an orange liqueur, not real gold.
examples.professional: The chemistry handout gives the symbol Au for aurum, the Latin name for gold.
examples.analytical: The chemical symbol Au comes from the Latin aurum, which shows how older alchemical language still shapes modern science.

nuance.analogy: Aurum is the old Latin name on the periodic table's gold entry, like an heirloom label on a modern box.
nuance.etymology: From Latin aurum, gold, and related to aurora.
common_mistakes: Assuming aurum is a common English word for gold.
Pronouncing it AW-room, the classical Latin pronunciation, in an American context.
Confusing the liqueur brand Aurum with the metal.

senses.definition: A form of government in which the governing body has absolute, or almost absolute, control. Typically this control is maintained by force, and little heed is paid to public opinion or the judicial system.

core.definition: A system of government where a leader or small group holds nearly unlimited power, with little regard for public opinion or independent courts.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on TAIR, with a lighter stress on the first syllable. The -ian is pronounced 'ee-un', and the ending -ism is unstressed, sounding like 'iz-um'.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It describes a system that limits freedom and accountability, and Americans use it as a strong political criticism.
nuance.usage_note: You will hear this word in news, political science and political debate. In American politics, calling a leader or government authoritarian is a serious accusation. In everyday life, say strict or controlling for a boss or parent instead.

distinctions.note: Totalitarianism seeks control over all of life, including private belief; authoritarianism focuses on political power and may leave some private life alone.
Autocracy means rule by one person; authoritarianism can involve a small group or party and describes how power is exercised.

examples.everyday: My dad says the new rules are a step toward authoritarianism, but I think that's an overstatement.
examples.professional: The consultant warned that a rigid approval chain can slide into authoritarianism, where nobody below the director can make a call.
examples.analytical: Arendt argued that the isolation of modern masses made them vulnerable to authoritarianism, because people without shared public life are easily led.

nuance.analogy: Like a thermostat set to one temperature for everyone in the house, with no vote and no way to change it.
nuance.etymology: From authoritarian, from French autoritaire, from Latin auctoritas 'authority'; the -ism suffix marks a system.
common_mistakes: Using authoritarianism as a casual word for 'strict'; in American English it is a strong political term.
Stressing the -ism ending; the main stress falls on TAIR.

senses.definition: An AI agent that works toward goals with little or no human direction.

core.definition: An AI system that pursues goals with little or no step-by-step human direction, choosing its own actions to complete a task.

pronunciation.tip: In this phrase, the noun 'agent' carries the strongest stress, with AY as the most prominent syllable, while 'autonomous' keeps its stress on TAH. The vowel in 'agent' is a clear AY, not 'ih'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and technical. It is a standard term in AI research and product discussions, and it can carry a note of caution in policy debates.
nuance.usage_note: Engineers and AI researchers use this phrase to describe systems that plan and act toward a goal, often using tools, such as software that books travel or runs tests. In a meeting, you might say 'We're building an autonomous agent for code review.' Americans often discuss the risks of autonomous agents in policy and safety conversations.

distinctions.note: An AI assistant usually responds to requests one at a time with a person in the loop. An autonomous agent plans multiple steps and acts toward a goal with little supervision.
A chatbot mainly produces text in conversation. An autonomous agent can take actions, such as calling tools or changing files, based on its own plan.

examples.everyday: My friend said his company is testing an autonomous agent that books the team's travel, but they still check the final itinerary.
examples.professional: Before we give the autonomous agent write access to the repository, let's agree on the permissions it needs and the approval steps.
examples.analytical: An autonomous agent blurs the line between tool and actor, which forces us to ask who is accountable when its chosen actions cause harm.

nuance.analogy: An autonomous agent is like a junior project manager who receives a goal, builds a plan, and checks in only when a decision is risky.
nuance.etymology: Autonomous comes from Greek autonomos, 'self-governing'; agent comes from Latin agens, 'doing,' from agere, 'to drive or act.'
common_mistakes: Saying 'autonomous agent' with stress only on AH-tuh-nuh-mus and dropping the stress on AY-jent, which sounds flat in American speech.
Using 'agent' in the sense of a sales representative when talking about AI systems.

conversation.text: An autonomous agent pursues a goal over many steps with little or no human input.
The more autonomous the agent, the more important it is to restrict its permissions.
Regulators are asking who's accountable when an autonomous agent makes a costly mistake.

senses.definition: A system that automatically increases or decreases the resources available to a process depending on need and availability.
senses.example: Our Kubernetes cluster adds pods during traffic spikes because the autoscaler watches CPU usage.

core.definition: A cloud or computing system that automatically adds or removes resources, such as servers or containers, based on current demand.

pronunciation.tip: The primary stress is on AW and the secondary stress is on skay.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a technical noun with no emotional meaning.
nuance.usage_note: In American tech work, people refer to 'the autoscaler' as a component, for example 'the autoscaler kicked in'. The word is standard in cloud and container contexts. Outside those contexts, people describe the same idea as 'automatic scaling'.

distinctions.note: A load balancer distributes incoming requests across existing servers, while an autoscaler changes how many servers exist.
An orchestrator deploys and manages containers, while an autoscaler decides how many of them should run at a given time.
A scheduler assigns work to available machines, but it does not usually change the total number of machines.

examples.everyday: Ask Dan about the website, since he set up the autoscaler that handles our busy weekends.
examples.professional: The autoscaler added four replicas after CPU usage stayed above 70 percent for five minutes.
examples.analytical: An autoscaler is only as reliable as the metric it reacts to, so a poorly chosen signal can cause the system to oscillate.

nuance.analogy: A thermostat for servers: it turns capacity up when the room fills and turns it back down when people leave.
nuance.etymology: From autoscale plus the agent suffix -er, 'one that does'.
common_mistakes: Adding an extra z sound, as in AW-tohz-skay-lur, which is not standard pronunciation.
Confusing the autoscaler with the load balancer, which spreads traffic but does not add capacity.

senses.definition: Traditionally the third of the four seasons, when deciduous trees lose their leaves, and temperatures and daylight hours decrease; typically regarded as spanning the months of September, October, and November in the Northern Hemisphere, and the months of March, April and May in the Southern Hemisphere.
senses.example: autumn leaves

senses.definition: The time period when someone or something is past its prime.
senses.example: The band's autumn lasted a decade after its hits faded.

senses.definition: A person with relatively dark hair and a warm skin tone, seen as best suited to certain colors in clothing.
senses.example: At the color consultation, the stylist said I was an autumn, so earthy tones suited me best.

senses.definition: To spend the autumn (in a particular place).
senses.example: Every year the family autumns in Vermont, renting a cabin near the foliage trails.

senses.definition: To (cause to) undergo the changes associated with autumn, such as leaves changing color and falling from trees.
senses.example: The cold snap autumned the maples early, and the leaves were falling by mid-September.

core.definition: The season between summer and winter, roughly September through November in the Northern Hemisphere, when leaves change color and fall from trees.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on AW, and the second syllable is a weak schwa vowel followed by m, so it has only two syllables. Do not add an extra vowel or say AW-toom.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to warm. The word often carries a poetic or reflective feeling.
nuance.usage_note: Most Americans say 'fall' in everyday speech, as in 'this fall' or 'in the fall'. 'Autumn' sounds more formal, literary, or poetic, and it is common in writing about seasons, weather reports, and older or British-influenced contexts. If you are talking with neighbors or coworkers, 'fall' is the natural choice.

distinctions.note: Fall is the everyday American word for the same season, while autumn sounds more formal or literary.
Autumn is the noun for the season, while autumnal is the adjective meaning 'of or like autumn'.

examples.everyday: I love autumn in New England, when the leaves turn red and the air gets crisp.
examples.professional: Our retail team plans the holiday promotions for autumn, so inventory has to be locked by August.
examples.analytical: In the poem, autumn stands for the slow approach of death, when the year itself seems to grow old.

nuance.analogy: Like the middle act of a play, autumn is when the year's color turns and the story starts winding down toward winter.
nuance.etymology: From Latin autumnus, of uncertain origin.
common_mistakes: Saying the word as AW-toom with a long vowel instead of a weak schwa in the second syllable.
Using autumn in everyday American conversation where fall is the natural word.

autumn.etymology: Middle English *autumpne*, from Middle French *automne*, from Old French *automne*, *autonne*, from Latin *autumnus*.

senses.definition: An open declaration of affirmation or admission of knowledge.
senses.example: His avowal of loyalty to the team surprised everyone who had doubted him.

core.definition: A public and open declaration of a belief, feeling, or commitment.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the second syllable. The final -al is a weak, reduced syllable, not a strong 'ahl,' so it sounds like 'uhl.'

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive. It usually describes a sincere, open statement of belief or love.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use avowal in formal writing, speeches, or serious discussion, often about faith, love, or commitment. In everyday speech they say statement, declaration, or admission instead. It can sound overly formal in casual talk.

distinctions.note: An admission is often a reluctant confession, especially of a fault, while an avowal is an open declaration, often proud or sincere.
A confession often reveals a wrongdoing or secret, while an avowal states what one believes or feels.

examples.everyday: Her avowal that she was done with the job surprised everyone at the lunch table.
examples.professional: The CEO's public avowal of transparency helped calm the investors after the earnings miss.
examples.analytical: Her avowal of atheism is not a mere absence of belief but a considered position about the grounds of knowledge.

nuance.etymology: From avow and the noun suffix -al, from Old French avouer, from Latin advocare.
common_mistakes: Using avowal as a verb, as in 'He avowal his love.' The correct verb is avow.
Misspelling it as 'avowel,' which looks like a vowel.

senses.definition: A bachelor's degree.
A high school completion exam and qualification awarded in many countries (e.g. Finland, France, Moldova, Romania), designed to enable students to pursue higher education.
senses.example: She spent the summer studying for the baccalaureate, the exam that would decide her university options.

senses.definition: A farewell address in the form of a sermon delivered to a graduating class.
senses.example: At the baccalaureate, the chaplain urged the graduates to serve their communities with humility.

senses.definition: The International Baccalaureate.
senses.example: Her school offers the International Baccalaureate, so she takes rigorous courses in three languages.

core.definition: A bachelor's degree, the first degree awarded by a college or university.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the -LOR- syllable. The vowel in lor is a clear r-colored sound, and the final -ate is reduced to a quiet schwa, not a full 'ayt.'

nuance.connotation: Neutral and formal, describing an academic credential or a formal ceremony.
nuance.usage_note: In the United States, people usually say 'bachelor's degree' in everyday talk. Baccalaureate appears in formal writing, university announcements and the name of a religious service, the baccalaureate, held before graduation. The sense of a national high school exam is mainly used in other countries, such as France.

distinctions.note: They mean the same thing, but bachelor's degree is the everyday American term and baccalaureate is more formal.
Commencement is the graduation ceremony itself, while the baccalaureate is a separate religious service or address held before it.

examples.everyday: She finally earned her baccalaureate after six years of night classes, and the whole family came to celebrate.
examples.professional: Applicants must hold a baccalaureate in computer science or a closely related field to be considered for this role.
examples.analytical: The baccalaureate sermon traditionally asks graduates to see their degree not as an endpoint but as a vocation to serve others.

nuance.analogy: Like a first driver's license: a broad foundation that lets you go on to specialize later.
nuance.etymology: From Medieval Latin baccalaureatus, from baccalaureus, meaning bachelor.
common_mistakes: Assuming baccalaureate always means a religious service or the French bac exam; in American usage it usually means a bachelor's degree.
Stressing the wrong syllable, as in 'bak-uh-LAIR-ee-ate.'

baccalaureate.etymology: French *baccalauréat*, from Medieval Latin *baccalaureātus*, from Medieval Latin *baccalaureus*, an alteration made to *baccalārius* (“young man aspiring to knighthood, apprentice, bachelor”) for it to resemble *bacca lauri* (“laurel berry”).

senses.definition: Refusing to proceed or cooperate.
senses.example: a balky horse

core.definition: Stubbornly refusing to move, cooperate or work properly, said of machines, animals or people.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on BAW, and the final y is pronounced as a long ee sound. Avoid adding a second syllable, as in 'bal-kee-ee'.

nuance.connotation: Mildly negative. It describes frustrating unwillingness to cooperate, often in a humorous or affectionate way when describing animals or old equipment.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use balky most often for machines, such as an engine or printer that suddenly stops working, and for mules or horses that refuse to move. It is informal and vivid, so it works well in casual conversation, storytelling, and technical comments. For people, stubborn or uncooperative is more common in polite speech.

distinctions.note: Stubborn is general and describes a person's fixed will, while balky suggests a sudden refusal to move forward, often for machines or animals.
Reluctant means hesitant but may still comply, while balky means actively refusing or stopping.
Recalcitrant is more formal and is used for persistent defiance, especially by institutions or officials.

examples.everyday: My old lawn mower is balky in the morning, so I always give it a few tries before I call it quits.
examples.professional: The deployment script is balky on Windows machines, so we run it from Linux for now.
examples.analytical: A balky institution resists reform not out of malice, but because its incentives reward stability over change.

nuance.analogy: Like a mule planting its feet in the mud, refusing to take another step no matter how much you pull.
nuance.etymology: From balk, plus the -y suffix forming an adjective.
common_mistakes: Spelling it balkey, which is a common error; the correct spelling is balky.
Confusing balky with bulky, which means large and awkward in size.
Using balky for people in formal writing, where stubborn or uncooperative is usually better.

senses.definition: A rigid bracelet or anklet, especially one with no clasp.
To beat about in the air; flutter: said of a hawk which does not rise steadily and then swoop down upon its prey.
senses.example: The hawk bangled over the meadow for a long moment before it finally plunged on the vole.

senses.definition: To flap or hang down loosely, as a hat brim or an animal's ear.
senses.example: The spaniel's long ears bangled against his face as he trotted through the grass.

core.definition: A stiff bracelet or anklet, usually without a clasp, worn as jewelry and slipped over the hand or foot.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable and make the g a clear, hard sound. The final -le is a syllabic l, so it sounds like 'gul' with no extra vowel between the g and the l.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It describes jewelry and fashion without emotional weight.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'bangle' for stiff, circular bracelets, often in sets, such as gold or silver bangles worn with a dress or sari. For a bracelet with links or a clasp, Americans say 'bracelet' or 'chain bracelet.' The verb senses in the dictionary, meaning to flutter or hang loosely, are rare and mostly literary or technical.

distinctions.note: A bracelet is the general word for any wrist ornament, while a bangle is specifically a rigid one with no clasp or flexible links.
A cuff is a wide, open bracelet that you slide on or bend around the wrist, usually more substantial than a bangle.

examples.everyday: She wore a stack of colorful bangles that jingled every time she waved.
examples.professional: Our jewelry line includes simple bangles in sterling silver and gold-plated brass.
examples.analytical: The bangle, unlike a flexible bracelet, holds its shape and so reveals the craftsmanship of a single continuous band.

nuance.analogy: A bangle is like a small hoop that stays put on your wrist, like a ring that has been stretched into a bracelet.
nuance.etymology: From Hindi bangṛī, a glass or metal bracelet, borrowed into English through Hindustani.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it 'BANG-ul' without the hard g.
Using 'bangle' for any bracelet, when Americans would say 'bracelet' for one with a clasp or chain.
Confusing it with 'banger', which is slang.

senses.definition: Any set of machine-readable parallel bars or concentric circles, varying in width, spacing, or height, encoding information according to a symbology.
senses.example: The cashier scanned the barcode on each item before printing the receipt.

senses.definition: A portion of a gene that identifies a particular species.
senses.example: Scientists used a short DNA barcode to identify each beetle species in the sample.

senses.definition: An instance of self-harm, typically with multiple parallel cuts along a line, similar in form to a machine barcode.
To apply a barcode (machine-readable code) to.
senses.example: The warehouse crew barcoded every pallet before it left the loading dock.

core.definition: A pattern of parallel lines and spaces, or a similar code, that a scanner reads to identify a product.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, and make the second syllable a long 'oh' sound followed by a clear 'd.' Do not say 'cod,' which has a short vowel. The r in 'bar' is strong in American speech.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a practical, everyday word with no emotional charge.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use barcode in stores, warehouses, and at work, as in 'scan the barcode.' The numbers under the bars are usually the UPC, or Universal Product Code, which is what the cashier sees if the scanner fails. In casual speech, people say 'scan it' rather than naming the code.

distinctions.note: A barcode is a one-dimensional pattern of lines, while a QR code is a two-dimensional square that can store more data and is often scanned with a phone.
A UPC is a specific standard for product codes in the US, and a barcode is the broader visual form that carries it.

examples.everyday: The cashier couldn't scan the barcode on the bottle, so she typed in the price by hand.
examples.professional: Our warehouse team barcodes every pallet before it ships, so inventory counts match the system.
examples.analytical: A barcode reduces a physical object to a machine-readable identifier, separating what a product is from the name a person gives it.

nuance.analogy: A barcode is like a fingerprint for a product: a unique pattern that identifies it quickly.
nuance.etymology: A compound of bar, meaning a stripe, and code, referring to the striped pattern of the symbol.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it as 'BAR-cod' with a short vowel.
Using barcode to mean a QR code on a phone screen; Americans usually say 'QR code' for that.

conversation.text: The barcode won't scan. Can you type in the number?
Hold the barcode under the red light at self-checkout.
You can scan the barcode with your phone to compare prices.

senses.definition: A cereal of the species Hordeum vulgare or its grains, often used as food or to make beer and other malted drinks.
senses.example: We planted barley in the north field because it tolerates cold, dry springs.

core.definition: A grain crop whose seeds are used for food, animal feed, and making beer and other malt drinks.

pronunciation.tip: The first syllable has the vowel of car, not bear. Pronounce the r clearly and keep the second syllable short and light.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; in cooking and farming it is ordinary, and in Scripture it often stands for humble, everyday food.
nuance.usage_note: In everyday US life, barley shows up in soups, salads and grain bowls, usually as pearled barley in the rice or grains aisle. Americans also talk about barley when discussing beer, since most American beers use malted barley. It is an uncountable grain, so you buy barley rather than barleys.

distinctions.note: Wheat is the main grain in American bread and pasta, while barley is chewier and more often used in soups and salads.
Oats are often eaten at breakfast as oatmeal; barley is more often used in savory dishes and beer.

examples.everyday: I made a barley soup with carrots and mushrooms for dinner.
examples.professional: Our brewery buys malted barley from a farm about two hours north of here.
examples.analytical: The barley harvest mentioned in Ruth 1:22 marks the time of Ruth's arrival in Bethlehem, a seasonal detail that anchors the story in agricultural life.

nuance.analogy: Barley is the plain, dependable grain of the pantry, good in many dishes.
nuance.etymology: From Old English bærlic, from bere, barley.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the first syllable like bear, as in BAIR-lee; the vowel is the one in car.
Using barley as a countable noun, as in three barleys; it is usually uncountable.
nuance.biblical_note: Barley was the staple grain of ordinary people in ancient Israel and was harvested earlier than wheat. In the Bible it appears as humble food and as a sign of abundance or disaster. In Exodus 9:31 the hail destroys the flax and barley in Egypt, and in John 6:9 a boy offers five barley loaves and two fish that Jesus uses to feed the crowd. Ruth 1:22 mentions the beginning of the barley harvest when Ruth and Naomi return to Bethlehem.

barley.etymology: From Middle English *barly*, *barli*, from Old English *bærlīċ* (“barley-like”), from *bere* (“barley”), from Proto-Germanic **baraz*, from Proto-Indo-European **bʰers-* (“spike, prickle”).

senses.definition: An exchange of goods or services without the use of money.
senses.example: We had no money so we had to live by barter.

senses.definition: The goods or services used in such an exchange.
senses.example: The man used his watch as barter to pay for his tab.

senses.definition: To exchange goods or services without involving money.
senses.example: She bartered a bonsai for one of the rare books in my library.

core.definition: An exchange of goods or services for other goods or services, without using money.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable and keep the r clear. In fast speech the t often becomes a soft flap that sounds like a quick d, so say 'BAR-der' lightly.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It describes a practical exchange and can sound friendly or resourceful.
nuance.usage_note: Barter is common in everyday talk about swapping services, such as trading babysitting for car repairs, and it is also used in economics for money-free trade. Americans often say trade or swap in casual speech. In the US, barter income is taxable, so it should be reported on your taxes if you earn money this way.

distinctions.note: Trade is the broader word and can involve money, while barter specifically means exchanging goods or services without money.
Swap is an informal exchange of items, often between friends, and does not always involve equal value.
Exchange is a general word that may or may not involve money, while barter always excludes money.

examples.everyday: Our neighbor fixed my fence, and I paid him back by watering his plants while he was away, a sort of barter.
examples.professional: The startup's first deal was a barter of software credits for office space.
examples.analytical: Economists often use the barter example to show why money emerged as a convenient way to avoid the problem of double coincidence of wants.

nuance.analogy: Barter is like trading your lunch cookies for a friend's apple, with no coins involved.
nuance.etymology: From Old French barater, meaning to cheat or to exchange, of uncertain origin.
common_mistakes: Saying 'barter money' when money is involved, which is not barter.
Using 'barter with' without naming the item exchanged, or using 'barter for' incorrectly.

barter.etymology: Late Middle English, from Old French *barater*.

senses.definition: A benchmark interest rate, from which other interest rates are calculated; a policy rate.
senses.example: On loans to higher-risk customers, the bank charges 5% above the base rate.

senses.definition: The background rate of occurrence of any phenomenon, which informs any logical analysis of its rate of occurrence under any subset of circumstances; especially, the proportion of individuals in a population who have a certain characteristic (e.g. trait, experience, circumstance), irrespective of any treatment effects in a treatment group of a scientific study.
senses.example: Ignoring the base rate, the test seemed far more accurate than it really was.

core.definition: In statistics, the background proportion of a population that has a given condition or outcome, before any specific evidence about an individual is considered.

pronunciation.tip: As a compound noun, base rate is usually stressed on BASE, so it sounds different from base as a verb. The word rate is a weaker, secondary-stressed syllable with a clear long a, and the t is a crisp American t before a vowel-less pause.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a precise technical term, though the idea it names is often ignored in everyday reasoning.
nuance.usage_note: Statisticians, epidemiologists, and data scientists use this phrase often in reports and reasoning about tests. In American finance, base rate can also mean a benchmark interest rate, but the more common US term is prime rate. In everyday talk, Americans might say the normal rate or how common something is.

distinctions.note: Prevalence is the share of a population that has a condition at a given time; base rate is the same idea used as a prior in probabilistic reasoning.
The prime rate is what US banks charge their best borrowers, while base rate in statistics means the background frequency of an outcome.

examples.everyday: The base rate for getting a parking ticket downtown is pretty high, so I just pay for the garage.
examples.professional: We need to adjust the model's predictions using the base rate of fraud in our transaction data.
examples.analytical: Judgments about a single case should begin from the base rate, since a test's accuracy alone cannot tell us the posterior probability.

nuance.analogy: The base rate is like the normal weather in a city before you read today's forecast; it is the starting point before you look at the evidence.
nuance.etymology: Base comes from Latin basis, and rate comes from medieval Latin rata, meaning a fixed amount.
common_mistakes: Confusing base rate with the result rate of a single test
Ignoring base rates when judging how likely something is

senses.definition: To bathe in warmth; to be exposed to pleasant heat.
senses.example: to bask in the sun

senses.definition: To expose oneself to heat, especially sunlight, in order to raise body temperature, as a form of thermoregulation.
senses.example: My lizard likes to spend his days basking on the stone near the lamp.

senses.definition: To take great pleasure or satisfaction; to feel warmth or happiness.
senses.example: to bask in someone’s favor

senses.definition: The act of bathing in warmth.
senses.example: Most cats enjoy a bask in the sunshine.

senses.definition: A group of crocodiles.
senses.example: A bask of crocodiles lay motionless on the riverbank in the afternoon sun.

core.definition: To sit or lie in warm sunshine, or to enjoy something pleasant such as praise, success, or happiness for a while.

pronunciation.tip: This is one syllable with a short a as in 'cat'. The final sk is a clean cluster, so do not add a vowel between s and k, and do not turn it into bass-kuh.

nuance.connotation: Positive and relaxed. It suggests calm enjoyment, though it is sometimes used ironically about someone who enjoys praise too much.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use bask mostly in writing, news, and descriptive speech about sitting in the sun or enjoying success. In casual talk, people more often say soak up the sun or sunbathe. The phrase bask in the glory is common in sports and business news.

distinctions.note: Sunbathe means deliberately lying in the sun, often to get a tan, while bask focuses on the pleasant feeling of warmth.
Relish means to enjoy something intensely, while bask suggests lingering in a warm, comfortable state.

examples.everyday: We lay on the dock and basked in the sun after our swim.
examples.professional: The team basked in the praise from leadership after the launch, but we still have open bugs to fix.
examples.analytical: Many classic essays on happiness warn against basking in pleasure without reflecting on its sources.

nuance.analogy: Basking is like a cat stretched out on a warm windowsill, soaking up heat without any hurry.
nuance.etymology: It comes from Old Norse baðask, meaning to bathe oneself.
common_mistakes: Using bask as a noun for getting a tan
Saying bask at instead of bask in

bask.etymology: Middle English *basken*, from Old Norse *baðask* (“to take a bath”), mediopassive form from underlying *baða* (“to bathe”) + *sik* (“oneself”), from Proto-Germanic **baþōną* and **sek*.

senses.definition: Any plant of several genera of the taxonomic family Fabaceae that produces large edible seeds or edible seedpods.
senses.example: Beans belong to the legume family, which is why they fix nitrogen in the soil.

senses.definition: The large edible seed of such a plant (for example, a broad bean, navy bean, or garbanzo bean).
senses.example: We soaked the dried navy beans overnight before making the chili for dinner.

senses.definition: The edible seedpod of such a plant.
senses.example: Green beans, also called French beans, can be pickled.

senses.definition: The bean-like seed of certain other plants, such as a vanilla bean or (especially) a coffee bean.
senses.example: Scrape the seeds from one vanilla bean into the warm cream before simmering.

senses.definition: An object resembling a pea or bean in shape, often made from plastic or styrofoam and used in large numbers as packing material or as stuffing for beanbags and similar items.
senses.example: The box was packed with foam beans so the glass vase would not break.

senses.definition: The head or brain.
senses.example: Use your bean for once and check the math before you submit the report.

senses.definition: The human clitoris.
senses.example: The doctor explained that the bean is highly sensitive, containing thousands of nerve endings.

senses.definition: A person; especially, a baby.
senses.example: Grandma called the newborn her little bean the moment she held him.

senses.definition: Clipping of JavaBean.
senses.example: Our Java application uses a JavaBean to store each customer's order details.

senses.definition: Any form of tablet, especially benzedrine (benny).
senses.example: He swallowed a bean before the exam and stayed up all night studying.

senses.definition: Clipping of toe bean.
senses.example: The puppy's soft toe beans felt cool against my palm.

senses.definition: To hit with a projectile, especially a deliberately aimed blow to the head.
senses.example: The pitcher beaned the batter, rather than letting him hit another home run.

core.definition: The edible seed of a plant in the pea family, or the pod that holds it, eaten as a vegetable or as a dried food.

pronunciation.tip: Use a long, tense 'ee' vowel that rhymes with 'green' and 'queen'. Do not shorten it to 'bin'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; beans are ordinary, inexpensive, everyday food.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say 'green beans' for the whole pod eaten as a vegetable, and 'string beans' is a casual older term. Dried beans like 'pinto' and 'black' are staples in American cooking. Informally, 'bean' can also mean the head, as in 'use your bean', and 'to bean someone' means to hit them on the head.

distinctions.note: Peas and beans are both legumes, but Americans usually mean round, small green peas by 'peas', while beans are usually longer or kidney-shaped.
'Legume' is the broader term for the plant family and its pods, while 'bean' names a specific kind of legume.

examples.everyday: Could you grab a can of black beans from the pantry? I'm making tacos tonight.
examples.professional: We need to order more green beans and black beans for the cafeteria menu this week.
examples.analytical: Ezekiel 4:9 lists beans and lentils among the grains mixed into a single bread, which shows how ordinary such foods were in ancient Israel.

nuance.analogy: A bean is like a seed tucked in a pod, and the pod exists to protect it until it is ready.
nuance.etymology: From Old English bēan.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing 'bean' with a short vowel, as in 'bin'
Saying 'a bean' for food when Americans usually say 'some beans' or 'a can of beans'
nuance.biblical_note: Hebrew pōl (פּוֹל), the broad bean or fava bean. 2 Samuel 17:28 lists beans among the supplies brought to David and his men at Mahanaim. Ezekiel 4:9 names beans among the ingredients the prophet is to mix into bread.

senses.definition: (poetic) Beautiful.
senses.label: poetic

core.definition: Beautiful, especially in a poetic or literary way; a formal word for something very lovely to look at.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The ending -eous is two light syllables, tee-us, not tay-us, and the final s is a simple us sound.

nuance.connotation: Positive and elevated; it sounds poetic and can seem overly formal or melodramatic in everyday talk.
nuance.usage_note: Americans find beauteous mainly in poetry, hymns, older novels, and formal speeches. Using it in conversation can sound affected unless the setting is deliberately poetic or playful. In ordinary speech, say beautiful, lovely, or gorgeous.

distinctions.note: Beautiful is the everyday word, while beauteous is literary and rare.
Gorgeous is informal and often describes vivid, striking appearance, while beauteous is poetic and formal.

examples.everyday: At the wedding toast, Uncle Joe called the bride beauteous, and everyone laughed at the old-fashioned word.
examples.professional: Our data visualization won an award, and one judge called it beauteous, a word I have never heard in a design review.
examples.analytical: Augustine's notion of a beauteous creation depends on an order of being, so the adjective carries a theological claim as well as an aesthetic one.

nuance.analogy: Beauteous is to beautiful what a formal portrait is to a snapshot: the same subject, presented with ceremony for an occasion.
nuance.etymology: Formed from beauty with the adjective suffix -ous, meaning full of or having the quality of.
common_mistakes: Using beauteous in casual conversation, where it can sound overly dramatic.
Pronouncing the ending as tay-us instead of tee-us.

beauteous.etymology: From Middle English *beautevous*, *bewteose*, *beautuous*, *boyteous*, *beuteus*, *beuteowse*, *bewtyvows*, equivalent to *beauty* + *ous* and/or *beauty* + *eous*.

senses.definition: The act or process by which something becomes.
senses.example: The becoming of a scientist is a slow process of failure and revision.

senses.definition: Pleasingly suitable; fit; congruous; beautiful.
Decent, respectable.
senses.example: Her grandmother insisted that a young woman's conduct should always be becoming.

core.definition: Suitable and flattering in appearance; making someone look attractive, fitting and pleasing to see.

pronunciation.tip: The stress is on the second syllable, BUM-ing sounds wrong; the first syllable is a reduced 'bih.' The final -ing is a light, unstressed 'ing,' not 'een.'

nuance.connotation: Positive. It praises appearance or manner as attractive and fitting, though it can sound old-fashioned in casual speech.
nuance.usage_note: Americans most often hear 'becoming' in fashion writing, formal compliments or older speakers, as in 'That hat is very becoming on you.' In everyday talk, 'flattering' or 'that looks great on you' is more natural. The older senses 'decent' or 'proper' are rare now. In philosophy, 'becoming' as a noun contrasts with 'being,' so readers may meet both forms in the same text.

distinctions.note: 'Flattering' usually describes a style or color that makes someone look slimmer or younger, while 'becoming' is a broader, more formal word for looking attractive and well suited.
'Suitable' means appropriate for a situation, while 'becoming' describes how a thing looks on a person.

examples.everyday: Your mom's new haircut is really becoming on her, and it suits her face.
examples.professional: The stylist recommended a softer neckline, which is more becoming for the client's photos in the annual report.
examples.analytical: Good portraiture is becoming to its subject, flattering without falsifying what the sitter actually is.

nuance.analogy: Like a well-tailored coat that fits the wearer, a becoming outfit looks as though it was made for the person.
nuance.etymology: From become, in the sense 'to suit or befit,' plus the adjectival -ing ending.
common_mistakes: Treating 'becoming' as an everyday word for any compliment: 'You look nice' is more natural than 'You look becoming' in casual speech.
Confusing the adjective 'becoming' with the verb form in 'He is becoming a lawyer,' which has a different meaning.

core.definition: In the New Testament, a name for Satan as prince of demons, used by Jesus's opponents to accuse him of working by demonic power.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the second syllable, EL. The last syllable rhymes with rub, not with bee. Many learners stress the first syllable or pronounce the first vowel as a long ee, which marks the name as foreign.

nuance.connotation: Strongly negative. It names the devil or chief of demons and carries strong religious and dramatic weight.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use Beelzebub mainly in religious, literary or humorous speech. In church or a Bible study, people may use it as a formal name for Satan. Calling a person a Beelzebub in casual speech is a dramatic or joking insult. The most common everyday word for the devil is Satan or the devil.

distinctions.note: Beelzebul is the spelling in the Gospel of Matthew, Mark and Luke in the Revised Standard Version; Beelzebub is the form used in the Latin Vulgate and the King James Version and remains popular in English.
Satan is the most common name for the devil in English; Beelzebub is a specific name for the chief of demons in the Gospel accusations.

examples.everyday: Some people in our Bible study use Beelzebub as just another name for the devil.
examples.professional: When I teach Mark 3, I explain that Beelzebub is the name Jesus's opponents use to accuse him of working with the devil.
examples.analytical: Mark presents Beelzebub as the prince of demons, so the accusation depends on the claim that Jesus casts out demons by the power of the demons themselves.

nuance.analogy: Beelzebub is like a family nickname for a notorious rival: everyone knows who it refers to, and the name carries the reputation.
nuance.etymology: From Greek Beelzeboul, from Hebrew Baʿal-zəḇūḇ, meaning lord of flies.
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable (BEE-lzeh-bub) instead of the second syllable (bih-EL-zuh-bub).
Writing it as a common noun, when it is a proper name and should be capitalized.
Confusing it with Baal-zebub of 2 Kings, which is a Philistine god at Ekron, though the two names are related.
nuance.biblical_note: The name is Greek Beelzeboul, from a Hebrew or Aramaic form of Baal-zebub, probably meaning lord of flies. In 2 Kings 1:2 the Israelite king Ahaziah sends to Baal-zebub, the god of Ekron, for an oracle about his illness, and Elijah rebukes him for it. In the Gospels, Jesus's opponents accuse him in Matthew 12:24 and Mark 3:22 of casting out demons by the prince of demons, which is the name used for Beelzebub. Jesus answers that a divided kingdom cannot stand, so the accusation is false.

senses.definition: A person who begs.
A person suffering from extreme poverty.
A mean or wretched person; a scoundrel.
senses.example: What does that silly beggar think he's doing?

senses.definition: A minced oath for bugger.
The last placer in Tycoon.
To make a beggar of someone; impoverish.
To exhaust the resources of; to outdo or go beyond.

core.definition: A person who lives by asking strangers for money, food, or shelter because they have no means of support.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, and the final -er is a light, reduced r sound, not 'ah.' Don't add an extra syllable like 'BEG-uh-ruh.'

nuance.connotation: Negative or pitying; calling someone a beggar can sound harsh, so polite speech usually avoids it.
nuance.usage_note: In American speech beggar is blunt and is used mostly in literature, history, or old sayings. Americans usually say 'homeless person' or 'someone asking for money' out of respect. The idiom 'beggars can't be choosers' is common and means people in need must accept what they get.

distinctions.note: Panhandler is the common American word for someone who asks for money in public places, and it sounds less old-fashioned than beggar.
Pauper is a formal term for someone who is destitute; it appears in history and law more than in daily speech.

examples.everyday: There was a man outside the grocery store asking for money, so I bought him a sandwich.
examples.professional: Our outreach team works with people who are often called beggars, but we prefer to say unhoused neighbors in reports.
examples.analytical: Jesus' parable of Lazarus shows a beggar at a rich man's gate, whose need the wealthy man is too comfortable to see.

nuance.analogy: Like an empty bowl held out in the street: it asks for what it cannot provide for itself.
nuance.etymology: From Middle English beggare, from beg; the origin of beg itself is uncertain.
common_mistakes: Using beggar as a neutral term in polite conversation, where it can sound insulting
Stressing the second syllable as bih-GER
nuance.biblical_note: Hebrew 'ebyon, 'needy' or 'poor,' and Greek ptochos, 'poor' or 'beggar.' Psalm 113:7 says God raises the poor from the dust and lifts the needy from the ash heap. 1 Samuel 2:8 describes God's care for the poor in similar terms. Luke 16:19-31 tells of Lazarus, a poor man at a rich man's gate, whose need goes unanswered.

beggar.etymology: From Middle English *beggere*, *beggare*, *beggar* (“beggar”), from Middle English *beggen* (“to beg”), equivalent to *beg* + *ar*.

senses.definition: The feeling that one belongs.
senses.example: I have a feeling of belonging in London.

senses.definition: Something physical that is owned.
senses.example: Make sure you take all your belongings when you leave.

senses.definition: (dated) Family; relations; household.
senses.example: Grandfather wrote that the whole of his belonging would gather for Christmas at the farm.
senses.label: dated

core.definition: The feeling of being accepted and part of a group, community or place where you fit.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the second syllable, LONG, and keep the ng sound clean at the end of both syllables. The final -ing is a short unstressed vowel, not a long ee.

nuance.connotation: Positive: it describes warmth, acceptance and community, and it is often used in personal or workplace contexts.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'belonging' often in talk about community, schools, workplaces and churches, as in 'a sense of belonging'. It is a fairly emotional word, so it sounds natural in personal sharing but may sound too abstract in very casual chat. The meaning 'something owned' is rare, and Americans normally say 'belongings' for personal possessions.

distinctions.note: Belongings are personal possessions, like bags and clothes, while belonging is the feeling of acceptance.
Membership is formal and means being officially enrolled in an organization, while belonging is emotional and may exist without formal status.

examples.everyday: Since we moved here, the neighbors have made me feel a real sense of belonging.
examples.professional: Our onboarding program is designed to build a sense of belonging for new engineers during their first month.
examples.analytical: Scholars of religion sometimes treat belonging as prior to belief, since people often join a community before they can articulate its doctrines.

nuance.analogy: Like finding your seat at a long table where everyone already knows you will be sitting.
nuance.etymology: Formed from belong with the suffix -ing.
common_mistakes: Using 'belonging' to mean personal possessions instead of 'belongings'.
Treating it as a countable noun, as in 'a belonging', when the feeling sense is usually uncountable.

senses.definition: An act of doing good; a benefit, a blessing.
senses.example: Her quiet kindness was a benefaction to everyone who worked beside her.

senses.definition: An act of charity; almsgiving.
senses.example: The church relied on the generous benefactions of parishioners to feed the hungry each winter.

core.definition: A gift, usually money or property, given to help a person, school, hospital, or other cause in need.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the third syllable, FAK, and keep the 'ben' and 'uh' syllables light. Do not stress 'ben' at the start; the stress shift from 'benefit' to 'benefaction' is a common error.

nuance.connotation: Positive; it describes generosity and charity, often in a respectful or slightly formal tone.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use benefaction mostly in formal writing, such as university histories, museum descriptions, or articles about donors. In daily conversation, people say 'donation' or 'gift' instead. You will see it on plaques or in wills, so it is worth recognizing, but you can use 'donation' in most speech.

distinctions.note: A donation is the everyday word for giving money or goods; benefaction sounds more formal and often refers to a large, meaningful gift.
A benefit is an advantage or good effect; a benefaction is an act of giving, not an advantage.

examples.everyday: The library got a huge benefaction from a local family, so the children's room finally got new furniture.
examples.professional: The foundation's benefaction will fund two new research positions in the medical school.
examples.analytical: Historians debate whether the benefaction was motivated by genuine generosity or by a desire for social status.

nuance.analogy: Like a seed planted by a donor, which grows into something the whole community can use.
nuance.etymology: From Latin benefactio, from benefacere, 'to do good'.
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable (BEN-uh-fak-shun) instead of the third.
Confusing benefaction with benefit, which means an advantage rather than a gift.
Using 'benefaction' in casual speech where 'donation' would sound more natural.

senses.definition: The state of being bilious.

core.definition: Queasiness or nausea from an upset stomach; in older usage, also irritability. This is an old-fashioned term.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable. The '-ious' ending is pronounced as one syllable, 'yus', so the word has three syllables, not five.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It describes an unpleasant physical or mood state, and sounds old-fashioned.
nuance.usage_note: Most Americans today would say 'nausea,' 'an upset stomach' or 'feeling queasy' instead. Biliousness appears mostly in older books, historical medical writing and occasional literary descriptions. Using it in ordinary conversation will sound odd or quaint.

distinctions.note: Nausea is the modern medical and everyday word for the feeling of wanting to vomit, while biliousness is an older, vaguer term.
Indigestion is discomfort or heartburn after eating, while biliousness was once a broad label for many digestive complaints.

examples.everyday: Grandpa blamed his biliousness on a greasy breakfast, though it was probably just the flu.
examples.professional: The 1890s clinic records list biliousness as a common complaint, which tells us how diagnosis has changed.
examples.analytical: Nineteenth-century physicians often diagnosed biliousness, a catch-all complaint that modern medicine has replaced with more precise terms.

nuance.analogy: Biliousness is like an old, vague weather report that says 'unsettled' where a modern forecast gives exact numbers.
nuance.etymology: From bilious (from Latin bilis, bile) plus the suffix -ness.
common_mistakes: Mispronouncing it as bil-ee-US-ness, with the stress on the wrong syllable.
Using it to mean anger in general, when it refers to a stomach or digestive state.

senses.definition: Biological; pertaining to biology or to a living organism.
senses.example: The pharmaceutical company's new biologic drug is grown in engineered cells rather than synthesized chemically.

senses.definition: An extremely complex drug, vaccine or antitoxin that is made from a living organism, or from products of a living organism.

core.definition: A complex drug, vaccine, or antitoxin made from living cells or from the products of living organisms, rather than by chemical synthesis.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on LAH, and the middle syllables are quick and reduced to uh. Don't stress the first syllable or pronounce the final -ic as 'eek'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a precise medical term, and in news about drug prices or approvals it carries no positive or negative judgment.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'biologic' mostly in medicine, pharmaceutical news, and talk with doctors about treatments such as those for rheumatoid arthritis, psoriasis, or some cancers. The plural 'biologics' is the more common form in headlines and industry reports. Ordinary Americans often just say 'a biologic shot' or 'a biologic drug' when describing a medication their doctor prescribed.

distinctions.note: A biosimilar is a biologic shown to be highly similar to an already approved biologic, usually sold at a lower price after patents expire.
Small-molecule drugs are chemically synthesized and much smaller, while biologics are large proteins or antibodies made in living cells.

examples.everyday: My sister is on a biologic for her psoriasis, and it has made a big difference for her.
examples.professional: The pipeline review shows three biologics in phase two trials, all targeting the same inflammatory pathway.
examples.analytical: Regulators classify insulin and monoclonal antibodies as biologics because their manufacture depends on living cells rather than chemical synthesis.

nuance.analogy: A biologic is like bread made with live yeast rather than mixed from chemicals: the product is grown by living organisms.
nuance.etymology: From Greek bios 'life', with the adjective suffix -ic; the noun use arose in pharmaceutical regulation.
common_mistakes: Using 'biologic' for any drug; it refers only to large drugs made from living sources.
Saying 'biologic' as a singular for several products; the plural form 'biologics' is used for the category.

senses.definition: Having two parts (two principal or main parts).
Having two participants; joint.
Having vertices that can be divided into two independent sets (see bigraph)
senses.example: In a bipartite graph, every edge connects a user node to a product node, never two users.

senses.definition: Divided into two at the base.
senses.example: The leaf has a bipartite base, split into two lobes that meet the stem.

core.definition: Having two parts, or involving two participants, such as a bipartite agreement; in mathematics, a graph whose vertices split into two groups.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on PAR, the second syllable, and the final -ite sounds like 'tight'. Do not say bi-PAR-tit with a short i at the end.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a precise term used in legal, business, and mathematical writing.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use bipartite mostly in legal, business, and math settings, such as a bipartite agreement or a bipartite graph. It is more formal than 'two-part' and rarely appears in casual talk. Do not confuse it with bipartisan, which refers to political parties.

distinctions.note: Bipartisan means supported by two political parties, while bipartite means consisting of two parts or participants.
Two-part is plain and everyday; bipartite is more formal and common in legal or technical writing.

examples.everyday: The lease is a bipartite agreement between me and the landlord, so nobody else has to sign it.
examples.professional: We modeled the recommendation system as a bipartite graph linking users to products, so each edge connects a user and an item.
examples.analytical: A bipartite structure makes certain problems tractable, such as matching, because the two sets of vertices can be treated separately.

nuance.analogy: A bipartite graph is like a dance with two groups of partners: dancers connect only across the two groups, never within one.
nuance.etymology: From Latin bipartitus ('divided into two parts'), from bi- ('two') and partitus ('divided').
common_mistakes: Confusing bipartite with bipartisan, since bipartite is about two parts or participants, not political parties.
Stressing the final syllable and saying bye-par-TITE.

bipartite.etymology: From Latin *bipartītus* (“bisected”), perfect passive participle of *bipartiō* (“to divide into two parts, bisect”).

senses.definition: Having or involving exactly two variables.
A polynomial or function with exactly two variables.
senses.example: The homework asked us to factor the bivariate and identify its three terms.

core.definition: Involving exactly two variables, such as a study that measures the relationship between height and weight.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on VAIR, the second syllable, not on bye. The r is pronounced, and the final -ate ending reduces to a light it sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a precise statistical term.
nuance.usage_note: Data scientists and statisticians use bivariate all the time in analysis reports, papers and meetings. Americans will say a bivariate analysis or bivariate correlation. For more than two variables, they switch to multivariate, so avoid using bivariate for a complex model.

distinctions.note: Univariate involves one variable, while bivariate involves exactly two variables that are analyzed together.
Multivariate means three or more variables; bivariate is the narrow case with exactly two.

examples.everyday: My sister's research looks at the bivariate relationship between sleep and mood, so it only uses two measurements.
examples.professional: Before we build the full model, let's run a bivariate analysis to check the correlation between tenure and churn.
examples.analytical: A bivariate model isolates the covariance between two variables, but it cannot rule out confounding by a third factor.

nuance.analogy: Like a graph with an x-axis and a y-axis: two dimensions, no more.
nuance.etymology: From bi- (two) plus variate, from Latin variare, to vary.
common_mistakes: Using bivariate for any model with several predictors; use multivariate when there are more than two variables.
Stressing the first syllable (BYE-var-ee-it); the stress belongs on VAIR.
Confusing the adjective with the noun; in some texts a bivariate is a two-variable function, but the adjective is far more common.

senses.definition: Resembling a block in shape.
senses.example: The oldest video games had crude, blocky graphics.

core.definition: Shaped like a block, with a square or rectangular form and heavy, solid sides.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, and end with a long ee sound. The vowel is the open ah of 'bloc,' not the short u of 'block' as it is said in some other accents.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to slightly negative, describing a chunky, angular look that may seem clumsy.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use blocky for furniture, robots, cars, or the pixelated look of old video games, as in 'blocky graphics.' For cars and buildings, 'boxy' is often more natural. The word describes shape only and is not usually an insult, though it can suggest a heavy or unrefined appearance.

distinctions.note: Boxy describes a square, upright shape like a box, often a car or room; blocky suggests heavier, chunkier pieces.
Chunky refers to thick, substantial pieces, often for clothing or food, and it is usually more positive than blocky.

examples.everyday: My old couch is kind of blocky, but it's really comfortable.
examples.professional: The first mockup looked blocky, so the designer rounded the corners to make the app feel friendlier.
examples.analytical: Early video game characters were blocky, and their simplified forms forced players to imagine the details that the graphics omitted.

nuance.analogy: Like a set of wooden toy blocks stacked into a rough shape.
nuance.etymology: From block plus the suffix -y, which forms adjectives.
common_mistakes: Using blocky for smooth or rounded shapes; the word always suggests angular, square forms.
Pronouncing the final -y as a short i, as in 'bloky'; it is a long ee sound.

senses.definition: Out of focus; partially obscured; smudged.
senses.example: blurred image

core.definition: Not sharp or clear; made fuzzy, smudged or partly out of focus.

pronunciation.tip: It is one syllable, and the -ed is silent, so it rhymes with 'heard' and 'word'. Keep the r-colored vowel and do not say 'bluh-red'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it describes loss of clarity in vision, images or boundaries, and can be used figuratively.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use blurred for photos, vision, lines and boundaries, as in 'the photo came out blurred' or 'the lines are blurred between work and home.' It is neutral in tone. In speech about eyeglasses, 'blurry' is more common, while 'blurred' sounds more descriptive or written.

distinctions.note: Blurry is more casual and common in everyday speech, while blurred emphasizes that something was smudged or made unclear, often by a process or action.
Fuzzy suggests soft, indistinct edges, sometimes pleasant or like fabric, while blurred suggests a loss of clear definition.

examples.everyday: The photo came out blurred because the kids were moving too fast.
examples.professional: The chart looked blurred on the projector, so I re-exported it at higher resolution before the meeting.
examples.analytical: The distinction between knowledge and belief is often blurred in ordinary speech, which complicates philosophical analysis.

nuance.analogy: Like a window fogged with breath: the shapes are still there, but the edges have lost their definition.
nuance.etymology: From blur, originally meaning to smear or stain, plus -ed, the past participle ending.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing -ed as a separate syllable; blurred has only one syllable.
Pronouncing the vowel like the 'ow' in 'blow' instead of the r-colored vowel in 'word'.

senses.definition: A corset-like sleeveless overgarment for women, sometimes provided with detachable sleeves.
senses.example: She laced her velvet bodice tightly over the linen chemise before the ball.

senses.definition: A blouse; any shirt for women, particularly the upper part of a two-piece dress or similar European folk costume.
senses.example: Her grandmother still sews embroidered bodices for the folk dancers at the Oktoberfest parade.

senses.definition: The upper portion of a women's one-piece dress, equivalent to a shirt, sometimes specifically excluding the sleeves.
senses.example: The dress had a fitted silk bodice and a long flowing skirt.

senses.definition: An underbodice: an undershirt for women.
senses.example: She wore a thin cotton bodice under her sheer blouse for modesty.

core.definition: The upper part of a woman's dress, from the shoulders to the waist, fitted closely around the chest and torso.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, and the second syllable is a short 'dis' with a reduced vowel. Do not say 'bo-dees' with a long o or add a final 'ee' sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it describes clothing and can sound romantic or old-fashioned in descriptions of gowns.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use bodice mainly when talking about dresses, especially formal, wedding or costume dresses. In everyday talk, people often just say 'the top' of the dress. The word is not used for a separate shirt; for that, Americans say blouse or top.

distinctions.note: A blouse is a separate top worn with a skirt or trousers, while a bodice is the upper part of a one-piece dress.
A corset is an undergarment that shapes the torso, whereas a bodice is part of the outer dress, though some bodices are boned like corsets.

examples.everyday: I love the lace bodice on that dress, but the skirt is a little too long for me.
examples.professional: The costume designer asked the tailor to reinforce the bodice before the wedding fitting.
