nuance.usage_note: Americans use dial-in number in meeting invitations, emails and chat messages. People often ask What's the dial-in number? or Can you send the dial-in? A reply can be Here it is, or Dial-in info is in the invite. It is a standard workplace term and sounds natural in professional settings.

distinctions.note: An access code is the PIN you enter after dialing, while the dial-in number is the number itself.
Conference line is a broader term for the phone system used for a call, while dial-in number is the specific number you dial.

examples.everyday: Text me the dial-in number for the family video chat, and I'll call from the car.
examples.professional: The dial-in number is in the calendar invite, along with the access code and a backup number.
examples.analytical: A dial-in number separates the audio channel from the video link, so participants can join by phone even when their internet connection fails.

nuance.analogy: A dial-in number is like the side door of a building: you can still get in when the front entrance is closed.
nuance.etymology: Formed from dial, to call by phone, plus in and number.
common_mistakes: Using dial-in number for a web link; a dial-in number is a telephone number.
Forgetting the access code: many dial-in numbers require a second code after you call.

conversation.text: The dial-in number is in the calendar invite.
I lost the dial-in number; can you send it again?
Call the dial-in number and enter the meeting ID.

senses.definition: A reference work listing words or names from one or more languages, usually ordered alphabetically, explaining each term's meanings or senses, often also containing information on its etymology, pronunciation, usage, semantic relations, translations, as well as other relevant information.
senses.example: If you want to know the meaning of a word, look it up in the dictionary.

senses.definition: A synchronic dictionary of a standardized language held to only contain words that are properly part of the language.
senses.example: The publisher's dictionary excludes slang and regional expressions, listing only standard English words.

senses.definition: A reference work on a particular subject or activity in which the entries are arranged alphabetically; an alphabetical encyclopedia.
senses.example: a law dictionary

senses.definition: The collection of words used or understood by a particular individual.
senses.example: By age six, the child's dictionary had grown to several thousand words.

senses.definition: Someone or something regarded as a repository or compendium of information.
senses.example: walking dictionary

senses.definition: An associative array; a data structure where each value is referenced by a particular key, analogous to words and definitions in a dictionary (noun sense 1).
senses.example: In Python, a dictionary stores each user ID as a key pointing to that user's profile.

senses.definition: To look up in a dictionary.
senses.example: She dictionaried every unfamiliar term in the Latin passage before starting her translation.

senses.definition: To add to a dictionary.
senses.example: Please dictionary the new acronyms so the spellchecker stops flagging them every time.

senses.definition: (rare) To compile a dictionary.
senses.example: After ten years of fieldwork, the linguist finally dictionaried the dialect of her grandmother's village.
senses.label: rare

core.definition: A reference book that lists words alphabetically and gives their meanings, pronunciations, spellings and usage.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, DIK. The middle is pronounced 'shuh', and the last syllable is weak 'ee'. Many learners stretch it into 'dic-tion-air-y' with full vowels.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It refers to a standard, practical tool.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use dictionary for any reference book of words, in print or online, and often say look it up in the dictionary. Common dictionaries include Merriam-Webster and the American Heritage dictionary. A thesaurus is a different book that lists synonyms, so do not confuse the two. If you need a dictionary that explains English words in English, just say an English dictionary.

distinctions.note: A thesaurus lists synonyms and related words; a dictionary defines words and gives pronunciation and usage.
A glossary is a short list of specialized terms, usually at the back of a book; a dictionary is broader and general.

collocations: look it up in the dictionary

examples.everyday: Can you check the dictionary for me? I'm not sure how to spell that word.
examples.professional: Our product documentation links to a shared data dictionary so every team uses the same field names.
examples.analytical: A dictionary is not a neutral record, since its choice of senses and examples reflects decisions about which usage counts as standard.

nuance.analogy: Like a map of a language: each entry marks the place where a word stands and how to get around it.
nuance.etymology: From Medieval Latin dictionarium, a collection of words, from Latin dictio 'word, saying'.
common_mistakes: Confusing dictionary with thesaurus
Mispronouncing the middle as a long vowel or stressing the last syllable

senses.definition: To make smaller.
To become less or smaller.
To make appear smaller than in reality; to dismiss as unimportant.
senses.example: He tended to diminish his own achievements, calling his research just a side project.

senses.definition: To lessen the authority or dignity of; to put down; to degrade; to abase; to weaken; to nerf (in gaming).
senses.example: The rival faction tried to diminish the mayor's authority by leaking private memos.

senses.definition: To taper.
senses.example: The river's width began to diminish near the canyon, narrowing into a shallow creek.

senses.definition: To disappear gradually.
senses.example: The pain in her knee began to diminish after a week of rest and ice.

senses.definition: To take away; to subtract.
senses.example: Each refund will diminish the store's total revenue for the quarter.

core.definition: To make something smaller, weaker, or less important, or to become less over time.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the second syllable 'MIN.' The final syllable is short, like 'ish.' Non-native speakers often stress the last syllable or lengthen the 'i' vowels.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to negative, since it describes a loss of size, strength, or importance. It can be used to belittle someone's contribution.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'diminish' in writing, speeches, and formal conversation, while in casual talk they more often say 'go down,' 'shrink,' or 'lessen.' It is common in business and science contexts, such as 'diminishing returns.' Saying someone 'diminishes' your work can sound stiff but clearly critical.

distinctions.note: Decrease is the neutral, everyday word for a drop in number or amount; diminish often suggests a loss of importance, strength, or quality.
Reduce is an active choice to make something smaller; diminish can happen gradually and without a clear agent.

examples.everyday: The noise from the street diminishes after midnight, so the apartment gets much quieter.
examples.professional: Our margins diminished this quarter because of higher shipping costs, so we need to review pricing.
examples.analytical: Critics argue that the emphasis on individual achievement diminishes the communal dimension of religious life.

nuance.analogy: Diminish is like a candle burning down: it gets smaller and dimmer as time passes.
nuance.etymology: From Old French diminuir, from Latin diminuere, 'to break into small pieces,' from de- and minuere, 'to make small.'
common_mistakes: Using 'diminish' when 'decrease' is more natural in everyday speech.
Stressing the last syllable instead of the second.

diminish.etymology: Formed under the influence of both diminue (from Old French *diminuer*, from Latin *dīminuo*) and minish.

senses.definition: Tending to cause discomfort, uneasiness or alarm.
senses.example: Even with a safety harness, losing one's grip that high up is disconcerting.

senses.definition: Gerund of disconcert.

core.definition: Causing someone to feel unsettled, uneasy, or alarmed, often because of something unexpected.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the third syllable, SUR. The final -ing is light and unstressed, and the r is rhotic, so the vowel sounds like 'er' in 'her.'

nuance.connotation: Negative or mildly negative. It describes something unexpected that makes people feel unsettled.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use disconcerting for situations or statements that are surprising and somewhat troubling, such as a strange silence in a meeting or an odd reaction from a customer. It is more formal than weird or creepy and sounds natural in news reports, reviews, and professional talk. In casual speech people might say it's kind of creepy or it threw me off.

distinctions.note: Discomforting describes a steady unease, while disconcerting suggests a surprising shock that breaks someone's composure.
Unsettling is a close synonym and slightly more emotional, while disconcerting is more formal and often used for unexpected events.
Alarming implies danger or a strong warning, whereas disconcerting is milder and focuses on confusion or unease.

examples.everyday: It was a little disconcerting when the bus driver stared at me without saying a word.
examples.professional: The disconcerting drop in conversion rates last week led us to recheck the tracking code.
examples.analytical: The text's sudden shift from praise to accusation is disconcerting, because it leaves the reader unsure whether the author is sincere.

nuance.analogy: A disconcerting moment is like a stair that isn't there when you expect it: your body and mind must suddenly adjust.
nuance.etymology: From disconcert plus the suffix -ing, forming an adjective describing an effect.
common_mistakes: Using disconcerting for a fixed condition; it describes an effect that surprises, not a permanent quality.
Confusing it with disconcerted, which describes the person who feels unsettled.
patterns: it is disconcerting to do sth

senses.definition: The act of cleaning the dishware.
senses.example: Dishwashing after dinner is my least favorite chore, so we take turns.

core.definition: The act of washing dishes, plates, glasses and cooking utensils, by hand or in a machine.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on DISH, the first syllable, and the second word 'wash' is weaker. Pronounce the 'ah' vowel of 'wash' as in 'cot', not 'wash' with an open 'aw' sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It describes a routine household or kitchen task.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say 'do the dishes' or 'wash the dishes' much more often than they use 'dishwashing' as a noun. The word is most common in compounds like 'dishwashing liquid' or in describing a job. 'Dishwasher' can mean the machine or the person who does the work.

distinctions.note: A dishwasher is either the appliance or the person who washes dishes, while dishwashing is the act itself.
Washing up is common in British English, while Americans usually say 'doing the dishes' or 'washing the dishes'.

examples.everyday: I'll do the dishwashing tonight if you handle the laundry.
examples.professional: The restaurant needs a second dishwashing shift to keep up with the dinner rush.
examples.analytical: Feminist historians have shown how dishwashing, long treated as trivial household labor, reveals who holds domestic authority.

nuance.analogy: Like a daily tide that washes away the mess of the day.
nuance.etymology: From dish plus washing, the gerund of wash.
common_mistakes: Using 'dishwashing' as a verb, as in 'I dishwashing', instead of 'I do the dishes'.
Confusing the act 'dishwashing' with the machine 'dishwasher'.

senses.definition: When a neutral-seeming policy or system harms one group disproportionately.

core.definition: A situation where a seemingly neutral policy or system harms one group much more than others.

pronunciation.tip: Both words have primary stress on their first syllable in a compound sense, with 'IM' in 'impact' the key stressed part. Avoid stressing 'pact' at the end, and keep the flapped t sound in 'impact' soft.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It points to unfair outcomes, often in law, hiring, lending, or algorithms.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use disparate impact mainly in legal, policy, and technology discussions about discrimination, such as hiring tests or loan approvals. It contrasts with 'disparate treatment,' which means intentional discrimination. In everyday talk people would say 'hurts certain groups more' instead. In data science, it is often discussed when a model looks neutral but produces unequal results.

distinctions.note: Disparate treatment is intentional discrimination, while disparate impact is about unequal results even without intent.
Bias is a broader term for systematic error or prejudice, while disparate impact specifically describes unequal outcomes for groups.
Discrimination is a general word for unfair treatment, while disparate impact is a specific legal and statistical concept.

examples.everyday: My friend says the new apartment rule hurts families with kids more, even though it looks fair to everyone.
examples.professional: Before we deploy the hiring model, we need to test it for disparate impact across gender and race categories.
examples.analytical: A policy may create disparate impact even when no one intends harm, which is why courts examine outcomes as well as motives.

nuance.analogy: Disparate impact is like a ramp built for everyone that still leaves some people unable to reach the door because of a step they cannot climb.
nuance.etymology: 'Disparate' from Latin 'disparatus' (separated); 'impact' from Latin 'impactus' (pushed against), used in the legal sense from the 1960s onward.
common_mistakes: Saying 'disparate impact' with the stress on the second word alone, when both words carry meaning and the first is key in the phrase.
Confusing 'disparate impact' with 'disparate treatment,' which means intentional discrimination.

conversation.text: Disparate impact is when a seemingly neutral practice disproportionately harms a protected group.
In U.S. hiring, the four-fifths rule is a common rule of thumb for flagging disparate impact.
Even without race as a feature, the model could have disparate impact through proxies like ZIP code.

senses.definition: Unattractive, dislikable, objectionable.
senses.example: After the hurricane, the building was structurally sound but aesthetically displeasing.

core.definition: Unpleasant or objectionable; causing dislike, disapproval, or a bad impression.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the second syllable, -PLEE-. Keep the final sound of 'displease' as a voiced z, not an s, and do not reduce the 'ee' vowel.

nuance.connotation: Negative, describing something that causes dislike or disapproval; it is milder than 'offensive' or 'repulsive'.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'displeasing' mainly in writing, reviews, and formal evaluations to describe things, such as a smell, a design, or behavior. In casual speech, 'unpleasant', 'gross', or 'not great' are more common. It sounds deliberate and slightly formal when used in conversation.

distinctions.note: Unpleasant is the everyday, general word for something not enjoyable, while displeasing suggests a stronger sense of disapproval.
Objectionable implies something morally or socially wrong or worthy of protest, which is stronger than displeasing.
Unappealing means not attractive, a matter of taste, whereas displeasing can also involve judgment about quality or conduct.

examples.everyday: That burnt-popcorn smell is kind of displeasing, honestly.
examples.professional: The cluttered dashboard layout is displeasing to users, and the drop-off rate in our analytics shows it.
examples.analytical: A theory that makes moral outcomes depend on arbitrary luck is displeasing not only in its results but in its arbitrariness.

nuance.analogy: A displeasing quality is like one sour note in a song that spoils your enjoyment of the whole piece.
nuance.etymology: Formed in English from displease (dis- 'not' + please) and the suffix -ing.
common_mistakes: Saying 'The movie was displeased'; use 'displeasing' for the thing and 'displeased' for the person.
Pronouncing the final sound of 'displease' as s, when it should be a voiced z.

displeasing.etymology: Perhaps a calque of Old French *desplaisant*, from the verb *desplere* (“to displease”).

senses.definition: To eliminate or to get rid of something.
senses.example: I dispose of my trash in the garbage can.

senses.definition: To distribute or arrange; to put in place.
To deal out; to assign to a use.
senses.example: The committee will dispose the grant funds among the three regional clinics.

senses.definition: To incline.
senses.example: In these uncertain times, I am disposed towards caution.

senses.definition: Behavior; disposition.
senses.example: Her calm dispose won over even the most anxious clients.

core.definition: To get rid of something, or to arrange things in a particular place or order.

pronunciation.tip: The stress is on 'POHZ', and the final 's' is pronounced as a 'z' sound. Don't add an extra syllable at the end.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it sounds more formal than 'throw away' in everyday talk.
nuance.usage_note: In everyday American English, people usually say 'throw away' or 'get rid of.' 'Dispose of' is common in formal writing, signs, and instructions, such as 'dispose of batteries properly.' The phrase 'dispose of' is usually followed by an object.

distinctions.note: 'Throw away' is informal and everyday; 'dispose of' is more formal and used in instructions or policies.
'Arrange' means to organize things neatly; 'dispose' used as arranging is formal and less common.

examples.everyday: Just dispose of the old batteries at the recycling center.
examples.professional: We need to dispose of the outdated servers before the migration next week.
examples.analytical: The regime sought to dispose of its critics by confining them to remote prisons.

nuance.analogy: To dispose is to clear a table after a meal: you take everything away and it is gone.
nuance.etymology: From Latin 'disponere,' to arrange in different places.
common_mistakes: Saying 'dispose the trash' without 'of.'
Confusing 'dispose' with 'deposit'.

senses.definition: Subject to disruption.
senses.example: The disrupted power grid left thousands of homes without electricity for hours.

core.definition: Interrupted or thrown into disorder, so that something no longer works or proceeds in its normal way.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on RUHP, and the -ed ending is pronounced /ɪd/ after the t sound. Do not drop the final syllable.

nuance.connotation: Negative; it describes something that is not functioning well, though sometimes the disruption is temporary and minor.
nuance.usage_note: Americans often use this adjective for sleep, internet service, flights, schedules and routines: 'My sleep was disrupted by the noise.' It implies a temporary break in normal function rather than permanent damage. A natural comment is 'Sorry, our service was disrupted this morning.'

distinctions.note: Broken means not working at all. Disrupted means the normal pattern or process was interrupted, often only temporarily.
Interrupted describes a single stop in an action. Disrupted suggests the overall system or routine has been thrown into disorder.

examples.everyday: Our internet was disrupted during the storm, so I couldn't stream the game last night.
examples.professional: The team's sprint was disrupted by three unplanned production incidents, so we pushed the launch to next month.
examples.analytical: The argument is disrupted by an unexamined assumption about causation in its second premise.

nuance.analogy: A disrupted routine is like a train that is delayed at one station: the whole line runs late until the signal is repaired.
nuance.etymology: From disrupt, from Latin disrumpere 'to break apart'.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the final -ed as 'd' alone, when it is /ɪd/ after a t sound.
Using 'disrupted' where 'broken' is more accurate for a device that has completely stopped working.

senses.definition: Capable of distorting.
senses.example: Heavy compression can be distortionary, flattening the vocals until they sound harsh.

senses.definition: Causing distortion, especially in prices.
senses.example: Government price caps have distortionary effects that discourage grocers from restocking shelves.

core.definition: Tending to push prices, incentives or markets away from their natural or efficient level.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress is on STOR, with a lighter secondary stress on the nair syllable. The -tion is pronounced shuh, and the final -ary sounds like 'air-ee'.

nuance.connotation: Negative in economics: it implies a tax, subsidy or policy that bends markets and reduces efficiency.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use distortionary almost only in economics, public policy and academic writing: distortionary taxes, distortionary subsidies. In casual talk people say it messes up the market or it skews things. It is precise, so it may sound stiff at a party, but it is natural in a policy meeting.

distinctions.note: Distorting is the general word for changing a shape or meaning; distortionary is a narrower technical term for economic effects.
Inefficient means wasteful in general; distortionary specifically means that a policy pushes behavior away from the market's natural outcome.

examples.everyday: My economics professor kept saying that farm subsidies are distortionary, and I still don't fully understand why.
examples.professional: Carbon pricing is less distortionary than a broad tax on labor, so the team recommends it.
examples.analytical: Economists argue that a distortionary tax reduces efficiency even when it raises revenue for public goods.

nuance.analogy: Like a referee who keeps favoring one team: the game goes on, but the result no longer reflects skill alone.
nuance.etymology: From distortion plus -ary, from Latin distortio, 'a twisting apart'.
common_mistakes: Stressing the wrong syllable, as in dis-tor-SHUN-air-ee.
Using it for any harmful effect; it refers specifically to economic or policy distortion of incentives.

senses.definition: Separation (disintegration) of a union; lack of union where union would be desirable.
senses.example: The war deepened the disunion between the northern and southern states.

core.definition: The breaking apart or separation of a union, group, or alliance; a loss of the unity that should hold them together.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the second syllable, YOON, and pronounce the 'yoo' sound clearly. The final -ion is said as 'yun', not 'ee-un' or 'shun'.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It describes a serious breakup or division.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'disunion' mainly in history, political writing, and formal or literary contexts, especially about the sectional crisis before the Civil War. In everyday speech they say 'breakup', 'split', or 'division'. The word is not used for minor disagreements.

distinctions.note: 'Disunity' is the more common word for a lack of agreement or cooperation among people, while 'disunion' suggests an actual separation.
'Secession' is the formal withdrawal of a state or group from a larger union, while 'disunion' is broader and describes the state of being separated.

examples.everyday: The fight over the house split the family, and now there's real disunion between my brothers.
examples.professional: Without clear shared goals, the merger risked disunion between the two engineering teams.
examples.analytical: Lincoln framed the war as a question of whether disunion could be allowed to become permanent.

nuance.analogy: Disunion is like a rope whose strands have come apart: each strand is still there, but they no longer hold together as one line.
nuance.etymology: From dis- and union, from Latin unio, 'unity, oneness'.
common_mistakes: Using 'disunion' where 'disunity' is more natural, such as for a team that disagrees internally.
Stressing the first syllable as in 'DIS-yoo-nyun' instead of the middle syllable.

senses.definition: The act of divining; a foreseeing or foretelling of future events.
senses.example: Ancient Greeks consulted oracles for divination before making major decisions about war.

senses.definition: The apparent art of discovering secrets or the future by preternatural means.
An indication of what is to come in the future or what is secret; a prediction.
senses.example: Her grandmother read the sudden rain as a divination that a hard year was coming.

core.definition: The attempt to foresee the future or discover hidden knowledge by supernatural or mystical means.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the syllable -NAY-, and the final -tion is pronounced "shun." Keep the middle vowels short and unstressed.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in scholarly or historical contexts; often negative or cautionary in religious contexts, where it may be seen as forbidden.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use divination mostly in academic, religious or literary contexts, for example when discussing ancient cultures, the Bible, or fiction. In casual speech people say "fortune-telling" or "predicting the future." Religious Americans are likely to use the word with disapproval, since many traditions forbid it.

distinctions.note: A prediction can be based on data or reasoning; divination relies on supernatural or mystical means such as omens or cards.
Forecasting is a technical, evidence-based process; divination is a mystical practice and is not considered reliable knowledge.

examples.everyday: My grandmother never believed in divination, but she loved reading her tea leaves for fun.
examples.professional: Our research team does not use divination; we rely only on statistical models trained on historical data.
examples.analytical: Scripture consistently treats divination as a rival source of knowledge that displaces trust in God.

nuance.analogy: Divination is like reading the weather from a sprained knee: it feels like knowledge, but it lacks a reliable link to the thing it claims to predict.
nuance.etymology: From Latin divinatio, from divinare (to foresee, to be inspired), from divinus (divine).
common_mistakes: Confusing divination with divine, which is an adjective or verb meaning godly or to discover.
Using divination in casual talk to mean ordinary forecasting or guessing.
Stressing the first syllable (DIV-ih-NAY-shun) instead of the third.
nuance.biblical_note: In the Hebrew Bible, divination is forbidden to Israel; the Hebrew word qosem refers to one who practices divination. Deuteronomy 18:10-11 lists divination among the practices that the nations used and that Israel must not imitate. Acts 16:16 describes a slave girl with a spirit of divination, whose fortune-telling Paul drives out.

senses.definition: Solemnly or ponderously sad.

core.definition: Expressing deep, heavy sadness in a solemn or serious way.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable. The middle syllables are reduced, and the r is clearly American.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It suggests heavy, solemn sorrow, often in a dramatic or old-fashioned way.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use dolorous mainly in literature, sermons, formal writing or to describe a serious, sad tone. In everyday talk they would normally say sad, miserable or gloomy. Using it casually may sound pretentious, so reserve it for written or formal descriptions.

distinctions.note: Doleful suggests a gloomy, down-hearted look or sound, while dolorous suggests deeper, more solemn grief.
Sorrowful is more common and neutral, whereas dolorous is more formal and literary.

examples.everyday: He gave a dolorous sigh when the game was rained out again.
examples.professional: The report had a dolorous tone that made the whole team feel worse about the failed quarter.
examples.analytical: The poet's dolorous language transforms personal grief into a meditation on mortality.

nuance.analogy: A dolorous mood is like a heavy gray cloud that refuses to move and blocks out the sun.
nuance.etymology: From Latin dolor, meaning pain or grief.
common_mistakes: Confusing it with 'dolerous' or 'doleful' in spelling
Using it in casual speech where 'sad' is more natural

dolorous.etymology: From Middle English *dolorous*, from Old French *dolerous* (modern French *douloureux*), from Late Latin *dolōrōsus* (“painful”), from Latin *dolor*.

senses.definition: A scalar product.
senses.example: To find the angle between the two vectors, compute their dot product and divide by the magnitudes.

core.definition: A single number computed from two vectors by multiplying their matching components and adding the results.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on "PRAH" in "product," and "dot" is weakly stressed. The vowel in "dot" is the same as in "hot" in General American. The "t" in "product" is aspirated and clear.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a precise mathematical term with no emotional tone.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use "dot product" in linear algebra, physics, machine learning, and computer graphics. In textbooks it may also be called the scalar product or inner product. In a meeting, a data scientist might say "the dot product of the two embeddings" to refer to a similarity calculation.

distinctions.note: The dot product gives a scalar, while the cross product gives a vector perpendicular to both inputs and exists only in three dimensions.
A matrix product is a general operation on matrices, while the dot product is specifically for two vectors and returns one number.

examples.everyday: My physics homework asked us to find the dot product of two force vectors, so I had to multiply the matching parts and add them.
examples.professional: We use the dot product of the query and document embeddings as a fast similarity score in the search index.
examples.analytical: The dot product is bilinear and symmetric, and its value equals the product of the magnitudes times the cosine of the angle between the vectors.

nuance.analogy: The dot product is like measuring how much two arrows point in the same direction, returning one number that rises when they align.
nuance.etymology: "Dot" refers to the dot symbol used in the notation, and "product" comes from Latin productus, "brought forth."
common_mistakes: Saying "dot product" as one word or with the stress on "dot."
Confusing it with the cross product, which gives a vector rather than a number.

dot-product.etymology: In reference to the symbol · used to denote the operation.

senses.definition: One who requires proof before believing.
One who finds belief difficult. (Can we add an example for this sense?)
senses.example: My brother is a real doubting Thomas, and he won't believe the good news until he sees proof.

core.definition: A person who refuses to believe something until they have clear proof, often used playfully or critically.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on 'DOWT' and on 'TAH', and the 'Thomas' ending is a reduced 'muss'. In General American the vowel in 'Thomas' matches the cot vowel, so it sounds like 'TAH'.

nuance.connotation: Mildly negative, though often said playfully about a friend who needs evidence.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say this when someone insists on seeing proof, as in 'Don't be a doubting Thomas, I really did fix it.' It is usually lighthearted among friends and coworkers. In religious settings it is a reference to the apostle, so it may sound pointed when used about a person's faith.

distinctions.note: A skeptic habitually questions claims, while a doubting Thomas specifically wants physical or direct proof before believing.
A cynic assumes the worst about people's motives, while a doubting Thomas simply wants evidence.

examples.everyday: Don't be a doubting Thomas, I really did pick up the dry cleaning this time.
examples.professional: Our CFO is a doubting Thomas about forecast models until she sees the backtests on real data.
examples.analytical: Thomas's demand to see the wounds before believing has become a model for insisting on evidence without rejecting faith.

nuance.analogy: Like a customer who will not trust the store's new price until he sees it on the receipt in his own hand.
nuance.etymology: Named for the apostle Thomas in John 20; Thomas comes from Aramaic t'oma, meaning twin.
common_mistakes: Writing 'doubting thomas' in lowercase in formal writing; the name is usually capitalized.
Using it to mean someone who doubts only in general, without the idea of demanding proof.
nuance.biblical_note: In John 20:24-29 the apostle Thomas, called Didymus, says he will not believe that Jesus has risen until he sees the nail marks and touches them. Jesus later appears to the group, including Thomas, and invites him to touch the wounds. Thomas answers with the confession 'My Lord and my God!' The Greek name Didymos means twin.

doubting-thomas.etymology: Originates from the story of the Apostle Thomas in the Gospel of John, where he refuses to believe that Jesus has risen from the dead unless he can see and touch the wounds of Jesus himself.

senses.definition: To compose (a document), especially following a standard form; prepare a plan.
senses.example: I asked my lawyer to draw up a new will.

senses.definition: To arrange in order or formation.
senses.example: Sergeant, please draw the men up in ranks of three.

senses.definition: To cause to come to a halt.
senses.example: Draw up the carriage just around the corner!

senses.definition: To come to a halt.
senses.example: The tractor drew up alongside the haystack.

senses.definition: To withdraw upwards.
senses.example: The crane drew up the steel beam slowly above the construction site.

core.definition: To write up a formal document such as a contract, plan or list, or to bring a vehicle to a stop.

pronunciation.tip: Stress UP, with the short uh vowel of cup. In casual speech the two words link into one smooth phrase, with the r of draw clearly pronounced.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it is typical in business, legal and planning contexts.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use draw up for paperwork, as in draw up a contract or draw up a will, and lawyers and business people say it often. For a car, Americans more often say pulled up. In casual talk, put together or come up with is more natural than draw up a plan.

distinctions.note: Write up means to turn notes or results into a finished written report; draw up suggests preparing a formal document with set terms.
Draft means to prepare an initial version; draw up often refers to producing the final formal document.

examples.everyday: We need to draw up a list of who's coming to the party.
examples.professional: Legal will draw up the agreement, and we'll review it before the vendor signs.
examples.analytical: The committee drew up a framework that separated principles from procedures, clarifying its purpose.

nuance.analogy: It is like sketching a rough floor plan before the builders arrive, except the document is formal and binding.
common_mistakes: Using draw up to mean draw out or to mean making a picture; draw up means preparing a formal document.
Forgetting that the particle can separate the phrase: draw up the contract or draw the contract up.

senses.definition: Tending to droop; sagging; wilting.

core.definition: Tending to hang down or sag; limp, wilting or lacking firmness.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable with a long oo sound. The final y is a light ee, not a long ie sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to mildly negative; it can describe a plant, a mustache or a dog's ears, and it often sounds humorous or affectionate.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use droopy casually for things that hang down: droopy eyelids, a droopy mustache, droopy leaves. It is a friendly, descriptive word in everyday speech and is common in writing for children. In formal writing, drooping is usually preferred.

distinctions.note: Floppy means loose and flexible, moving easily; droopy means hanging down or sagging.
Drooping describes a current state, while droopy describes a more lasting or characteristic quality.

examples.everyday: The flowers look droopy, so I think they need water.
examples.professional: The droopy trend line on the dashboard suggests retention is falling.
examples.analytical: The argument's droopy middle section never recovers the force of its opening.

nuance.analogy: Like a wet sock hung on a line: heavy, limp and sagging toward the ground.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the final y as a long ie sound, saying DROO-pie.
Using droopy in formal writing where drooping is more natural.

droopy.etymology: Middle English *drupi*, from *drup* (“sad”), from Old Norse *drúpr* (“drooping sadness”); related to, *droupen* (“to sag, droop”), also from Old Norse.

senses.definition: Exhibiting duality.
senses.example: The novel's dual themes of faith and doubt make it richer on every reread.

senses.definition: Being the space of all linear functionals of (some other space).
senses.example: In functional analysis, the dual space of a Banach space consists of all continuous linear functionals.

senses.definition: Being the dual of some other category; containing the same objects but with source and target reversed for all morphisms.
senses.example: Reversing every arrow gives the dual category, which is useful when studying limits and colimits.

senses.definition: Characterized by having two (usually equivalent) components.
senses.example: a dual-motor vehicle

senses.definition: Pertaining to two, pertaining to a pair of.
senses.example: dual engine failure

senses.definition: Pertaining to a grammatical number in certain languages that refers to two of something, such as a pair of shoes.
senses.example: Modern Arabic displays a dual number, as did Homeric Greek.

senses.definition: Of a regular polyhedron with V vertices and F faces, the regular polyhedron having F vertices and V faces.
senses.example: The octahedron is the dual of the cube. The icosahedron is the dual of the dodecahedron.

senses.definition: Of a vector in an inner product space, the linear functional corresponding to taking the inner product with that vector. The set of all duals is a vector space called the dual space.
senses.example: For any vector v, its dual is the linear functional that takes the inner product with v.

senses.definition: Of an item that is one of a pair, the other item in the pair.
senses.example: Every sock I own has a dual somewhere in the laundry, but never the one I need.

senses.definition: The dual number.
senses.example: The dual numbers, which include an infinitesimal term, are useful for automatic differentiation in code.

senses.definition: A head-to-head match or meet between two teams, such as two high schools or colleges.
senses.example: Our high school's wrestling team faces the rival school in a dual this Friday night.

senses.definition: To convert from single to dual; specifically, to convert a single-carriageway road to a dual carriageway.
senses.example: The state plans to dual the old two-lane highway between the two cities next year.

core.definition: Having two parts, aspects, or functions; combining two things of the same kind, such as a dual-core processor or dual citizenship.

pronunciation.tip: Americans say 'DOO-ul', with no y sound; the stress is on the first syllable, and the second syllable is a light 'ul'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral, descriptive and precise.
nuance.usage_note: In everyday American speech, people more often say 'two' or 'double', but 'dual' is common in technical contexts like 'dual monitors' or 'dual citizenship'. It sounds formal in casual conversation. In mathematics, it has specialized meanings like 'dual space'.

distinctions.note: Double is the everyday word for two of something; dual is more formal or technical and emphasizes two distinct functions or aspects.
Twin refers to two similar or paired things, often identical in form; dual stresses two roles or functions within one thing.

examples.everyday: My sister has dual citizenship, so she carries both passports when she travels.
examples.professional: Our new laptop has dual monitor outputs, which makes it easier to run the dashboard and the notebook side by side.
examples.analytical: The author argues that the text has a dual purpose: it is both a historical record and a theological argument.

nuance.analogy: Like a coin with two faces, each side different but part of the same object.
nuance.etymology: From Latin 'dualis', from 'duo' (two).
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it with a y sound, like 'JOO-ul'.
Using 'dual' in casual speech where 'two' or 'double' sounds more natural.

dual.etymology: Borrowed from Latin *dualis* (“two”), from *duo* (“two”) + adjective suffix *-alis*.

senses.definition: Synonym of due date (“the date of payment in financial arrangements”)

core.definition: The day of the month or week when a regular payment or obligation is owed; a less common synonym of due date.

pronunciation.tip: Stress due, and give the second word a clear ay diphthong. Keep the final day as a full syllable without reducing it to dee.

nuance.connotation: Neutral
nuance.usage_note: Americans use due date far more often than due day. Due day appears mainly for recurring obligations, such as the due day for rent, a credit card or membership dues, where the day of the month matters. In everyday talk, say due date unless you specifically mean a monthly schedule.

distinctions.note: Due date is the standard American term for any date when something is owed; due day stresses a recurring day in a schedule.
Payday is when you receive your wages; due day is when you must pay a bill.

collocations: the due day of the month

examples.everyday: The car payment's due day is the fifteenth, so I set a reminder on my phone.
examples.professional: Each vendor's due day falls on the first business day of the month, so finance runs the batch then.
examples.analytical: Calling it a due day shifts attention from a single obligation to a recurring calendar rule, which matters for scheduled payments.

nuance.analogy: Like a recurring alarm on a calendar, it repeats the same obligation on a fixed day.
nuance.etymology: Due from Old French deu, from Latin debere; day from Old English dæg.
common_mistakes: Using due day for a one-time deadline, where due date is the normal American term.
Pronouncing day as dee, which sounds unnatural and can be confused with another word.

senses.definition: A period of time in which a system or component remains in a given state.
senses.example: The sensor's dwell in the idle state lasted nearly twenty seconds before the alarm sounded.

senses.definition: A brief pause in the motion of part of a mechanism to allow an operation to be completed.
senses.example: The cam's dwell lets the feeder arm pause long enough for the bottle to fill.

senses.definition: A planned delay in a timed control program.
senses.example: The controller program includes a five-second dwell before the valve opens to the tank.

senses.definition: In a petrol engine, the period of time the ignition points are closed to let current flow through the ignition coil in between each spark. This is measured as an angle in degrees around the camshaft in the distributor which controls the points, for example in a 4-cylinder engine it might be 55° (spark at 90° intervals, points closed for 55° between each).
senses.example: Adjusting the points gap changes the dwell angle, which sets how long the coil charges.

senses.definition: To live; to reside.
To linger (on); to remain fixated. [with on ‘a particular thought, idea, etc.’]
senses.example: Stop dwelling on the past!

senses.definition: To be in a given state.
senses.example: Many workers dwell in uncertainty while the company decides on layoffs.

senses.definition: To abide; to remain; to continue.
senses.example: Let the Lord's peace dwell in your heart as you go through the day.

core.definition: To keep thinking or talking about something for a long time, or to live in a place. The everyday sense is to linger on a thought or worry.

pronunciation.tip: It is one syllable with a short e, like 'bell'. Do not add a vowel after the d, and do not say 'dwell-uh'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to slightly negative when used with 'on', because it suggests spending too much mental energy on something. Neutral when it means to live somewhere, which sounds formal or literary.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say 'don't dwell on it' or 'she dwelled on her mistakes' in casual talk, usually to mean you should stop worrying about something. The sense 'to live in a place' sounds biblical, poetic or formal, so in everyday speech Americans say 'live' instead. A natural reply to someone who keeps worrying is 'Yeah, I know, but let's move on.'

distinctions.note: 'Live' is the ordinary everyday word for where you reside, while 'dwell' sounds formal or literary.
'Linger' suggests staying somewhere a little longer than needed, while 'dwell' usually refers to staying in your mind on a topic, often too long.
'Ponder' means to think carefully and deliberately about something, while 'dwell' often suggests unhealthy or repetitive focus.

collocations: dwell in the house of the Lord

examples.everyday: Don't dwell on the bad review; most people loved the show.
examples.professional: We shouldn't dwell on last quarter's delays; let's focus on the fix for next sprint.
examples.analytical: The author dwells on the inner conflict of the protagonist rather than on the external plot.

nuance.analogy: Like a song stuck in your head, a thought you dwell on keeps playing again and again.
nuance.etymology: From Old English dwellan, meaning 'to lead astray or delay', later 'to remain'.
common_mistakes: Saying 'dwell at home' or 'dwell in Boston' in casual speech, where 'live' is more natural.
Pronouncing it with a long vowel, as in 'dwail'.
Using 'dwell' for a short visit or passing thought, when 'think about' is more natural.
nuance.biblical_note: In Scripture, 'dwell' often means to live in the presence of God or to have God's presence among people. The Hebrew shakhan means 'to dwell or settle', and the Greek skenoo means 'to tabernacle' or pitch a tent. Psalm 23:6 speaks of dwelling in the house of the LORD forever. John 1:14 says the Word dwelt among us. Psalm 91:1 describes the one who dwells in the shelter of the Most High.

senses.definition: Great energy, drive, force, or power; vigor of body, mind, or personality; oomph or pizzazz.
senses.example: The new sales director brought a dynamism to the team that had been missing for years.

senses.definition: Dynamic reality; active energy; continuous change, progress, or activity.
senses.example: The fact that the war is no longer the main issue in the election points to the dynamism of foreign affairs.

senses.definition: Any of several philosophical theories that attempt to explain the universe by an immanent force.
senses.example: Leibniz's dynamism rejected the view that matter is merely extended substance without inner force.

core.definition: Great energy, drive and readiness for change and action, especially in a person, team or organization.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, 'DY'. The middle syllable is a reduced schwa, 'nuh', and the final syllable is a weak 'um'.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It praises energy, initiative and momentum.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'dynamism' in business writing, reviews and speeches to praise an organization's energy, as in 'the company's dynamism attracted investors'. In everyday talk people would say 'energy', 'drive' or 'a lot of go-getter spirit'. It can sound a little stiff in casual speech, so use it in writing or formal presentations.

distinctions.note: 'Energy' is the everyday word for vitality, while 'dynamism' is more formal and suggests a continuous, forward-moving force.
'Drive' suggests ambition and determination, while 'dynamism' emphasizes vigor and capacity for change.

examples.everyday: My grandmother has a lot of dynamism for her age; she still goes hiking every morning.
examples.professional: The new director brought real dynamism to the sales team, and our numbers rose within a quarter.
examples.analytical: Hegel's account of history emphasizes a dynamism in which contradictions drive the development of ideas.

nuance.analogy: Dynamism is like a river in spring, full of force and always moving forward.
nuance.etymology: From 'dynamic', from Greek dynamis, 'power' or 'force', plus the suffix -ism.
common_mistakes: Confusing 'dynamism' with 'dynamics' when talking about group interactions.
Pronouncing the stress on the second syllable, 'dy-NAM-iz-um'.
Using 'dynamism' for physical strength alone when 'vigor' or 'energy' is more natural.

dynamism.etymology: From English *dynamic* (or directly from Ancient Greek *δύναμις* (“power”)) + *ism*.

senses.definition: A subscriber to the philosophy of dynamism.

core.definition: A person who holds the philosophy of dynamism, the view that reality consists fundamentally of forces or activity rather than inert matter.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, DY. The second syllable is a weak 'nuh' and should not be pronounced as a full 'nah' or 'nay' sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. The word names a philosophical position without implying approval or disapproval.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this word almost only in philosophy and the history of ideas, mostly in academic writing or lectures. It is rarely heard in everyday life. If you need to use it, name the thinker, as in a Leibnizian dynamist, so listeners know the context. Do not use it to describe an energetic person; for that, say dynamic or a dynamo.

distinctions.note: A dynamicist studies physical forces and motion, while a dynamist holds a philosophical view that force or activity is basic to reality.
Dynamic as an adjective describes energy or change in general, whereas dynamist names a person committed to a specific doctrine.

examples.professional: In the strategy meeting, Dana described herself as a dynamist, meaning she believes the company should focus on change rather than fixed structures.
examples.analytical: Leibniz's rejection of pure extension made him a dynamist, since he took force rather than matter alone to be the basis of bodies.

nuance.analogy: A dynamist sees the world as a river rather than a set of stones, so what matters most is the flow of force rather than the fixed pieces.
nuance.etymology: From dynamism, from Greek dynamis 'power', with the suffix -ist denoting an adherent.
common_mistakes: Confusing dynamist with dynamicist, the scientist who studies motion; the two words refer to very different kinds of people.
Using dynamist to mean an energetic person; in English, say dynamic or dynamo.

senses.definition: A ruler or governor, especially a hereditary ruler or someone who founded or is part of a dynasty.
senses.example: The dynast ruled the valley for forty years, passing his title to his eldest son.

core.definition: A ruler, especially a hereditary one, who belongs to a family that holds power across several generations.

pronunciation.tip: Stress DY. The vowel in the second syllable is a short 'a' as in cat, not 'ah' or 'ay'. Don't add a final vowel sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral, though it can suggest concentrated and inherited power.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this word in history, political writing, and literature about royal or ruling families. In everyday speech they would say ruler, monarch, or a member of the royal family. Dynast sounds bookish in conversation and is most natural in an essay or a history discussion.

distinctions.note: A monarch is any sovereign ruler, while a dynast emphasizes membership in a ruling family line that passes power by inheritance.
A dictator seizes or holds power by force, whereas a dynast holds power through family inheritance.
King is the everyday word; dynast is broader and can refer to any ruler from a hereditary line, or to a founder of one.

examples.everyday: Some of the old families in that small town act like dynasts, passing the mayor's seat from father to son.
examples.professional: The report on the family-owned company described its chairman as a dynast who had controlled the board for three generations.
examples.analytical: Machiavelli distinguishes the hereditary dynast, whose authority is accepted by custom, from the new prince, who must win power and keep it by his own effort.

nuance.analogy: A dynast is like the heir to a family house: the title passes down through the bloodline rather than through a vote.
nuance.etymology: From Greek dynastes 'lord, ruler', from dynasthai 'to be able'.
common_mistakes: Confusing dynast, a person who rules, with dynasty, a family line of rulers or the period of their rule.
Using dynast as a casual word for a rich family; the word refers to rule and power rather than wealth.

dynast.etymology: From Late Latin *dynastēs*, from Ancient Greek *δυνάστης* (“lord, ruler”), from *δύναμαι* (“to be powerful”).

senses.definition: Of, pertaining to, or being a dysphemism.
senses.example: Calling the new policy a money grab was a dysphemistic label that angered the city council.

core.definition: Using a harsh, insulting, or deliberately offensive word or phrase in place of a neutral one.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the MIS syllable, as in dysphemism. The unstressed syllables are weak schwa sounds, and dys- is pronounced like 'dis'.

nuance.connotation: Negative, since it describes harsh or insulting language.
nuance.usage_note: Linguists, rhetoricians, and writers about language use this word. Ordinary Americans would say an insulting term or a harsh word. It is the opposite of euphemistic, which describes a softer word. Use it to describe a word or phrase, not a rude person.

distinctions.note: Euphemistic describes a soft or polite word used to avoid a harsh one, while dysphemistic describes using the harsh word itself.
Blunt describes direct speech without tact, while dysphemistic describes the specific harsh word choice.
Slang is informal vocabulary used by a group, and a slang word may or may not be dysphemistic.

examples.everyday: My dad calls the gym the torture chamber, which is pretty dysphemistic, but he goes every single morning.
examples.professional: Let's avoid dysphemistic labels for the legacy system in the documentation and describe it neutrally.
examples.analytical: Scholars of political rhetoric note that dysphemistic labels can make an opponent seem hostile before the argument even begins.

nuance.analogy: A dysphemism is like a sharp elbow in a crowded room: it gets attention and hurts, while a euphemism is a polite hand on the shoulder.
nuance.etymology: Formed on the model of euphemism, from Greek dys- 'bad, ill' and phēmē 'speech'.
common_mistakes: Confusing dysphemistic with euphemistic; the first means harsh, the second means polite.
Using dysphemistic for any rude word; it describes a harsh substitute for a neutral term.

senses.definition: Commercial activity conducted via the Internet.
senses.example: Our small bakery grew fast after we launched e-commerce on our website.

core.definition: Buying and selling goods or services over the Internet, or the business sector that does this.

pronunciation.tip: The first 'e' is the letter name 'ee'. The stress is on 'com', the second syllable, and the 'merce' ending is a reduced, r-colored vowel, not 'mace'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral: it names a business sector or practice without judging it.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use e-commerce in business, news and tech writing for online retail and related services. In everyday talk people say 'shopping online' or 'buying on Amazon'. The spelling ecommerce without a hyphen is also common in American writing.

distinctions.note: Online shopping describes what a consumer does. E-commerce describes the business activity and industry as a whole.
M-commerce means buying through mobile devices and apps. E-commerce is the broader term that includes computers and phones.

examples.everyday: My sister runs a small e-commerce shop selling handmade candles.
examples.professional: Our e-commerce team needs the checkout data to fix the abandoned-cart problem before the holiday season.
examples.analytical: E-commerce has reshaped retail by lowering entry barriers, though it also concentrates market power in a few platforms.

nuance.analogy: E-commerce is like a shopping mall that never closes and has no physical doors.
nuance.etymology: From electronic (abbreviated e-) plus commerce, from Latin commercium 'trade'.
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable as 'EE-kom-merce'.
Pronouncing the 'e' as 'eh' instead of the letter name 'ee'.
Using e-commerce for a single website when it means the broader business activity.

senses.definition: Intense pleasure.
A state of emotion so intense that a person is carried beyond rational thought and self-control.
senses.example: an ecstasy of remorse

senses.definition: A trance, frenzy, or rapture associated with mystic or prophetic exaltation.
senses.example: The mystic fell into ecstasy, speaking words the congregation could not follow.

senses.definition: The drug MDMA, a synthetic entactogen of the methylenedioxyphenethylamine family, especially in a tablet form.
senses.example: Police seized several packets of ecstasy at the nightclub entrance last Saturday.

senses.definition: (dated) A state in which sensibility, voluntary motion, and (largely) mental power are suspended, and the body is erect and inflexible.
senses.example: The physician described the patient's ecstasy as a rigid trance, body stiff and unmoving.
senses.label: dated

senses.definition: To experience intense pleasure.
senses.example: Fans would ecstasy over every new album release, screaming and dancing in the aisles.

senses.definition: To cause intense pleasure in.
senses.example: The sweet melody ecstasied the audience, drawing cheers from every row.

core.definition: Intense, overwhelming joy or pleasure; a feeling of being carried away by emotion.

pronunciation.tip: Stress is on the first syllable. The "-sy" ending sounds like "see", and the middle vowel is a weak schwa.

nuance.connotation: Positive when describing joy or spiritual rapture. In American English it can also refer to the drug MDMA, so context matters.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use ecstasy for very strong happiness, usually in writing or in dramatic speech, as in "pure ecstasy" or "in ecstasy." In everyday talk, "ecstatic" is more common. In contemporary American speech, "ecstasy" often refers to the club drug, so avoid it in casual joking unless you mean that.

distinctions.note: Happiness is a general, calm state of contentment; ecstasy is an intense, overwhelming peak of joy.
Joy is deep gladness; ecstasy suggests a stronger feeling that takes you out of ordinary awareness.

examples.everyday: She danced with pure ecstasy when she heard the band play her favorite song.
examples.professional: The team was in ecstasy when the model finally passed every test in the release.
examples.analytical: Mystics have long described ecstasy as a movement of the soul beyond ordinary thought.

nuance.analogy: Ecstasy is like a wave that lifts you off your feet, sweeping you past your usual awareness.
nuance.etymology: From Greek ekstasis, "standing outside oneself", from ek- "out" and histanai "to stand".
common_mistakes: Using "ecstasy" in casual talk where a listener may think of the drug; "ecstatic" is safer.
Saying "I am ecstasy" instead of "I am ecstatic".
nuance.biblical_note: In the New Testament the Greek word ekstasis, meaning a state of being outside one's normal mind, appears in Acts 10:10 and Acts 11:5, where Peter falls into a trance and sees a vision. In Mark 5:42 the same Greek root describes the amazement of the onlookers when a girl is restored to life. The Septuagint also uses ekstasis for the deep sleep that fell on Adam in Genesis 2:21.

ecstasy.etymology: From Old French *estaise* (“ecstasy, rapture”), from Latin *ecstasis*, from Ancient Greek *ἔκστασις*, from *ἐξίστημι* (“to displace”), from *ἐκ* (“out”) and *ἵστημι* (“to stand”).

senses.definition: The boundary line of a surface.
senses.example: The knife's edge was so smooth that it sliced through the paper.

senses.definition: A one-dimensional face of a polytope. In particular, the joining line between two vertices of a polygon; the place where two faces of a polyhedron meet.
senses.example: Each edge of the cube connects two vertices and joins two adjacent faces.

senses.definition: An advantage.
senses.example: I have the edge on him.

senses.definition: The thin cutting side of the blade of an instrument, such as an ax, knife, sword, or scythe; that which cuts as an edge does, or wounds deeply, etc.
senses.example: Speaking with a metallic edge to her voice.

senses.definition: A sharp terminating border; a margin; a brink; an extreme verge.
senses.example: The cup is right on the edge of the table.

senses.definition: Sharpness; readiness or fitness to cut; keenness; intenseness of desire.
senses.example: After the timeout there was a new edge to the team's play.

senses.definition: The border or part adjacent to the line of division; the beginning or early part (of a period of time)
senses.example: in the edge of evening

senses.definition: A connected pair of vertices in a graph.
senses.example: In this network graph, every edge links two nodes with a weighted cost.

senses.definition: A level of sexual arousal that is maintained just short of reaching the point of inevitability, or climax.
senses.example: They lingered at the edge together, savoring the tension before neither could hold back.

senses.definition: The point of data production in an organization (the focus of edge computing), as opposed to the cloud.
senses.example: Our sensors process video at the edge before sending summaries to the cloud.

senses.definition: A position or curved gliding movement favoring either the inside or outside edge of the blade against the ice surface, or the visible trace left on the ice when gliding on an edge.
senses.example: To jump a flip, the skater takes off from their backward inside edge and lands on a backward outside edge.

senses.definition: A shot where the ball comes off the edge of the bat, often unintentionally.
senses.example: The pitch was outside, and he got an edge that sailed over the slips.

senses.definition: To move an object slowly and carefully in a particular direction.
senses.example: He edged the book across the table.

senses.definition: To move slowly and carefully in a particular direction.
senses.example: He edged away from her.

senses.definition: To win by a small margin.
senses.example: The home team edged the visitors 3-2 in extra innings.

senses.definition: To trim the margin of a lawn where the grass meets the sidewalk, usually with an electric or gas-powered lawn edger.
senses.example: Before the party, Dad spent an hour edging the lawn along the sidewalk.

senses.definition: To furnish with an edge; to construct an edging.
senses.example: She edged the flower beds with river stones to keep the mulch in.

senses.definition: To furnish with an edge, as a tool or weapon; to sharpen.
senses.example: He edged the old scythe on a whetstone before cutting the hay.

senses.definition: To form a border to; to enclose, to border.
senses.example: Tall pines edged the gravel road as it wound toward the lake.

senses.definition: To make sharp or keen; to incite; to exasperate; to goad; to urge or egg on.
senses.example: His constant teasing edged his brother toward a furious fight.

senses.definition: To intentionally stay or keep someone extremely close to the point of orgasm for a long period of time.
senses.example: Jimmy has been edging for 6 hours straight; is his dick okay?

senses.definition: To agitate or exasperate (someone) due to constant delays of something.
senses.example: When are the developers going to release the update? They've been edging us for months with all of these trailers.

senses.definition: To hit the ball with an edge of the bat, causing a fine deflection.
senses.example: He edged the fastball into the backstop, barely grazing the bat.

core.definition: The outer limit or border of something, such as the side of a table, the cliff at the edge of a canyon, or the cutting side of a blade.

pronunciation.tip: It is one syllable with a short 'e' vowel and a soft 'j' ending. Do not add a vowel at the end, as in 'ej-uh'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a basic physical word, though 'on edge' carries a negative sense of anxiety.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use edge constantly for physical borders and in phrases like 'on the edge of town'. In competition, 'an edge' means an advantage, and in mood, 'on edge' means nervous. The meaning is clear from context, so listen for the phrase around it.

distinctions.note: Border usually means a dividing line between regions or countries; edge is the outermost part of an object or surface.
Rim is the edge of something round, like a cup or wheel; edge is more general.
Verge is the point just before something happens, as in 'on the verge of tears'; edge is the physical border.

examples.everyday: Don't set your coffee right on the edge of the counter; it might fall off.
examples.professional: Can you check whether the edge labels on the chart are cut off in the slide?
examples.analytical: The edge of a concept is where its meaning becomes unclear and contested, which is why definitions matter.

nuance.analogy: The edge is like a coastline, the line where solid land meets the sea.
nuance.etymology: From Old English ecg, meaning the cutting edge of a blade or sword.
common_mistakes: Confusing the physical sense (border) with the competitive sense (advantage); both are common in American English.
Saying 'on edge' for a physical border; 'on the edge of' is the correct form for location.

edge.etymology: From Middle English *egge*, from Old English *eċġ*, from **aggju*, from Proto-Germanic **agjō*, from Proto-Indo-European **h₂eḱ-* (“sharp”).

senses.definition: Having attained a level of higher education, such as a college degree.
Based on relevant information.
senses.example: an educated guess

senses.definition: Knowledgeable.
senses.example: She cast an educated eye over the antiques.

core.definition: Having completed formal education, such as a college degree, or being well informed and knowledgeable in a subject.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the first syllable. The final '-ed' is pronounced 'id' in this adjective, and the middle vowel is weak, so there is no separate 'yoo' sound.

nuance.connotation: Positive in most contexts, because it suggests knowledge and training. It can sound snobbish when it implies that less-schooled people lack good judgment.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use educated to describe someone with a college degree or serious schooling, and also to describe decisions based on good information, as in 'educated voters.' Be careful, because some people hear it as a class marker when it contrasts with 'uneducated'. In friendly conversation, 'well-read' or 'knowledgeable' may sound warmer.

distinctions.note: Learned sounds scholarly or literary and suggests deep study, while educated is the everyday word for having had schooling or being well informed.
Literate means able to read and write, which is a narrower skill than being educated in a broad sense.
Well-read means someone has read widely, which is only one part of being educated.

examples.everyday: My grandmother was a highly educated woman who read everything she could find.
examples.professional: We want educated decisions based on the data rather than guesses.
examples.analytical: A genuinely educated person knows the limits of what they know and can say so plainly.

nuance.analogy: Being educated is like having a well-stocked toolbox: you have tools, and you know which one fits which job.
nuance.etymology: Past participle adjective from educate, from Latin educare, 'to bring up, rear'.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it with an extra syllable like 'ed-yoo-KAY-ted'; the stress is on the first syllable.
Using 'educated' as a compliment for everyone with a degree when you mean the person is knowledgeable; a degree does not guarantee knowledge.

core.definition: In the Bible, the eldest son of Jesse and older brother of David, who scorned David when he came to the battle with Goliath.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, EL. The middle syllable is a short 'ee' and the final syllable rhymes with 'cab'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral as a name; in Bible study it often suggests jealousy or pride.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say EL-ee-ab, with the final syllable like 'cab'. It is used mostly in Bible study, sermons and religious writing, and is also a rare given name in the United States.

distinctions.note: Eli is the priest at Shiloh who raised Samuel. Eliab is David's older brother, a soldier in Saul's army.
Eliakim was a royal steward under King Hezekiah. Eliab is David's brother from the time of Saul.

examples.everyday: In Sunday school we talked about how David's brother Eliab got angry at him for coming to the battle.
examples.professional: When teaching the story of David, I point out that Eliab's reaction shows how easily people misjudge a younger sibling's calling.
examples.analytical: Eliab's rebuke in 1 Samuel 17 reveals a tension between family expectations and God's choice of David as king.

nuance.analogy: Like an older sibling who assumes the family's future belongs to him, only to be surprised when the younger one is chosen.
nuance.etymology: From Hebrew ʾĕlîʾāb, meaning God is father, from ʾēl, God, and ʾāb, father.
common_mistakes: Confusing Eliab with Eli, the priest, because the names sound alike.
Stressing the last syllable instead of the first.
nuance.biblical_note: Hebrew ʾĕlîʾāb, 'God is father'. In 1 Samuel 16:6–7 Samuel looks at Eliab and assumes he is the chosen king, but God tells him that people look at outward appearance while God looks at the heart. In 1 Samuel 17:28 Eliab angrily rebukes David for coming to the battlefield and accuses him of pride. In 1 Chronicles 2:13 Eliab appears in the genealogy as one of Jesse's sons.

senses.definition: Of or pertaining to an ellipse.
Of or pertaining to a broad field of mathematics that originates from the problem of calculating arc lengths of an ellipse.
senses.example: elliptic integral

senses.definition: That has coefficients satisfying a condition analogous to the condition for the general equation for a conic section to be of an ellipse.
senses.example: elliptic partial differential equation

senses.definition: Of, or showing ellipsis; having a word or words omitted; elliptical.
Oval, with a short or no point.
An elliptical function, equation, path, etc.

core.definition: Relating to an ellipse, or in mathematics, a branch of study involving curves and functions defined by elliptic integrals.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the second syllable, LIP. The final syllable is short -tik, not -teek. Do not pronounce the t as a flap, because it is a clear t here.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a precise technical term in mathematics and physics.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use elliptic almost only in mathematics and science classrooms or research. In most cases, elliptical is the more common everyday adjective, as in elliptical trainer or elliptical orbit. Elliptic is often used in phrases like elliptic curve or elliptic function.

distinctions.note: Elliptic is preferred in technical names such as elliptic curve. Elliptical is used more in everyday and general descriptions, like an elliptical orbit or gym machine.

examples.everyday: My cryptography class spends a week on elliptic curves, which is harder than I expected.
examples.professional: Our security team uses elliptic curve cryptography for the new key exchange because it offers strong protection with smaller keys.
examples.analytical: The elliptic integrals studied by Legendre and Jacobi provided the foundation for a broad theory of elliptic functions.

nuance.analogy: An elliptic curve is like a stretched circle with a special rule for points, which turns out to be very useful for secure codes.
nuance.etymology: From Greek elleipsis, a falling short or omission, via the ellipse.
common_mistakes: Using elliptic and elliptical interchangeably in all contexts, even when elliptic curve is the fixed term.
Stressing the first syllable as EL-ip-tik.

elliptic.etymology: From Ancient Greek *ἐλλειπτικός*, from *ἐλλείπω* (“I leave out, omit”).

senses.definition: To clasp (someone or each other) in the arms with affection; to take in the arms; to hug.
senses.example: After three years apart, the sisters finally embraced at the airport gate.

senses.definition: To seize (something) eagerly or with alacrity; to accept or take up with cordiality; to welcome.
senses.example: I wholeheartedly embrace the new legislation.

senses.definition: To submit to; to undergo.
senses.example: The soldiers embraced hardship and danger for months on the frozen front.

senses.definition: To encircle; to enclose, to encompass.
senses.example: Tall oak trees embraced the small cabin, shading it from the summer sun.

senses.definition: To enfold, to include (ideas, principles, etc.); to encompass.
senses.example: Natural philosophy embraces many sciences.

senses.definition: An act of putting arms around someone and bringing the person close to the chest; a hug.
senses.example: She gave her nephew a warm embrace before he boarded the bus.

senses.definition: An enclosure partially or fully surrounding someone or something.
senses.example: The valley's embrace of steep green hills made the village feel sheltered.

senses.definition: Full acceptance (of something).
senses.example: The company's full embrace of remote work changed how every department operated.

senses.definition: An act of enfolding or including.
senses.example: The new policy's embrace of part-time staff extended health benefits to more workers.

core.definition: To hold someone closely in your arms, usually as a greeting or sign of affection; also to accept something eagerly.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the second syllable, 'brace,' which rhymes with 'place.' The 'r' is clearly pronounced in American English, and the final 's' is a soft 's' sound, not a 'z.'

nuance.connotation: Positive and warm. It suggests affection, acceptance, or welcome, though 'embrace' a difficult idea can sound more formal.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say 'hug' for everyday affectionate contact and 'embrace' for a more formal, emotional, or literary hug. 'Embrace' also means to welcome an idea or change, as in 'embrace diversity,' which is common in business and public speech. Saying 'Let's embrace it' is a common, energetic way to accept a challenge at work.

distinctions.note: 'Hug' is the everyday word for putting arms around someone; 'embrace' is more formal, emotional, or literary.
'Accept' is neutral; 'embrace' adds enthusiasm and a sense of welcoming something you care about.

examples.everyday: When I saw my brother at the airport, we just embraced for a long minute without saying anything.
examples.professional: Our team needs to embrace the new reporting tool instead of sticking with the spreadsheets.
examples.analytical: The parable of the prodigal son shows a father who runs to embrace his returning child before any confession is spoken.

nuance.analogy: To embrace is like wrapping your arms around an idea or a person, holding it close and making it part of you.
nuance.etymology: From Old French 'embracier,' from 'em-' plus 'brace,' meaning arms, from Latin 'brachium.'
common_mistakes: Using 'embrace' for a quick, casual hug; 'hug' is more natural in everyday American talk.
Pronouncing the final 's' as 'z' (em-BRAYZ); the correct sound is a soft 's.'
nuance.biblical_note: In the Bible, embracing expresses reunion, greeting, or affection. The Hebrew word 'chabaq' (to embrace) appears in narratives of reconciliation, and the Greek 'aspazomai' (to greet, embrace) is used for welcome in the New Testament.

embrace.etymology: The verb is derived from Middle English *embracen* (“to clasp in one's arms, embrace; to reach out eagerly for, welcome; to enfold, entwine; to ensnare, entangle; to twist, wrap around; to gird, put on; to lace; to be in or put into bonds; to put a shield…

senses.definition: Decorated with embroidery; covered in decorative needlework.
Embellished; elaborate, especially when containing superfluous or fictitious details.
senses.example: His story about the fishing trip was so embroidered that nobody believed the ending.

core.definition: Decorated with embroidery, meaning stitched designs on fabric; also describing a story with added, exaggerated details.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the second syllable, BROY, and the final -ered is one reduced syllable sounding like 'erd', not 'ared'. The r in 'embr' is pronounced clearly.

nuance.connotation: Neutral when describing fabric or clothing; slightly negative when describing a story, meaning exaggerated or made up.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use embroidered for a shirt, pillow, or tablecloth with stitched designs, often with a monogram or logo. For stories, it suggests someone added details to make an account more interesting, often in a mildly critical way, as in 'His embroidered tale of the fishing trip grew larger each time.'

distinctions.note: Decorated is a broad word for anything made more attractive; embroidered specifically means decorated with needlework.
Exaggerated describes overstating facts in general, while embroidered in the figurative sense stresses added invented details.

examples.everyday: My grandmother gave me a pillow with embroidered flowers on it.
examples.professional: The uniform shop can add an embroidered company logo to every polo shirt.
examples.analytical: The memoir is embroidered with invented scenes that undermine its claim to historical accuracy.

nuance.analogy: Like a plain cloth with thread stitched on top, an embroidered account is a simple story with extra decoration added.
nuance.etymology: From embroider, from Middle French embroder, to ornament with needlework.
common_mistakes: Saying 'embroidered' as if it has two syllables in the middle; the word is three syllables before the ending: im-BROY-derd.
Using embroidered only for stories; in everyday American English it most often describes fabric.

senses.definition: Following or imitating a style popular during the First French Empire (1804–1814).
Having the waistline just below the bust; featuring an empire waist.

core.definition: Describing a dress or top with a high waistline just below the bust, called an empire waist.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, EM. The second part is one syllable ending in an r sound, so it sounds like 'pyer', not 'peer'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive in fashion talk. It describes a style that many people find flattering.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use empire mostly in shopping and fashion, as in 'an empire-waist dress'. It also refers to the early nineteenth-century style inspired by the First French Empire, which is more of a history or fashion-history term. When shopping, you can say 'Do you have this in an empire waist?' and a salesperson will understand.
