distinctions.note: An A-line dress is fitted at the top and flares out from the waist, while an empire waist is fitted just under the bust and falls loosely from there.
A drop waist sits at the hip, while an empire waist sits just below the bust.
A sheath is a close-fitting dress that follows the body, while an empire dress has a loose skirt below the high waistline.

examples.everyday: I bought an empire-waist dress for my cousin's summer wedding, and it fits really well.
examples.professional: The buyer wants the spring line to include two empire-waist dresses, since they sold well last season.
examples.analytical: The fashion for empire-waisted gowns in the early nineteenth century reflected the classical tastes of the period.

nuance.analogy: Like a belt set high under the chest, so the fabric falls straight down from there.
nuance.etymology: From empire, from Latin imperium, 'command' or 'rule'.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it as EM-peer, which sounds like a different word.
Confusing empire with imperial, which is the adjective used for the empire itself.

senses.definition: A person, firm or other entity which pays for or hires the services of another person.
senses.example: My employer offers health insurance and a retirement match for all full-time staff.

core.definition: A person, company or organization that hires people and pays them for their work.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the PLOY syllable. The final -er is a quick, r-colored schwa, not a full 'ur' vowel, and the ending is not 'ee'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; the word names the party that hires. Tone depends on context: 'good employer' is praise, while 'abusive employer' is negative.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use employer in HR, job applications and benefits talk. In everyday speech people say 'the company' or 'the firm'. On resumes you list your employer and your job title. 'Boss' is more informal and refers to a person rather than the organization.

distinctions.note: Boss is informal and refers to the person who supervises you; employer is the formal party that hires and pays you, which may be a company.
Company is everyday speech; employer is preferred in legal, HR and benefits language.

examples.everyday: My employer pays for half of my gym membership, which is nice.
examples.professional: Your employer will need your Social Security number to set up payroll.
examples.analytical: The moral obligations of an employer extend beyond the wage contract to the safety and dignity of the workforce.

nuance.analogy: An employer is like the owner of a restaurant who hires the cooks: the cooks do the work, but the owner sets the schedule and signs the checks.
nuance.etymology: From employ plus -er, 'one who employs'.
common_mistakes: Swapping employer and employee, which reverses the meaning; the employer hires and pays.
Using 'employer' for your direct manager; in American English your manager is your boss, while the employer is the company.

senses.definition: A technique in poetry whereby a sentence is carried over to the next line without pause.

core.definition: In poetry, the continuation of a sentence or phrase from one line to the next without a pause at the end of the line.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on JAM, the second syllable, and the final syllable is a reduced 'ment'. Pronounce the 'j' as in 'judge' and don't stress the first syllable.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; a neutral technical term from literary criticism.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use enjambment in poetry classes, literary criticism and discussions of poems. It is not used in everyday conversation, so you would only hear it in classrooms, reviews or literary discussion. A common reply in a class might be 'Yes, the enjambment creates tension because the reader has to keep going.'

distinctions.note: A caesura is a pause within a line, while enjambment is the lack of a pause at the end of a line.
An end-stop is a line that finishes with punctuation or a natural pause, the opposite of enjambment.

examples.everyday: My sister is taking a poetry class and keeps talking about enjambment, so I asked her to explain it.
examples.professional: For the grant report, we discussed how the poet's enjambment mirrors the sense of uncertainty in the text.
examples.analytical: Milton's enjambment in Paradise Lost forces the reader to carry the sentence across the line, enacting the movement of the argument itself.

nuance.analogy: Enjambment is like a conversation that keeps going without a breath, so the listener is pulled into the next line.
nuance.etymology: From French enjamber ('to stride over'), from en- and jambe ('leg').
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable, as in EN-jam-ment.
Pronouncing the 'j' as 'y' or using a hard 'g' sound.

senses.definition: Of or relating to a system of ceremonial magic involving the evocation and commanding of various spirits, and based on the 16th-century writings of Dr. John Dee and Edward Kelley.
senses.example: The occult bookseller stocked rare manuscripts on Enochian magic and John Dee's angelic conversations.

core.definition: Relating to the system of ceremonial magic and angelic language developed in the 1580s by John Dee and Edward Kelley.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the second syllable, NOH. The final -ian is weak, close to 'un', and learners often stress the first syllable or pronounce it like the name Enoch, which starts with EE.

nuance.connotation: Neutral: a precise historical and occult term, with no positive or negative charge in itself.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this word mainly in scholarly discussions of Renaissance history, the history of religion and science, and esoteric or occult studies. In everyday conversation you will almost never need it. Say 'Enochian magic' or 'the Enochian language' rather than using it alone, and do not confuse it with Enoch, the biblical patriarch.

distinctions.note: Enochian magic rests on the visionary revelations recorded by Dee and Kelley, while Kabbalah refers to a Jewish mystical tradition built on older texts such as the Zohar.
Hermetic refers to a broad occult tradition traced to the texts attributed to Hermes Trismegistus, whereas Enochian is one specific system within that wider world.

examples.everyday: My roommate collects old books, and she has a facsimile of an Enochian manuscript on her shelf.
examples.professional: Our historian of science is writing a chapter on Enochian manuscripts in Elizabethan England.
examples.analytical: The Enochian system presents a revealed language whose claims to angelic authority Dee never fully resolved.

nuance.analogy: Like a secret code its makers claimed had been dictated from heaven.
nuance.etymology: Named after the biblical patriarch Enoch, whom Dee associated with the revealed angelic language.
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable (EE-no-kee-un) instead of the second (ih-NOH-kee-un).
Confusing Enochian with Enoch, the biblical figure, and pronouncing it with a stressed EE at the start.
nuance.biblical_note: The word itself is not biblical, but it takes its name from Enoch, a figure in Genesis 5:18-24, where Enoch walked with God and was taken by him. Hebrews 11:5 says Enoch was taken up by faith so that he should not see death, and Jude 14 describes him as a prophet. Enoch's Hebrew name is Hanokh, and the Enochian system borrowed his name for its claimed revelations.

enochian.etymology: From *Enoch* + *ian*, with reference to the Book of Enoch in the Bible.

senses.definition: A logical fallacy resulting from the use of multiple meanings of a single expression.
senses.example: The argument fails through equivocation, since bank means a riverside in one premise and a lender in the other.

senses.definition: The use of expressions susceptible of a double signification, possibly intentionally and with the aim of misleading.
senses.example: The senator's equivocation about the scandal frustrated reporters who wanted a straight yes or no.

core.definition: Deliberately vague or misleading wording, or a logical fallacy where one word has two different meanings in an argument.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on KAY, the fourth syllable. The -tion ending is a 'shun' sound, not 'tee-on.'

nuance.connotation: Negative. It suggests dishonest evasion or a flaw in reasoning.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'equivocation' in political commentary, legal discussion, and philosophy. In logic classes, it names a specific fallacy. In everyday talk people more often say 'dodging' or 'spin.' Calling someone's answer 'an equivocation' is direct and can sound confrontational.

distinctions.note: 'Ambiguity' is a neutral property of language; 'equivocation' describes deliberate or fallacious use of multiple meanings.
'Evasion' is broader and covers any avoidance; 'equivocation' specifically involves wording that is technically true but misleading.

examples.everyday: Her answer about the budget was pure equivocation, so I still don't know if the project is funded.
examples.professional: The memo's claim about 'user data' is an equivocation, since the team used it to mean both raw logs and anonymized records.
examples.analytical: The argument fails because of an equivocation on the word 'cause,' which shifts from physical causation to explanatory reasons.

nuance.analogy: Like a magician using the same card name for two different cards, misleading the audience without technically lying.
nuance.etymology: From Medieval Latin aequivocatio, from aequivocare 'to call by the same name.'
common_mistakes: Using 'equivocation' as a synonym for 'equivalence' or 'equality.'
Confusing the noun with the verb 'equivocate' in sentences.

senses.definition: The state of being a hermit; seclusion from society.

core.definition: The way of life or condition of living as a hermit, withdrawn from ordinary society.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable. The ending '-ism' is pronounced 'iz-um' with a reduced final vowel. Keep the middle vowels short and quick.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it names a religious or philosophical practice without judgment.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this word in historical, religious, or scholarly contexts. In ordinary talk, people say 'living as a hermit' or 'living alone in seclusion'. It is not used for simple loneliness.

distinctions.note: 'Asceticism' is broader and refers to strict self-discipline and denial of comforts, while 'eremitism' specifically refers to living alone.
'Monasticism' refers to community religious life, while 'eremitism' refers to solitary life.

examples.everyday: My aunt talks about eremitism like it is a dream, but she only wants a quiet weekend away from her kids.
examples.professional: Our church history course spends two weeks on the rise of eremitism in the fourth century.
examples.analytical: Eremitism raised a theological question: can a person find holiness by withdrawing from the community that the gospel commands them to serve?

nuance.analogy: Eremitism is like taking a long walk alone to think, but pushed to a whole life.
nuance.etymology: From eremite, from Greek erēmos, 'desert, solitary', with the suffix '-ism'.
common_mistakes: Using it as a synonym for loneliness; it describes a chosen way of life.
Stressing the last syllable.

senses.definition: In the habit of making errors.
senses.example: Manual data entry is error-prone, so we automated most of the spreadsheet work.

senses.definition: Tending to cause errors.

core.definition: Likely to make mistakes, or likely to cause them; tending toward errors.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the second part, prone, which rhymes with own, not with pron as in pronunciation. Keep error weaker with a reduced second syllable.

nuance.connotation: Negative but neutral in tone. It describes a tendency or condition, and it is less personal than careless.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use error-prone for people, tasks, processes, and systems, such as error-prone manual data entry or an error-prone recipe. It describes conditions and tendencies rather than blaming someone, so it sounds more professional than calling a person careless. At work you might say that a process is error-prone to suggest a change.

distinctions.note: Careless blames a person's attitude or attention, while error-prone describes a process, task, or system that tends to produce mistakes.
Prone to is the phrase used with a following noun or gerund, as in prone to errors, while error-prone is a single compound adjective placed before a noun.

examples.everyday: I'm error-prone with numbers, so I always double-check the tip before I sign.
examples.professional: Manual data entry is error-prone, so we automated the intake form to reduce typing mistakes.
examples.analytical: Human judgment is error-prone under time pressure, which is why checklists and peer review exist in medicine and engineering.

nuance.analogy: Working in an error-prone process is like walking a tightrope on a windy day: each step carries some chance of a wobble.
nuance.etymology: Error comes from Latin errare, to wander; prone comes from Latin pronus, leaning forward or inclined.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing prone to rhyme with pron; the vowel is long, as in own.
Saying I am error prone with no hyphen before a noun; use the hyphen when the compound comes before a noun.
Using error-prone with a direct object; the usual pattern is error-prone process or prone to errors.

senses.definition: A system of doctrines concerning final matters, such as death.
senses.example: Her seminar on eschatology covered how different traditions understand death and the final destiny of the soul.

senses.definition: The study of the end times—the end of the world, notably in Christian and Islamic theology, the second coming of Christ, the Apocalypse, or the Last Judgment.
senses.example: Our pastor's sermon on eschatology focused on the second coming and the final judgment.

core.definition: The branch of theology that studies the last things: death, judgment, the end of the age, and the final destiny of humanity and the world.

pronunciation.tip: Primary stress falls on 'TAH', the third syllable. The 'ch' is a /k/ sound, not 'ch'. Many Americans pronounce the stressed vowel as 'ah' due to the cot-caught merger, and the last part is 'luh-jee'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and scholarly. It describes a field of study, though end-times topics can carry strong emotion in popular religion.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'eschatology' mainly in seminaries, theology classes, and religious studies. In popular American Christianity, the same topic appears as 'end times' or 'prophecy'. Theologians distinguish 'realized eschatology' (the end already begun) from 'future eschatology'. The word is also used loosely for any view of ultimate destiny.

distinctions.note: Apocalyptic is a literary and theological style with visions of cosmic upheaval; eschatology is the broader doctrine of last things.
Soteriology is the doctrine of salvation; eschatology is the doctrine of final events and destiny.
End times is the popular term for the future period before the end, while eschatology is the academic study.

examples.everyday: I'm taking a class on eschatology, which is basically what the Bible says about the end of all things.
examples.professional: This semester's seminar will survey major views of eschatology, from premillennialism to amillennialism.
examples.analytical: Jesus's teaching is often read through the lens of inaugurated eschatology, in which the age to come has already broken into the present without yet being fully realized.

nuance.analogy: Like reading the last chapter of a story to understand what the whole plot has been heading toward.
nuance.etymology: From Greek eschatos, 'last,' plus -logia, 'study of'; coined in the 19th century.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the 'ch' as in 'church' instead of /k/.
Stressing the first syllable: ES-kuh-tol-uh-jee.
Confusing it with 'scatology', which is a different word entirely.
nuance.biblical_note: The word comes from Greek eschatos ('last') and refers to biblical teaching about the last days. Daniel 12:2 speaks of many who sleep in the dust awakening to everlasting life or contempt. 1 Corinthians 15:51-57 describes the resurrection of the dead and the final victory over death. Revelation 21:1-4 envisions a new heaven and a new earth where God dwells with his people.

traditions.view: Orthodoxy affirms Christ's second coming, the resurrection of the dead, and the Last Judgment, with the Church already participating in the age to come through the liturgy. It generally avoids detailed timelines and does not teach purgatory.

Catholic teaching includes particular judgment at death, heaven, hell, and purgatory, followed by Christ's return, the general resurrection, and the Last Judgment. Detailed predictions of dates are discouraged.

Protestants affirm Christ's return, resurrection, and judgment but differ on details: premillennialists, amillennialists, and postmillennialists disagree on the millennium, and dispensationalists teach a rapture. Most reject purgatory.

senses.definition: Synonym of due date (“the date on which a pregnant female is expected to give birth”).
senses.example: Her estimated date of delivery is March 14, so she's planning to work until early March.

core.definition: The date a doctor predicts a pregnancy will end in birth, usually called the due date in everyday American speech.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on 'LIV' in 'delivery', while 'estimated' and 'date' are lighter. The word 'of' reduces to 'uv', and the -ed in 'estimated' sounds like 'tuhd'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and clinical. It is used on medical forms and by doctors, but friends say 'due date' in conversation.
nuance.usage_note: Americans normally say 'due date' when talking with friends, as in 'When's your due date?' The longer phrase appears on medical forms, ultrasound reports and insurance paperwork. Everyone understands that it is a prediction, and most babies arrive within a couple of weeks before or after it. A natural reply to a question about it is simply the month, such as 'Early March'.

distinctions.note: Due date is the everyday phrase for the same concept; the longer form is more formal and appears on medical documents.
In American business, a delivery date is when goods or packages arrive; in pregnancy talk it refers only to a baby's expected birth.
Expected date is a loose phrase that could refer to anything; estimated date of delivery is a specific medical estimate.

collocations: calculate the estimated date of delivery
confirm the estimated date of delivery
put the estimated date of delivery on the form
an estimated date of delivery in early May
revise the estimated date of delivery

examples.everyday: Her estimated date of delivery is in June, but she keeps saying the baby will come early.
examples.professional: The hospital's intake form asks for the estimated date of delivery, so please confirm the ultrasound dating.
examples.analytical: The estimated date of delivery is calculated from the last menstrual period or an early ultrasound, and it is a probability rather than a fixed day.

nuance.analogy: The estimated date of delivery is like a weather forecast for a baby: a useful target that few people expect to hit exactly.
nuance.etymology: Built from 'estimated' (from Latin aestimare, 'to value') and 'delivery' (from Old French delivrer, 'to set free').
common_mistakes: Saying 'delivery date' for a baby; in American English that phrase usually means when a package arrives.
Treating the date as exact; Americans know most babies arrive within a few weeks of it.

senses.definition: Of or pertaining to an aetiology.
senses.example: The team identified the etiologic factor behind the rise in cases.

core.definition: Relating to the cause or origin of a disease, condition or phenomenon, especially in medicine.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on LAH, the fourth syllable. The 'ae' or 'oe' spelling is pronounced as a long 'ee', and the ending -ic is 'ik'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a precise medical or scientific term.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'etiologic' in medicine and epidemiology, usually in professional writing. The American spelling drops the 'ae' of 'aetiologic', which is the British form. In everyday talk people say 'the cause' or 'what's causing it'.

distinctions.note: Pathogenic describes the ability to cause disease, while etiologic describes the cause or origin of a disease.
Diagnostic refers to identifying a condition, while etiologic refers to finding its underlying cause.

examples.everyday: The doctor said they still don't know the etiologic cause of my cough.
examples.professional: The epidemiology team is identifying the etiologic agent behind the outbreak.
examples.analytical: The study examines etiologic pathways that link early childhood stress to later depression.

nuance.analogy: Like tracing a river back to its spring: you follow the flow until you find where it began.
nuance.etymology: From Greek aitia (cause) and -logia (study), through medical Latin aetiologia, with the adjective ending -ic.
common_mistakes: Spelling it aetiologic, the British form; the American spelling is etiologic.
Pronouncing the first vowel as 'eh' or 'eth' instead of a long 'ee'.

senses.definition: A supporter of eudaemonism.

core.definition: A person who supports eudaemonism, the ethical view that happiness comes from living virtuously and flourishing as a human being.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on DEE, the second syllable. The final -ist is short, like the i in bit, and the middle syllable -muh- is reduced.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It describes a philosophical position held by a person without judgment.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this noun in philosophy and ethics discussions to describe thinkers who hold this view. The spelling eudaemonist is also common. People in everyday life would say someone who believes in living a good life.

distinctions.note: A hedonist seeks pleasure as the highest good, while a eudaimonist seeks flourishing through virtue.
A utilitarian aims at the greatest happiness for the greatest number, while a eudaimonist focuses on the excellence of a person's character and life.

examples.everyday: My brother calls himself a eudaimonist, which means he thinks a good life matters more than a good time.
examples.professional: Our leadership coach is a eudaimonist, so she asks the team whether their work helps them grow, not just whether they hit targets.
examples.analytical: Aristotle is often read as the classic eudaimonist, though later Stoic and Christian thinkers reshaped the idea of happiness in different ways.

nuance.analogy: A eudaimonist is like a gardener who cares about the health of the whole plant, not just the flowers that bloom this week.
nuance.etymology: From Greek eudaimonia, well-being or happiness, from eu, well, and daimon, spirit or fortune.
common_mistakes: Confusing eudaimonist with hedonist, who holds the opposite view.
Pronouncing the stressed syllable as DYE instead of DEE, as in yoo-DYE-muh-nist.

senses.definition: An instance of euphuism.
senses.example: His sermon was full of euphuism, with balanced clauses and elaborate alliteration throughout.

senses.definition: Misconstruction of euphemism.
senses.example: Her boss laughed at his euphuism, using rightsizing for layoffs when he meant firing.

senses.definition: (historical) An ornate style of writing (in Elizabethan England) marked by the excessive use of alliteration, antithesis and mythological similes.
senses.label: historical

core.definition: An ornate, affected style of English prose from Elizabethan England, marked by heavy alliteration, balanced antithesis and mythological comparisons.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, YOO. The middle -fyoo- is a single syllable, and the ending -ism is a reduced schwa, 'um.'

nuance.connotation: Negative in modern use. It suggests showy, overwrought or insincere writing.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use euphuism mainly in literary history, English classes, and criticism of wordy writing. It is not a casual word. In everyday talk people would just say 'flowery' or 'over-the-top.' Be careful not to confuse it with euphemism.

distinctions.note: A euphemism is a mild word used in place of a harsh one; euphuism is an ornate style of writing.
Purple prose is any excessively ornate writing; euphuism refers to a specific Elizabethan style with set patterns.

examples.everyday: Grandma's letters were full of flowery phrases that my cousin called euphuism.
examples.professional: The editor cut the euphuism from the proposal so the executives could read it quickly.
examples.analytical: Lyly's Euphues exemplifies euphuism, where antithesis and alliteration become the substance of the argument rather than its ornament.

nuance.analogy: Like a garden trimmed into elaborate shapes: impressive to look at, but it hides the natural growth.
nuance.etymology: From Euphues, the name of the witty young man in John Lyly's 1578 novel, from Greek euphyēs 'well-grown, graceful.'
common_mistakes: Confusing it with 'euphemism,' which means a gentle substitute for a harsh word.
Saying 'yoo-FYOO-iz-um' with the stress on the wrong syllable.

euphuism.etymology: From Euphues (Ancient Greek *ευφυής* (“graceful, witty”)) *ism*, after the titular character in John Lyly’s didactic romance Euphues: The Anatomy of Wit (1578).

senses.definition: Someone who writes with euphuism.

core.definition: A writer who uses euphuism, the ornate, artificial prose style of John Lyly's Euphues (1578).

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The opening eu sounds like 'you', so avoid 'you-FEW-ist'. Do not confuse it with euphemist, a person who uses polite substitute words.

nuance.connotation: Mildly negative. It labels a writer as excessively decorative, so it usually signals criticism rather than praise.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this word almost only in literary history, English courses and literary criticism. You might hear it when discussing Elizabethan prose or a writer whose style is overly showy. Calling a colleague a euphuist would sound pointed and a little pretentious, so reserve it for prose discussions.

distinctions.note: A stylist is anyone who cares about how writing sounds, which is often a compliment. A euphuist is a specific kind of stylist whose ornament has become excessive.

A euphemist softens unpleasant facts with mild words such as 'passed away'. A euphuist decorates a sentence with antithesis, alliteration and classical allusion, so the two words are not interchangeable.

examples.everyday: My uncle is a bit of a euphuist. He can't just say he's bored; he has to describe it with three metaphors.
examples.professional: The vendor's proposal was written by a euphuist, so the actual features are buried under flowery comparisons.
examples.analytical: Lyly remains the best-known euphuist, and his Euphues shows how antithesis and alliteration can swamp the meaning they are meant to serve.

nuance.analogy: A euphuist is like a jeweler who covers every object in gems until the object itself cannot be seen.
nuance.etymology: From Euphues, the name of the title character in John Lyly's 1578 novel, from Greek euphyes, meaning well-endowed or talented.
common_mistakes: Confusing euphuist with euphemist, which means someone who uses soft or polite substitute words.
Using euphuist as a general word for any writer; it refers specifically to the ornate Lylyan style.

euphuist.etymology: From Euphues *ist*, after the titular character in John Lyly’s didactic romance Euphues: The Anatomy of Wit (1578); see *euphuism* for more.

senses.definition: Of plants, especially trees, that do not shed their leaves seasonally.
senses.example: The evergreen trees in our backyard stayed green all through the harsh winter.

senses.definition: Continually fresh or self-renewing.
senses.example: Her novel's themes are evergreen, still resonating with new readers decades after it was published.

senses.definition: Being a clause which causes an automatic renewal of a contract unless action is taken.
senses.example: The gym membership includes an evergreen clause that renews it automatically every year unless you cancel.

senses.definition: Of a document, a piece of software, or a data set: kept continually up to date (as opposed to being published at regular intervals and outdated in the meantime)
senses.example: The research team maintains an evergreen dataset that updates nightly from the sensor feeds.

senses.definition: Suitable for transmission at any time; not urgent or time-dependent.
senses.example: The editors marked the feature as evergreen so they could publish it at any time.

senses.definition: A shrub or tree that does not shed its leaves or needles seasonally.
senses.example: Boxwood is a dependable evergreen that keeps its dark color all winter long.

senses.definition: A conifer tree.
senses.example: The nursery sold pines, spruces, and other evergreens for the holiday season.

senses.definition: A news story that can be published or broadcast at any time.
senses.example: Editors kept a few evergreens on file for slow news weeks when nothing urgent happened.

senses.definition: To extend the term of a patent beyond the normal legal limit, usually through repeated small modifications.
senses.example: The company tried to evergreen its patent by filing minor modifications every few years.

senses.definition: To set the repayment rate of a loan at or below the interest rate, so low that the principal will never be repaid.
senses.example: The lender's terms effectively evergreened the loan, since monthly payments never reduced the principal.

core.definition: Keeping its leaves or needles all year, not losing them in winter; said of trees and shrubs like pines and hollies.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, and keep the 'er' reduced and rhotic. The final 'green' is a long e sound, so avoid making the last syllable short.

nuance.connotation: Positive, suggesting freshness, endurance, and life in winter.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'evergreen' for plants and also for things that stay fresh over time, such as a holiday tree or a classic song. It is common in everyday speech and in home, garden, and holiday contexts. A natural reply to 'What kind of tree is that?' is 'It's an evergreen, a Douglas fir.'

distinctions.note: 'Deciduous' means losing leaves seasonally, which is the opposite of evergreen, and is common in botanical and gardening writing.
'Perennial' means living for many years, while 'evergreen' describes keeping leaves all year; a plant can be both.

examples.everyday: We put up an evergreen in the living room every December, and it smells wonderful.
examples.professional: The landscape plan uses evergreen shrubs along the parking lot so the screen works in winter too.
examples.analytical: Some traditions read the evergreen as a sign of persistence, while others treat it as a simple botanical fact.

nuance.analogy: Like a sweater that stays warm all winter, the plant keeps its covering when everything else drops it.
nuance.etymology: Compound of 'ever' (from Old English 'æfre') and 'green' (from Old English 'grēne').
common_mistakes: Stressing the second syllable, saying 'ev-er-GREEN' instead of 'EV-er-green.'
Using 'evergreen' to mean a plant that stays green in a dry climate, when the term refers specifically to keeping leaves or needles through the year.

senses.definition: In an evocative manner.

core.definition: In a way that vividly brings a memory, feeling or image to mind.

pronunciation.tip: The stress stays on VAH, the second syllable, as in the adjective. The final syllable is a clear 'lee,' and the middle vowels are quick schwas.

nuance.connotation: Positive; it describes something done in a vivid, emotionally powerful way.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use evocatively mostly in writing, reviews and critical discussion of art or literature. In speech they often say 'vividly' or 'beautifully' instead. It sounds literary, so use it when describing creative work or atmosphere.

distinctions.note: 'Vividly' describes clearness of detail, while 'evocatively' emphasizes emotional or memory-bringing power.
'Beautifully' focuses on aesthetic quality, while 'evocatively' focuses on bringing something to mind.

examples.everyday: The host described the old farmhouse so evocatively that I could almost smell the apple pie.
examples.professional: The brand video portrays our product evocatively, but the call to action needs to be clearer.
examples.analytical: The essay evocatively recreates the sensory world of rural Ohio, which makes its argument about memory persuasive.

nuance.analogy: Like a painter who uses a few strokes to make you feel a whole sunset.
nuance.etymology: From evocative plus the adverb suffix -ly, from Latin evocare, 'to call out.'
common_mistakes: Using 'evocatively' as a synonym for 'vaguely'; it means vividly, not unclearly.
Confusing 'evocatively' with 'evocative,' using the adverb where an adjective is needed, as in 'an evocatively image.'

senses.definition: The act of heaping or piling up.
senses.example: Hurried exaggeration of the sandbags along the riverbank left the wall taller than the engineers planned.

senses.definition: The act of exaggerating; the act of doing or representing in an excessive manner; a going beyond the bounds of truth, reason, or justice; a hyperbolical representation; hyperbole; overstatement.
senses.example: They say he's a millionnaire, but that's a massive exaggeration.

senses.definition: A representation of things beyond natural life, in expression, beauty, power, vigor.
senses.example: His story about catching a fish the size of a truck was pure exaggeration, but everyone laughed anyway.

core.definition: A statement or description that makes something seem bigger, better, or worse than it really is.

pronunciation.tip: The primary stress falls on RAY, the syllable before -shun, while the first syllable has a weaker stress. Americans say the r clearly, and the -tion ending sounds like 'shun'.

nuance.connotation: Negative to neutral. It usually suggests the speaker is not telling the full truth, but it can be playful in casual talk.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say 'That's an exaggeration' or 'No exaggeration' in ordinary conversation. 'No exaggeration' is often used to emphasize something true that sounds unbelievable. The word is common in both casual and professional speech.

distinctions.note: Hyperbole is the technical term for deliberate exaggeration as a figure of speech; exaggeration is the general everyday word.
Overstatement is more formal and common in reports and debate; exaggeration is more casual.

examples.everyday: When he said the pizza took three hours to arrive, that was a bit of an exaggeration.
examples.professional: The forecast of record traffic was a clear exaggeration, and we overprovisioned the servers.
examples.analytical: Such a reading treats the psalmist's language of cosmic collapse as literal, which is an exaggeration of the poetic intent.

nuance.analogy: An exaggeration is like a photo edited with the contrast turned all the way up: the details are still there, but the picture looks far more dramatic than the scene.
nuance.etymology: From Latin exaggeratio, from exaggerare 'to heap up', from ex- plus agger 'mound'.
common_mistakes: Saying 'exageration' by dropping the g, which is a common spelling error.
Stressing the final syllable instead of the -RAY- syllable.
patterns: [U, C] it's no exaggeration to say (that) …

senses.definition: The weighted average of outcome values, using probability as the weighting function.

core.definition: The long-run average of a random variable's possible outcomes, with each outcome weighted by its probability.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the second syllable of expected and the first of value. Say the -ed ending as a light "id" in expected, and don't pronounce the final vowel of value as a long "oo" in rushed speech.

nuance.connotation: Neutral
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this term in statistics, finance, data science, and decision analysis, and it appears in both classrooms and business meetings. In casual talk, people say "on average" or "the typical outcome" instead. In a meeting, saying "the expected value is about 40 dollars" sounds precise and natural.

distinctions.note: An average describes a set of observed data, while an expected value is a theoretical quantity computed from a probability distribution.
The mode is the single most probable result, but the expected value is the probability-weighted mean, which need not be a possible outcome at all.

collocations: expected value of a random variable

examples.everyday: If you bet a dollar on a coin flip that pays two dollars on heads, the expected value is a little better than zero.
examples.professional: Before we launch the A/B test, let's compare the expected value of each option so we know which one is worth the cost.
examples.analytical: The expected value of a random variable is defined as the sum, or integral, of each possible outcome multiplied by its probability, and it need not equal any outcome that can actually occur.

nuance.analogy: Think of expected value as the average of a fair-weighted lottery: each outcome counts in proportion to how likely it is.
nuance.etymology: Expect comes from Latin exspectare, "to look out for"; value comes from Latin valere, "to be strong, worth."
common_mistakes: Assuming the expected value must be a possible outcome; a die's expected value is 3.5, which cannot be rolled.
Calling it simply the average in technical writing, where the probability weighting matters.

senses.definition: To cough up fluid from the lungs.
To spit.

core.definition: To cough up phlegm or mucus from the lungs or throat and spit it out.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the second syllable, SPEK, and keep the middle syllable reduced to 'tuh'. The r is pronounced strongly in American speech, and the final syllable rhymes with 'rate'.

nuance.connotation: Negative or clinical. It describes an unpleasant bodily act, usually in medical or formal contexts.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use expectorate in everyday talk, where they say 'spit,' 'cough up' or 'hack up.' It appears mainly in medical settings, in pharmacy labels and in formal descriptions. Using it casually can sound stiff or humorous, so keep it for professional or precise contexts.

distinctions.note: Spit is the everyday word for forcing saliva or something from the mouth, while expectorate specifically refers to clearing phlegm from the airway.
Cough up is a casual phrase for bringing something up from the throat, while expectorate is precise and formal.

examples.everyday: The doctor told me to cough hard and try to expectorate the phlegm, which is more than I wanted to know.
examples.professional: The clinic asked patients to expectorate a sample into a sterile cup for the lab test.
examples.analytical: The cough reflex exists so the body can expectorate mucus that would otherwise block the airway.

nuance.analogy: To expectorate is like clearing a clogged drain: the body pushes out what is blocking the passage.
nuance.etymology: From Latin expectorare, 'to expel from the chest', from ex- 'out' and pectus 'chest'.
common_mistakes: Using 'expectorate' in casual conversation, where 'spit' or 'cough up' is more natural.
Confusing it with 'expect', which has a completely different meaning.

expectorate.etymology: From Latin *expectorātus*, past participle of *expectorō* (“ banish from the mind; expel from the breast)”), from *ex* (“out of”) + *pectus* (“the breast”).

senses.definition: In an expedient manner.

core.definition: In a way that is practical and effective for getting a result quickly, even if it is not ideal.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on spee. Keep the middle syllables short and reduced, and pronounce -ly as a light "lee."

nuance.connotation: Neutral
nuance.usage_note: Americans use expediently in formal writing and speech, such as reports or policy discussions. In everyday talk they would say "quickly" or "the easy way." It can imply that a choice was made to avoid a difficulty.

distinctions.note: Quickly only describes speed, while expediently suggests that the method was chosen because it was practical for the situation.
Efficiently emphasizes good use of resources, while expediently emphasizes practicality and getting past an obstacle.

examples.everyday: The mechanic fixed the leak expediently so we could still make it to the game.
examples.professional: The team resolved the outage expediently by rolling back the release instead of debugging it live.
examples.analytical: A government may act expediently in a crisis, but the long-term consequences of such action must still be weighed.

nuance.analogy: Acting expediently is like taking the nearest exit when a road is blocked: it gets you out of trouble, though it may not be the scenic route.
nuance.etymology: From expedient, from Latin expedire, "to free the feet, extricate."
common_mistakes: Using expediently to mean hurriedly or carelessly; it describes a practical choice.
Dropping the -ly ending in speech, which makes it sound like an adjective.

senses.definition: A spending or consuming, often a disbursement of funds.
senses.example: She went to great expense to ensure her children would get the best education.

senses.definition: The elimination or consumption of something, sometimes with the notion of loss or damage to the thing eliminated.
senses.example: Jones reached the final at the expense of Smith, who couldn't beat him.

senses.definition: To charge a cost against an expense account; to bill something to the company for which one works.
senses.example: It should be acceptable to expense a business lunch with a client.

core.definition: Money spent on something, especially a cost you must pay for work, daily life, or a specific purchase.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the second syllable, SPENS. The final s is a clear /s/ sound, not a /z/.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It becomes negative when the cost is high or when something is achieved 'at the expense of' someone or something else.
nuance.usage_note: Americans often use the plural 'expenses' for regular costs such as rent, groceries, and travel. The phrase 'at the expense of' means that something is sacrificed or harmed for a result, and 'on the expense' is not idiomatic. At work, 'expense' refers to costs you can claim, and the verb 'to expense' means to charge a cost to the company.

distinctions.note: Cost is the price of anything, while expense often refers to money spent in the course of work or living.
Expenditure is a more formal word used for large-scale spending by governments or organizations.
A fee is a specific amount paid for a service, while expenses are money spent on various things.

examples.everyday: After rent and groceries, my monthly expenses eat up most of my paycheck.
examples.professional: Please submit your travel expenses by Friday so finance can reimburse you before the month closes.
examples.analytical: Every doctrine has an expense, since some truths must be given up to keep others intact.

nuance.analogy: An expense is like water leaking from a bucket: it is always draining, and you have to keep track of how much is gone.
nuance.etymology: From Latin expensa, 'money spent,' from expendere, 'to weigh out.'
common_mistakes: Using the singular 'expense' for total living costs, where Americans usually say 'expenses' in the plural.
Saying 'with the expense of' instead of 'at the expense of.'

expense.etymology: From Middle English *expense*, from Anglo-Norman *expense* and Old French *espense*, from Late Latin *expēnsa*, from Latin *expendō*.

senses.definition: A person who expounds; a commentator.
senses.example: As an expositor of Romans, the professor walked students through every verse with patient clarity.

core.definition: A person who explains or interprets the meaning of a text, idea or theory, often in writing or public teaching.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on -SPAH-, and the root vowel is the American 'ah' of 'cot', so it sounds like 'pa', not 'po'. The final -or is a reduced /ɚ/ sound, like the end of 'teacher'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive; it describes a clear, knowledgeable explainer and can suggest learned authority.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use expositor mostly in academic, theological and literary contexts, for a scholar or preacher who explains a text or theory. In everyday speech, say 'explainer', 'teacher' or 'commentator'. The word can sound stiff in casual talk, so it works best in writing or formal introductions.

distinctions.note: A commentator often adds personal opinion or current analysis, while an expositor focuses on explaining the meaning of a text or idea accurately.
An interpreter translates or decides meaning across languages or contexts; an expositor explains meaning within the same text or subject.

collocations: a leading expositor of the theory

examples.everyday: My uncle is a good expositor of baseball rules, so I always ask him when I get confused.
examples.professional: She is the team's best expositor of the model, so she presents its assumptions to the stakeholders.
examples.analytical: Aquinas is a careful expositor of Aristotle, though he often reads the Greek text in light of Christian doctrine.

nuance.analogy: Like a museum docent who walks visitors through a painting, pointing out what each detail means.
nuance.etymology: From Latin expositor, 'one who explains', from exponere, 'to set out'.
common_mistakes: Stressing the second syllable as in 'expose' and giving the root a long 'o' vowel; the vowel is /ɑ/ in American speech.
Using expositor for any speaker; the word implies careful explanation, not just talking.

senses.definition: To rejoice; to be very happy, especially in triumph; to triumph (over).
senses.example: The crowd began to exult as the home team scored the winning goal in overtime.

core.definition: To feel or show great joy, especially after a success or a victory.

pronunciation.tip: The stress is on the second syllable, ZULT, with a short u like in "cut." Finish with a clear t and avoid making it sound like "ex-ult" with a long vowel.

nuance.connotation: Positive
nuance.usage_note: Americans use "exult" in writing, speeches, and news reports about triumph, such as "the crowd exulted." In everyday speech people say "celebrate" or "be thrilled." It sounds dramatic, so it suits a sports commentary or a formal toast more than a casual chat. Often followed by "in" or "over."

distinctions.note: Celebrate is the everyday word for marking a happy occasion; exult is more intense and literary, suggesting triumphant joy.
Rejoice is warmer and often religious or emotional; exult suggests a more triumphant, public joy after winning or overcoming.

examples.everyday: The fans exulted when the team scored the winning goal in the last minute.
examples.professional: Leadership exulted over the quarterly results, but we should still keep an eye on customer churn.
examples.analytical: The author argues that the hero exults in power too quickly, forgetting the cost of his victory.

nuance.analogy: Like a runner crossing the finish line with both arms raised: the joy is loud, open, and shared.
nuance.etymology: From Latin exsultare, to leap up or rejoice, from ex- (out) and saltare (to jump).
common_mistakes: Using "exult" in casual conversation where "celebrate" is more natural.
Forgetting the preposition: say "exult in victory" or "exult over the win," not just "exult the win."

exult.etymology: From Middle French *exulter*, from Latin *exsultō*, frequentative of *exsiliō* (“jump up”), from *ex-* + *saliō* (“jump, leap”).

senses.definition: Something that causes the eyes to open, or that opens the eyes.
Something that provides a sudden insight, or makes something clear that was previously mysterious.
A startling or shocking revelation.
senses.example: A visit to the slaughterhouse was a real eye-opener to anyone who thought they understood where their food came from.

senses.definition: A strong alcoholic beverage, especially one consumed in the morning.
senses.example: As soon as I got on the plane I asked the flight attendant for an eye-opener, but all he had to offer was orange juice.

core.definition: Something surprising that suddenly helps you understand a situation or see something more clearly than before.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first word, EYE, and give a lighter secondary stress to OH. The final -er is a weak, rhotic r sound, so say the word with a clear r at the end, not as 'eye-oh-pun-uh'.

nuance.connotation: Usually positive, since the new understanding is valuable, but it can be unpleasant if the surprise is shocking or sad.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say this for a fact, experience or moment that changes how they see something, as in 'That trip was an eye-opener.' In a bar or diner, eye-opener can also mean a morning drink such as coffee or, informally, an alcoholic drink. A natural reply to 'That was an eye-opener' is 'Right? I had no idea.'

distinctions.note: A revelation is a major, often dramatic disclosure and is more formal; an eye-opener is usually a smaller, everyday surprise.
A wake-up call is a warning that pushes you to act; an eye-opener gives you insight but does not necessarily demand a response.
A surprise is simply something unexpected; an eye-opener adds the idea of new understanding.

examples.everyday: That documentary about ocean plastic was an eye-opener; I had no idea how much of it there is.
examples.professional: The latency numbers from the new cluster were an eye-opener for the whole infrastructure team.
examples.analytical: Hume's critique of causation was an eye-opener for many students who had assumed that cause and effect are directly observed.

nuance.analogy: Like switching on a light in a dark room and suddenly seeing the furniture you have been bumping into all along.
nuance.etymology: Compound of eye and open, with the agent suffix -er; the literal sense of something that opens the eyes came first.
common_mistakes: Using eye-opener as an adjective; say eye-opening, as in 'an eye-opening talk'.
Stressing the last syllable, as in 'eye-oh-PEN-er'; the stress belongs on EYE.

senses.definition: To confront; to abash by stern looks.

core.definition: To confront someone or something boldly until they back down, or to stare someone into backing off.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on DOWN, with a lighter secondary stress on face. In fast speech, the two words link smoothly, so say 'fayss-DOWN'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive when describing courage; negative when describing intimidation.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use face down in conversation about conflict, sports, politics or work, as in 'She faced down the bully.' It is often used with a noun object placed between the verb and particle, or after the particle. A natural reply might be 'Good for her, she didn't let him intimidate her.' Do not confuse it with the physical sense of lying with the face toward the floor.

distinctions.note: Stand up to is a broad and everyday phrase for resisting pressure, while face down often implies a direct confrontation that wins or ends a standoff.
Stare down means to win a contest of looks, while face down can include both looks and direct confrontation.

examples.everyday: When the kid tried to bully him on the playground, Marcus refused to back down and faced him down until the kid walked away.
examples.professional: The new manager had to face down pushback from the vendor and insist on the original delivery date.
examples.analytical: A democracy that cannot face down its own demagogues risks letting fear, rather than public reason, govern its decisions.

nuance.analogy: To face down someone is like holding your ground in a narrow hallway: you stay where you are until the other person has to step aside.
nuance.etymology: The phrasal sense comes from face, from Old French face, plus the adverb down, meaning to overcome by a bold front.
common_mistakes: Using face down in the physical sense for lying on your stomach, which is confusing without context.
Placing the object after down only in a way that feels unnatural; 'faced him down' is more natural than 'faced down him'.

senses.definition: Pertaining to or consisting of objective claims.
senses.example: The report stuck to factual claims, leaving out the author's opinions and speculation entirely.

senses.definition: True, accurate, corresponding to reality.
Programs having content based on facts, such as documentaries.
senses.example: The BBC is increasing its budget for factual this year.

core.definition: Based on facts or actual events, and therefore true and accurate rather than opinion or imagination.

pronunciation.tip: The stress is on the first syllable, FAK. The 'tch' sound is a 'ch' sound, and the final syllable is often reduced to 'ul' with almost no 'oo' sound.

nuance.connotation: Positive or neutral; it signals reliability and seriousness, and it often contrasts with opinion or rumor.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'factual' often in news, science, debates, and business contexts, for example 'Is that factual?' or 'That's a factual error'. In casual conversation people usually say 'true' or 'real' instead. Saying 'That's factual' alone in a relaxed conversation may sound slightly stiff.

distinctions.note: 'True' describes whether something corresponds to reality in general, while 'factual' emphasizes that the statement is based on verifiable facts rather than opinion.
'Factitious' means artificial or contrived, not based on natural facts, so it is almost the opposite in meaning.

examples.everyday: I know it sounds unbelievable, but that story is factual; my uncle was actually there.
examples.professional: Before we publish the report, we need to verify every factual claim in the executive summary.
examples.analytical: The author distinguishes between factual statements, which can be tested against evidence, and normative claims, which cannot.

nuance.analogy: A factual statement is like a measuring tape: it gives a reading you can check against the object itself.
nuance.etymology: From 'fact', from Latin 'factum', meaning 'something done'.
common_mistakes: Confusing 'factual' with 'fact' as a noun in phrases like 'a factual of the matter'; the correct phrase is 'a matter of fact'.
Stressing the second syllable instead of the first.

senses.definition: The quality or state of being fainthearted.

core.definition: The quality of lacking courage or resolve, or a state of being easily frightened or hesitant.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, with a lighter secondary stress on 'heart'. The ending 'ness' is a reduced, unstressed syllable, so it sounds like 'nus', not 'ness' with a full vowel.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It names a lack of courage, usually in a critical or reflective tone.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'faintheartedness' mainly in writing, speeches and reflective discussion, not in everyday speech. Most people would say 'lack of courage' or 'being timid' in casual talk. The word appears more in essays, commentary and sermons than in conversation.

distinctions.note: 'Cowardice' is a stronger moral term for shameful fear, while 'faintheartedness' describes a more general hesitation or lack of nerve.
'Caution' is a sensible care that may be wise, while 'faintheartedness' suggests a failure of courage that holds someone back.

examples.professional: Faintheartedness in budget cuts will only delay the inevitable, so we should make the hard decisions now.
examples.analytical: Christian courage is often misunderstood as the absence of fear, yet it is the opposite of mere faintheartedness, a willingness to act despite fear.

nuance.analogy: Faintheartedness is like a candle in a strong wind: the flame is still there, but it flickers and hides when it should burn steadily.
nuance.etymology: From 'fainthearted', from 'faint' (weak) and 'heart' (courage), with the suffix '-ness'.
common_mistakes: Using the noun 'faintheartedness' in casual speech where 'timidity' or 'lack of courage' is more natural.
Mispronouncing the middle 'heart' as 'hart', which sounds like the animal; keep the 'ar' sound with a clear r.

senses.definition: An irresponsible or lazy person.

core.definition: A lazy person who avoids work and responsibility, especially someone who does nothing useful despite holding a position.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, FAYN, and keep the second syllable short and open as 'ant'. The word is pronounced 'fayn-ANT' in French, but Americans stress the first syllable.

nuance.connotation: Negative; it criticizes laziness or idleness, often with a note of disdain.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use 'fainéant' in conversation; it appears mainly in historical writing, such as about the 'do-nothing kings' of the Merovingian dynasty, or in literary criticism. If you want a common alternative, say 'slacker' or 'do-nothing'. Using it in a modern workplace would sound pretentious.

distinctions.note: 'Slacker' is informal American slang for someone who avoids effort, while 'fainéant' is formal, literary, and mostly historical.
'Idler' describes someone who spends time doing nothing, often by choice, while 'fainéant' suggests someone who is nominally in charge but does nothing.

examples.professional: The manager we inherited was a fainéant who signed off on nothing and answered no emails.
examples.analytical: Historians often describe the last Merovingian kings as fainéants, rulers who held the title while power passed to the mayors of the palace.

nuance.analogy: A fainéant is like a stage prop crown: it has the look of authority but does none of the work.
nuance.etymology: From French 'fainéant', from 'faire' (to do) with a negative sense, meaning one who does nothing.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it as 'fay-nee-ANT' with French stress; Americans stress the first syllable.
Using it as a common everyday word; it sounds unusually formal or pretentious in casual talk.

senses.definition: The fans of a thing or person taken as a group.
senses.example: Building a fan base is crucial to career development of a pop musician.

core.definition: The group of fans who follow a particular person, team, band, brand, or product, considered together.

pronunciation.tip: Americans stress the first word in this compound noun, so FAN is strong and base is lighter. Say the long a in base as 'bayss,' not 'bahss.'

nuance.connotation: Positive or neutral; it describes a group of supporters, often with pride or admiration.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use fan base often in sports, entertainment, and marketing news, as in 'The band has a loyal fan base.' It is a neutral, everyday phrase that is fine in both casual and professional settings. People often pair it with build, grow, or lose.

distinctions.note: A fan base is the whole group of supporters, while a fan club is an organized group with members and often official activities.
Audience refers to people who watch, listen, or read, while fan base suggests stronger loyalty and enthusiasm.

examples.everyday: My cousin has a huge fan base in Chicago because he plays in a cover band every weekend.
examples.professional: Our streaming series has built a loyal fan base, so we're planning renewal talks for next quarter.
examples.analytical: A brand's fan base is less a crowd than a community, held together by shared identity and a sense of belonging.

nuance.analogy: A fan base is like a stadium's crowd that keeps coming back, even when the team has a losing season.
nuance.etymology: Fan comes from fanatic, and base comes from Latin basis, 'foundation'; the compound is a modern English usage.
common_mistakes: Putting equal stress on both words; in American speech, FAN is stronger.
Using fan base for a single person; say 'my fans' or 'a fan' when talking about one person.
Saying 'fan basis' instead of 'fan base.'

senses.definition: Suitable for farming.
Capable of being farmed (used to produce an item or money in large quantities by grinding).
senses.example: This week's raid battle is especially farmable.

core.definition: Suitable for growing crops or raising animals; land that can be used for farming. In games and economics, also describes resources that can be gathered repeatedly.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, FAHR. The -able ending is weak and reduced to a quick 'buhl' sound, not stressed like 'bay-buhl'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; describes land, soil or resources rather than people.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use farmable mostly for land and soil, meaning it can be cultivated. In video games and online talk, farmable describes an item or resource a player can gather again and again. For precise agricultural writing, arable is the more technical word.

distinctions.note: Arable means land fit for growing crops, a technical term; farmable is looser and can also describe animals or game resources.

examples.everyday: There isn't much farmable land left around here since the developers moved in.
examples.professional: The team mapped which parcels in the county are farmable before we set the acquisition budget.
examples.analytical: Whether a landscape counts as farmable depends less on soil alone than on water access, slope and the cost of clearing it.

nuance.analogy: Like a garden plot: some ground is ready for planting, and other ground needs work first.
nuance.etymology: From farm (verb) plus the suffix -able, meaning able to be farmed.
common_mistakes: Stressing the -able ending, as in fahr-muh-BAYL; the ending is weak in American speech.
Using farmable to describe people or workers; it describes land, animals or resources.

senses.definition: Synonym of quick as a flash.
senses.example: She finished the spreadsheet fast as lightning, then asked for another.

core.definition: Extremely quick; happening in an instant, or moving with great speed.

pronunciation.tip: Lightning has the main stress on LYTE, and fast takes a secondary stress. In speech, as is reduced to uz, and the -ing ending is ing, not een.

nuance.connotation: Positive or admiring, describing someone's speed in a lively way.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use fast as lightning for a reply, reaction, or movement that happens very quickly, often with admiration. It is informal and mostly spoken. Quick as a flash is equally common, and a natural reply is Wow, that was quick.

distinctions.note: Both mean very quick; quick as a flash is equally common and a bit more playful in tone.
Fast is the basic word for speed, while fast as lightning is a vivid comparison used for emphasis.

examples.everyday: Ask Dad to fix the sink, he's fast as lightning with a wrench.
examples.professional: Our support lead answers urgent tickets fast as lightning, so customers rarely wait long.
examples.analytical: The argument moves fast as lightning from premise to conclusion, leaving readers little time to test each step.

nuance.analogy: Like a camera flash: the action is over before you can really notice it.
common_mistakes: Dropping as and saying fast like lightning, which sounds wrong in English.
Changing the phrase to faster as lightning, when the comparison is fixed as it is.

senses.definition: An important or main item.
senses.example: a water feature

senses.definition: A component that draws attention or interest.
senses.example: a water feature

senses.definition: A beneficial capability of a piece of software.
senses.example: The new photo editor has a useful feature that automatically removes red-eye from snapshots.

senses.definition: A long, prominent article or item in the media, or the department that creates them; frequently used technically to distinguish content from news.
senses.example: He was included in a feature that was written by the EspnCricinfo department on the media.

senses.definition: Ellipsis of feature film.
Any of the physical constituents of the face (eyes, nose, etc.).
senses.example: She has her father's features: the same dark eyes and strong jaw.

senses.definition: The cast or structure of anything, or of any part of a thing, as of a landscape, a picture, a treaty, or an essay; any marked peculiarity or characteristic.
senses.example: one of the features of the landscape

senses.definition: Something discerned from physical evidence that helps define, identify, characterize, and interpret an archeological site.
senses.example: A feature of many Central Texas prehistoric archeological sites is a low spreading pile of stones called a rock midden. Other features at these sites may include small hearths.

senses.definition: Characteristic forms or shapes of parts. For example, a hole, boss, slot, cut, chamfer, or fillet.
senses.example: The model includes a fillet feature on each corner to reduce stress concentrations.

senses.definition: An individual measurable property or characteristic of a phenomenon being observed; the input of a model.
senses.example: Our model uses twelve features, including age, income, and zip code, to predict churn.

senses.definition: The elements into which linguistic units can be broken down.
senses.example: Voicing is a feature of the consonants b, d, and g.

senses.definition: The act of being featured in a piece of music, as a collaborator. See verb sense below; also feat.
senses.example: The rapper's feature on the new single pushed the track up the charts.

senses.definition: To ascribe the greatest importance to something within a certain context.
senses.example: Our onboarding guide features data privacy above every other concern for new hires.

senses.definition: To star, to contain.
senses.example: The museum's new exhibit features paintings from over forty local artists.

senses.definition: To appear, to make an appearance.
senses.example: Her name features in the credits of three documentaries about urban farming.

senses.definition: (dated) To have features resembling.
senses.example: The baby features his mother more than his father, everyone at the party agreed.
senses.label: dated

senses.definition: To think about, understand, or imagine.
senses.example: Can you feature what our team would do with unlimited funding?

core.definition: A distinctive or important part or characteristic of something, such as a product, building, or face.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The final -ture is a single syllable pronounced 'cher,' with the r sounding in American English, not two separate syllables.

nuance.connotation: Positive or neutral. Features are usually described as advantages or interesting parts.
nuance.usage_note: Americans often talk about a product's 'key features,' 'safety features,' or 'standard features' when shopping. In media, 'feature story' or 'feature film' refers to a main article or a full-length movie. As a verb, 'the film features' means it stars or includes someone or something, and 'to feature' means to give special prominence to something.

distinctions.note: Characteristic is more neutral and analytical, describing a typical or defining quality, while feature is often more visible and sometimes a selling point.
Function means what something does or is for, while a feature is a part or quality of it.

examples.everyday: The best feature of this apartment is the big kitchen window.
examples.professional: The most requested feature in the new app is offline mode.
examples.analytical: Consciousness is a feature of human experience that resists purely physical explanation.

nuance.analogy: Like the distinctive shape of a letter that lets you recognize it at a glance.
nuance.etymology: From Old French 'faiture,' from Latin 'factura,' meaning a making or shaping; the facial sense came later.
common_mistakes: Using 'feature' to mean a movie in general; 'feature film' is the main or full-length movie.
Using 'feature' as a countable noun when you mean the whole product; say 'the product has features.'

feature.etymology: From Middle English *feture*, from Anglo-Norman *feture*, from Old French *faiture*, from Latin *factūra*, from Latin *factus*, from Latin *faciō* (“do, make”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European **dʰeh₁-* (“to do, put, place, set”).

senses.definition: Annoyed and out of patience with something that keeps happening.

core.definition: Annoyed and out of patience with something that keeps happening over and over.

pronunciation.tip: Stress 'FED' and 'up' lightly, with 'with' reduced to 'with' (a short 'wih-th'). Link the words smoothly: 'FED-up-with'.

nuance.connotation: Negative, showing frustration. It is casual and common in American conversation.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this expression to complain about something repeated, like noise, bad service, or bureaucracy. A natural reply is I hear you or Yeah, it's getting old. It is informal, so use it with friends, coworkers, and family rather than in formal letters.

distinctions.note: Fed up alone is an adjective; fed up with names the thing that frustrates you.
Sick of is slightly stronger and more informal; fed up with is common and a little more neutral.

examples.everyday: I'm fed up with the construction on my street, and it's been going on for months.
examples.professional: I'm fed up with the same bugs coming back, so let's fix the root cause this sprint.
examples.analytical: Many voters are fed up with a political system that promises reform and never delivers it.

nuance.analogy: Being fed up with something is like a dripping faucet that you have heard for weeks; eventually you can't ignore it anymore.
nuance.etymology: From feed (to supply) plus up and with; the phrase shows the sense of having been filled to the limit.
common_mistakes: Dropping with and saying I'm fed up the noise.
Using fed up with for one small annoyance; it fits better for repeated problems.

conversation.text: I'm fed up with my neighbor's dog barking all night.
She's fed up with her commute, so she's looking for a job closer to home.
We're all fed up with the rain this week.

senses.definition: United, as a federation, under a central government.
Interconnected, as a federation or supernetwork of independent and interoperable services.
senses.example: The hospital joined a federated network so patient records could be shared securely between clinics.

core.definition: Joined together as a federation, with separate member states or groups sharing a central government or common system.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable and make the final -ed a short, reduced 'id' sound, as in FEH-duh-ray-tid. Many learners pronounce the -ated ending as a full separate syllable with a long a and a clear final d.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It describes structure and organization without judgment.
nuance.usage_note: In American English federated appears in political and organizational writing, and in technology, where it describes systems that are connected but independent. Politically, it is more formal than saying united or joined. In technology, you may hear federated login or federated learning. Native speakers rarely use it in casual conversation.

distinctions.note: United means joined together in general, while federated specifically means joined in a structure where member groups keep some independence.
Unified implies a single, merged whole, whereas federated implies separate parts that keep their own identity.

examples.everyday: My company uses federated login, so I can sign into several apps with one password.
examples.professional: We are moving to a federated data architecture so each region keeps control of its own records.
examples.analytical: A federated state preserves regional self-government while sharing authority over common matters.

nuance.analogy: Like a shared building with a common lobby and elevator, where each tenant still runs their own apartment.
nuance.etymology: From federate, from Latin foederatus meaning united by treaty, with the past participle ending -ed.
common_mistakes: Mispronouncing the ending as -ay-ted with a long e; the final syllable is short and reduced.
Using federated as a synonym for federal, which describes the central government itself.

senses.definition: One who feeds, or gives food to another.
The participant in feederism who feeds the other (the feedee).
One who feeds, or takes in food.
One who, or that which, feeds material into something (especially a machine).
senses.example: The conveyor belt feeder jammed again, so the crew had to clear the gravel from the hopper.

senses.definition: That which is used to feed.
senses.example: bird feeder

senses.definition: A tributary stream, especially of a canal.
senses.example: The old feeder stream still carries snowmelt into the canal during the spring floods.

senses.definition: A branch line of a railway.
senses.example: Our commuter train now runs on a feeder line that connects the suburbs to the main station.

senses.definition: A transmission line that feeds the electricity for an electricity substation, or for a transmitter.
senses.example: A high-voltage feeder carries power from the substation to the new transmitter on the ridge.

senses.definition: Ellipsis of feeder school.
A feeder ship.
senses.example: The feeder ship carried containers from the small island ports to the big container terminal.

senses.definition: A judge whose law clerks are often selected to become clerks for the Supreme Court.
senses.example: Judge Patel is a known feeder, and several of her clerks have gone on to the Supreme Court.

senses.definition: A player whose character is killed by the opposing player or team more than once, deliberately or through lack of skills and experience, thus helping the opposing side.
senses.example: Stop being a feeder in ranked matches, or the rest of the team will keep losing.

senses.definition: Synonym of blower (“fissure from which firedamp issues”).
senses.example: Miners in the old coal seam warned that a feeder could release firedamp without any warning.

core.definition: A person or thing that feeds others, such as a device that supplies food to animals, or someone who gives food to another.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable and keep the 'ee' long. The 'd' between vowels is a quick flap, so it sounds close to 'FEE-ur'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. The word is ordinary and descriptive; in some contexts, like the 'feederism' sense, it has a sexual or fetish meaning that is rare and specialized.
nuance.usage_note: Americans most often use feeder for a bird feeder or a pet feeder, a container that dispenses food. For the general sense of a person who gives food, Americans more often say someone who feeds or whoever is feeding the animals. Avoid using feeder for a person in everyday talk unless the meaning is clear from context, since the fetish sense exists.

distinctions.note: In the US, a feeder road (also called a frontage road) runs beside a highway and gives access to it, a meaning unrelated to feeding.
Feeding is the act of giving food; a feeder is the person or device that does it or the container that holds the food.

examples.everyday: I filled the bird feeder this morning, and the cardinals showed up within minutes.
examples.professional: The feeder pipeline pulls raw logs from the servers every fifteen minutes and passes them to the model.
examples.analytical: A feeder in this sense is only a conduit, passing nourishment along without shaping what it carries.

nuance.analogy: A feeder is like a small stream that carries water into a larger lake: it supplies the main body without being the lake itself.
nuance.etymology: From Old English fēdan (to feed) with the agent suffix -er.
common_mistakes: Saying 'I did feeder' when the natural phrase is 'I fed the birds' or 'I filled the feeder'.
Using feeder for a person in general conversation without context, which can be misread because of the feederism sense.

senses.definition: The quality of being feral.

core.definition: The quality of being feral, meaning wild or living in a wild state after having been domesticated.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, FER. The word feral is often mispronounced as 'FEH-ral', but the first vowel is like the air in 'fair'. The final -ness is a reduced syllable.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to negative. It suggests wildness, danger, or a loss of domestication.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use feralness mainly in writing about animals, nature, or wild human behavior, and it is uncommon in casual speech. Most people say wildness or describe the animals as feral instead. In conversation, saying 'the feral cats' is more natural than talking about their feralness.

distinctions.note: Wildness is a general word for untamed nature; feralness specifically describes animals that were once domesticated and have reverted.
Savagery suggests cruelty or violence, while feralness focuses on a state of living without domestication.

examples.everyday: The feralness of the stray cats near our apartment made me keep my distance.
examples.professional: The shelter reported that the feralness of the colony made adoption difficult.
examples.analytical: The feralness of the colony raises questions about whether domestication is reversible in animals or permanent in their social behavior.

nuance.analogy: Feralness is like a house pet that has been left out in the woods so long that its manners have gone wild.
nuance.etymology: From feral, from Latin fera, wild beast, with the English suffix -ness added.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing feral as 'FEH-ral' rather than 'FER-ul'.
Using feralness in everyday speech where wildness is more natural.

senses.definition: A social system based on personal ownership of resources and personal fealty between a suzerain (lord) and a vassal (subject). Defining characteristics are direct ownership of resources, personal loyalty, and a hierarchical social structure reinforced by religion.
senses.example: Medieval peasants farmed the lord's land and owed him military service under feudalism.

core.definition: A medieval social system in which lords granted land to vassals in exchange for loyalty and military service.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The middle -al- is reduced to a quick uh, and the ending -ism sounds like 'iz-um'. Do not stress the -DAL- syllable.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in history, but critical when used to describe modern systems of dependence or control.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use feudalism mainly for European medieval history, but also as a political term, for example 'modern feudalism' or 'digital feudalism' for workers who depend on powerful owners. In political debate the word is pointed and critical. In casual talk, 'old-fashioned' or 'hierarchical' is more typical.

distinctions.note: Manorialism concerns the economic organization of estates and peasant labor, while feudalism concerns the political and military bonds between lords and vassals.
Serfdom is the legal bondage of peasants to land, which was one part of the broader feudal system.
Feudalism rests on personal ties and inherited obligations, while capitalism rests on markets and contracts between free workers.

examples.everyday: My history podcast spent a whole episode explaining how feudalism worked in medieval England.
examples.professional: The report argues that gig platforms have created a kind of digital feudalism, where workers depend on a few owners for income and access.
