pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, ICE, and the second syllable, BREAK, is secondary. Keep the flapped vowel in break clear, and do not reduce the final -ing to -in' in careful speech.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a precise technical description with no emotional charge.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use icebreaking mainly in shipping, Arctic, and engineering contexts, such as an icebreaking ship or icebreaking hull. For social situations, Americans say icebreaker for an activity meant to start conversation, and icebreaker or ice-breaker for the ship as well. The adjective is rarely used outside technical or news writing.

distinctions.note: Icebreaker is the usual noun for either a ship or a social activity, while icebreaking is the adjective describing what breaks ice.
Icebreaking implies forcing through thick ice, usually by a heavy hull, while ice-cutting can refer to any cutting of ice, such as for blocks or sculpture.

examples.everyday: The coast guard sent an icebreaking ship to free the fishing boats stuck in the bay.
examples.professional: The icebreaking vessel will clear a channel before the supply convoy arrives at the station.
examples.analytical: An icebreaking hull is designed to ride up onto the ice and crush it under its own weight.

nuance.analogy: An icebreaking ship works like a bulldozer for ice, pushing forward until the frozen surface gives way.
nuance.etymology: From ice (Old English is) and breaking, the present participle of break (Old English brecan).
common_mistakes: Using icebreaking for a social activity, where icebreaker is the normal noun.
Stressing BREAK as the main stress instead of ICE in the compound.

senses.definition: Cold tea, a beverage.
senses.example: Could you bring me some iced tea please?

senses.definition: Sweetened iced tea, flavored with lemon.
A serving of cold tea.
senses.example: I would like an iced tea with my sandwich, please.

core.definition: Tea brewed hot, then chilled and served cold over ice, usually sweetened or with lemon.

pronunciation.tip: The word 'iced' ends in a clean /st/ cluster, so don't add a vowel after the s. Stress falls on 'tea', with the first word lighter; link the words smoothly so it sounds like 'eyes-TEE'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and friendly; it is an ordinary, everyday drink order.
nuance.usage_note: Americans order iced tea at nearly every restaurant, often without being asked whether they want it sweet. In the South, 'sweet tea' is the usual default and can be very sweet, so if you prefer less sugar, say 'unsweetened' or 'not sweet.' A common reply to 'What can I get you to drink?' is 'Iced tea, please.'

distinctions.note: Sweet tea is a Southern term for iced tea sweetened heavily with sugar; in most of the US, plain iced tea is served unsweetened unless you ask.
Hot tea is served steaming and is usually drunk without ice; iced tea is the cold version of the same drink.

examples.everyday: Could I get a glass of unsweetened iced tea, please?
examples.professional: Let's grab some iced tea and coffee for the afternoon workshop.
examples.analytical: Iced tea illustrates how a familiar drink changes meaning across regions: in the South, the word sweet is often assumed.

nuance.analogy: Iced tea is like cold lemonade's quieter cousin: the same glass and ice, but the tea sets the flavor.
nuance.etymology: 'Tea' comes from a Chinese dialect word (Min te); 'iced' comes from Old English 'is', meaning ice.
common_mistakes: Saying 'ice tea' instead of 'iced tea' in writing or ordering.
Assuming all iced tea is sweet; in most American restaurants it comes unsweetened unless you ask for sweet.

conversation.text: I'll have an iced tea, unsweetened, please.
Can I get a refill on my iced tea?
Is the iced tea fresh brewed?

senses.definition: Assigning an image to one of a set of categories.
senses.example: We fine-tuned a convolutional network for image classification on the medical scan dataset.

core.definition: A machine learning task in which a model assigns an image to one category from a set of predefined labels.

pronunciation.tip: The first word stresses IM, and the second phrase stresses kay in classification. Americans say 'IM-ij' with a short i, and the -ification ending is reduced to ih-fih-KAY-shun.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a precise technical term used in AI and data science.
nuance.usage_note: In American data science and AI work, image classification is the standard name for labeling a whole image, such as 'this photo is a cat.' Engineers often compare it with object detection, which also locates objects in the image. In a meeting, say 'it's an image classification problem' when the output is one label per image.

distinctions.note: Image recognition is a broader, everyday umbrella term for identifying content in images; image classification is the specific task of assigning one label.
Object detection locates objects with bounding boxes and labels them, while image classification gives one label for the whole image.

collocations: a deep learning image classification task

examples.everyday: My phone can tell whether a photo is a beach or a mountain, which is a kind of image classification.
examples.professional: For the first sprint, let's build a simple image classification model and measure its accuracy on the validation set.
examples.analytical: The paper argues that image classification benchmarks reward pattern matching more than true visual understanding.

nuance.analogy: Image classification is like sorting mail into labeled bins: each picture goes into exactly one bin.
common_mistakes: Saying 'image classify' as a verb phrase; Americans say 'classify images'.
Confusing it with object detection, which also finds locations in the image.

conversation.text: Image classification assigns a single label to the whole image, like "cat" or "dog."
Image classification tells you a defect exists; object detection tells you where it is.
We pretrain on a large image classification dataset and fine-tune on medical scans.

senses.definition: The image-making power of the mind; the act of mentally creating or reproducing an object not previously perceived; the ability to create such images.
senses.example: Imagination is one of the most advanced human faculties.

senses.definition: Particularly, construction of false images; fantasizing.
senses.example: You think someone's been following you? That's just your imagination.

senses.definition: Creativity; resourcefulness.
senses.example: His imagination makes him a valuable team member.

senses.definition: A mental image formed by the action of the imagination as a faculty; something imagined.
senses.example: The ghost in the story was just my imagination during that sleepless night.

core.definition: The mind's ability to form mental pictures of things not present, and to create new ideas.

pronunciation.tip: The primary stress falls on NAY, with a lighter secondary stress on the first syllable. The -tion ending sounds like 'shun', and the unstressed vowels are reduced to a schwa.

nuance.connotation: Positive when it means creativity and originality. It shifts negative when it means something unreal, as in 'It's all in your imagination.'
nuance.usage_note: Americans use imagination both to praise creativity ('Use your imagination') and to say that a worry is unfounded ('It's just your imagination'). The second use can sound dismissive if you say it to someone who is genuinely upset. In professional settings, the word usually describes creative problem-solving.

distinctions.note: Creativity is the ability or process of producing something new and valuable; imagination is the mental faculty of forming images and ideas that may lead to it.
Fantasy usually means an elaborate, often escapist daydream or invented world, while imagination is the broader faculty behind it.

examples.everyday: Kids need a lot of imagination to turn a cardboard box into a spaceship.
examples.professional: Our team needs more imagination if we want this product to stand out from the competition.
examples.analytical: Kant treats imagination as the faculty that mediates between sensory intuition and the concepts of the understanding.

nuance.analogy: Imagination is the mind's workshop, where it builds new pictures out of parts it has already seen.
nuance.etymology: From Latin imaginatio, from imaginari 'to picture to oneself', from imago 'image'.
common_mistakes: Adding an extra vowel and spelling it 'imagenation'.
Saying the -tion ending as 'tee-on' instead of 'shun'.
nuance.biblical_note: In Genesis 6:5 (RSV), the imagination of the thoughts of man's heart is described as evil continually; the Hebrew word is yetzer, meaning inclination or the formed bent of the mind. Genesis 8:21 repeats this observation after the flood, saying the imagination of man's heart is evil from youth, and God responds by promising not to curse the ground again. In Luke 1:51, in Mary's song, God scatters the proud in the imagination of their hearts; the Greek word there is dianoia, meaning thought or understanding.

imagination.etymology: From Middle English *ymaginacioun*, from Old French *imaginacion*, *ymaginacion*, from Latin *imāginātiō*.

senses.definition: Not concerned with material things.
senses.example: She was a deeply immaterialistic person who cared little for money, cars, or fashion.

senses.definition: Of or pertaining to the philosophy of immaterialism.
senses.example: His immaterialistic account of perception troubled the students who expected a more physical explanation.

core.definition: Not concerned with money or possessions, or relating to the philosophy that denies matter exists.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on LIS, the fifth syllable. The word has many syllables, so Americans reduce most of them and keep only the strong beat on LIS.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in philosophy, and mildly positive when describing someone who is spiritually or intellectually focused rather than materially focused.
nuance.usage_note: In ordinary American speech, people more often say someone is 'not materialistic' or 'not into material things.' Immaterialistic is rare and sounds formal or academic. It has the philosophical sense as well, so context matters.

distinctions.note: Unmaterialistic is a rare, plain-sounding alternative that means the same as immaterialistic in the everyday sense, but it is less formal.
Spiritual refers to matters of the spirit or religion. Immaterialistic describes a lack of attachment to material things, and in philosophy it describes a specific metaphysical view.

collocations: an immaterialistic view of the mind

examples.everyday: She is pretty immaterialistic, and she would rather spend her paycheck on books than on clothes.
examples.professional: Our founder has an immaterialistic approach to budgeting that focuses on people rather than equipment.
examples.analytical: Berkeley's immaterialistic position denies that physical substance exists apart from the minds that perceive it.

nuance.analogy: An immaterialistic person is like someone who looks through a window at the view and does not bother about the frame.
nuance.etymology: Formed from immaterial with the suffixes -ist and -ic.
common_mistakes: Using immaterialistic to mean unimportant, which is the job of the word immaterial.
Confusing it with materialistic, which means focused on possessions.

senses.definition: Able to be impeached (of a person).
senses.example: Critics argued that the official's conduct was clearly impeachable, not merely politically embarrassing.

senses.definition: That warrants impeachment (of an offense).

core.definition: Open to impeachment, meaning a public official who can be formally charged with serious misconduct, or an offense serious enough to warrant it.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on PEECH, the second syllable. The -able ending is reduced to 'uh-buhl'. Americans say 'PEECH', with a clear 'ch' like in 'church'.

nuance.connotation: Negative; it implies serious wrongdoing, often in a political context.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use impeachable mostly in news and political talk, often in the phrase 'impeachable offense'. The U.S. Constitution uses the phrase 'high crimes and misdemeanors'. People sometimes use the phrase loosely for any shocking misconduct, even when no impeachment is pending.

distinctions.note: Unimpeachable means beyond criticism or doubt; impeachable means open to impeachment or serious charges. The meanings are nearly opposite.
Removable is a general term; impeachable refers specifically to charges brought by a legislature against an official.

examples.everyday: My neighbor says the mayor's lies are impeachable, but he doesn't really follow politics.
examples.professional: The inspector general's report describes conduct that some lawmakers are calling impeachable.
examples.analytical: Whether a president's conduct is impeachable depends on the meaning the Framers gave to high crimes and misdemeanors.

nuance.analogy: Like a badge that can be taken back: the office is held only while the official behaves.
nuance.etymology: From Old French empeechier ('to hinder'), from Late Latin impedicare ('to entangle').
common_mistakes: Using impeachable to mean unimpeachable (beyond doubt); the two words have nearly opposite meanings.
Stressing the first syllable; say im-PEECH-uh-buhl.

senses.definition: Not noticeably; such that it cannot be detected, through being too small or too fast, etc.
senses.example: No one noticed that he had moved imperceptibly backwards.

core.definition: In a way that is too slight or gradual to be noticed.

pronunciation.tip: Stress is on SEP. The final '-ibly' is 'uh-blee', and the 'bly' is a light, clear sound with no separate 'i' sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It describes gradual change and can be used in both casual and formal speech.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'imperceptibly' when describing slow change, such as 'The light faded imperceptibly.' In casual talk they might say 'little by little' or 'so slowly you can't tell.' It sounds more polished than everyday, so it fits writing or careful speech.

distinctions.note: 'Gradually' describes change over time; 'imperceptibly' stresses that the change is so slight it cannot be noticed while happening.
'Slowly' describes speed; 'imperceptibly' describes how little of the change you can actually observe.

examples.everyday: The kids grew so imperceptibly this year that I only noticed when their jeans got short.
examples.professional: Our churn rate rose imperceptibly over the quarter, so the dashboard barely showed it.
examples.analytical: The author's argument shifts imperceptibly from description to judgment across the chapter.

nuance.analogy: Imperceptibly is like the hour hand of a clock: it is always moving, but you only see the change after you look away and come back.
nuance.etymology: From imperceptible plus the English adverb ending '-ly'.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the final syllables as 'im-per-SEP-ti-bly' with a stressed last syllable.
Using it for a large or obvious change, where 'noticeably' fits better.

senses.definition: Not practical; impracticable.

core.definition: Not sensible or realistic; not suited to actual use, real conditions or everyday needs.

pronunciation.tip: The stress is on 'PRAK,' the second syllable. The unstressed 'i' in 'practical' is a short 'ih,' and the final syllable is a reduced 'kul,' so it is not 'practi-CAL.'

nuance.connotation: Negative or mildly critical. It can be a gentle criticism of a plan, or a sharp dismissal of an idea.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'impractical' constantly, in both casual and professional talk. It can describe a person, such as 'an impractical dreamer,' or a plan, such as 'that idea is impractical.' Saying something is impractical is often a polite way to reject a suggestion in a meeting, but calling a person impractical can sound like a personal criticism.

distinctions.note: Impracticable means cannot be done in practice. Impractical is more everyday and means not sensible or useful, even if it could be done.
Unrealistic describes expectations or beliefs that do not match reality. Impractical focuses on whether something works or makes sense to use.

examples.everyday: A car with only two seats is impractical for a family of five.
examples.professional: Building a custom database for this small report would be impractical; a spreadsheet will do the job.
examples.analytical: Kant's ideal of perfect moral law may seem impractical, but he argued that it is the standard by which all actual maxims must be judged.

nuance.analogy: An impractical idea is like a key that fits no lock: it might be beautifully made, but it will not open the door you need.
nuance.etymology: From 'practical' with the prefix im- 'not,' from Latin 'practicus' and Greek 'praktikos,' meaning active or concerned with action.
common_mistakes: Using 'impractical' to mean 'impossible'; something impractical can still be done but is not worth the effort.
Mispronouncing the stress as 'im-prak-TI-kal'; the primary stress is on 'PRAK.'

senses.definition: That has been made better; enhanced.

core.definition: Made better than before; enhanced, or having become more effective or of higher quality.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the second syllable and pronounce the ending as a single /d/ sound after the v. Don't add an extra 'ed' syllable.

nuance.connotation: Positive; it signals progress and is common in product descriptions and everyday reports.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use improved to describe products, versions, conditions, or results, as in 'an improved version' or 'his health is much improved.' Marketers often say 'new and improved,' which people sometimes joke about. It usually describes a state that has already changed, while 'improving' describes ongoing change.

distinctions.note: Better is more general and everyday; improved suggests a deliberate change or upgrade to something that already exists.
Enhanced is more formal and often means that something has been given added features or value; improved refers to general quality.

examples.everyday: The new coffee maker is much improved, and it doesn't leak all over the counter anymore.
examples.professional: The improved reporting tool cut our monthly close from five days to two, which the finance team really appreciates.
examples.analytical: Scholars debate whether the improved manuscript tradition of the fourteenth century reflects careful editing or simply later scribal habits.

nuance.analogy: Like a fresh coat of paint on a house that was already sound: the basic structure is the same, but it now looks and works better.
nuance.etymology: From improve (see improve) plus the past-tense suffix -ed.
common_mistakes: Adding an extra syllable and saying 'im-PROO-vid' instead of 'im-PROOVD'.
Using 'improved' when you mean ongoing change; say 'improving' for progress that is still happening.

senses.definition: Inherently; viewed independently, without reference to anything else.
senses.example: Oxygen is not flammable in itself, but it supports combustion.

core.definition: Considered by itself, apart from anything else; intrinsically. Used to say something matters or is judged on its own merits.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on SELF, not on IN or IT, and the first syllable of itself is a quick reduced vowel. Keep the final f clear and do not add a vowel after it.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it is an analytical phrase that often introduces a point about what something is worth on its own.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this phrase in discussion, writing and argument to say that something matters or is judged on its own, as in 'The money isn't the problem in itself.' It works in both conversation and professional writing. In casual speech people often say 'by itself' or the more emphatic 'in and of itself'.

distinctions.note: 'By itself' means alone or without help; 'in itself' means intrinsically, considered on its own merits, and often introduces a contrast.
The meaning is the same, but 'in and of itself' is more emphatic and more rhetorical, and it is very common in American speech and writing.

examples.everyday: The cake isn't bad in itself, but it's way too sweet for me.
examples.professional: The outage wasn't serious in itself, but it exposed a gap in our monitoring.
examples.analytical: A right to property is not, in itself, a justification for any particular distribution of goods.

nuance.analogy: Like a single brick: ordinary in itself, and meaningful only when you consider the whole wall.
nuance.etymology: Formed from 'in' and 'itself', the reflexive form of 'it' with 'self'.
common_mistakes: Writing 'in it self' as two words instead of 'in itself'.
Stressing IT (IN-it-SELF) instead of SELF, which makes the phrase sound unnatural.

senses.definition: Not subject to being alienated, that is, surrendered, taken away, or transferred to another.
senses.example: An inalienable right is a right that cannot be given away nor taken away.

senses.definition: Of or pertaining to a noun belonging to a special class in which the possessive construction differs from the norm, especially for particular familial relationships and body parts, regarding permanence.
senses.example: Just as some languages have a "be" for permanent states (which are essential) and a different "be" for temporary states (which are incidental), some languages have a "have" for unchangeable possession (which is inalienable) and a different "have" for changeable possession (which is alienable).

core.definition: Impossible to take away or give up; belonging to a person by right and not transferable.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on AY. The -able ending is reduced to 'uh-bul', and the -ian part is said as 'yun' or 'ee-un' in relaxed speech.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It emphasizes dignity, rights and protection, and it is often used in political or moral speech.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use inalienable mainly in political, legal and moral contexts, most famously 'inalienable rights' in the Declaration of Independence. In everyday talk, people rarely use it. Saying 'basic rights' or 'rights no one can take away' is more natural in casual speech.

distinctions.note: Unalienable is an older spelling still found in the Declaration of Independence; Americans today usually write inalienable.
Inviolable means must not be violated or broken; inalienable means cannot be transferred or taken away, often applied to rights.

examples.everyday: My grandmother always said that dignity is inalienable, no matter what happens to you.
examples.professional: The policy team argues that data access is an inalienable right for users, not a premium feature.
examples.analytical: Locke's account of property depends on the claim that the rights to life and liberty are inalienable.

nuance.analogy: Like your own shadow: no one can sell it or take it from you, because it is part of you.
nuance.etymology: From in- (not) plus alienable, from Latin alienare, 'to make foreign or transfer'.
common_mistakes: Stressing the wrong syllable; the stress is on AY, not on -lee-.
Confusing inalienable with unalienable in formal writing; both occur, but inalienable is standard in modern American English.

inalienable.etymology: Borrowed around 1645 from French *inaliénable*, from *in-* + *aliénable* (“alienable”), equivalent to *in-* + *alienable*.

senses.definition: Something that motivates, rouses, or encourages.
senses.example: I have no incentive to do housework right now.

senses.definition: A bonus or reward, often monetary, to work harder.
senses.example: Management offered the sales team a $500 incentive for each car sold.

senses.definition: Inciting; encouraging or moving; rousing to action; stimulating.
senses.example: An incentive speech from the coach rallied the tired team for one final push.

senses.definition: Serving to kindle or set on fire.
senses.example: Old accounts describe the incentive flames that spread through the dry wooden barns.

core.definition: Something that motivates you to act, especially a reward or bonus given to encourage more effort or better performance.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on SEN. The final -tive is a short 'tiv', not 'teev', and the first syllable is a reduced 'in'.

nuance.connotation: Positive; an incentive is usually a reward or something attractive.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this word constantly in business, schools, and government, as in 'incentive program' or 'tax incentive'. In everyday talk parents use it for rewards ('a dollar for every chore is a good incentive'). A natural reply to an offer is 'That's a good incentive', meaning it gives you a reason to act.

distinctions.note: Motivation is the inner drive to act; an incentive is an external reward or push that produces it.
A bonus is one specific payment; an incentive is anything that motivates, which may include a bonus.
A disincentive discourages action, while an incentive encourages it.

examples.everyday: My kids get a dollar for every chore they finish, and honestly that's a pretty good incentive.
examples.professional: The sales team has a quarterly incentive tied to hitting the new revenue targets.
examples.analytical: Economists argue that incentives shape behavior more reliably than exhortation when rewards and costs are clear.

nuance.analogy: An incentive is like a carrot dangled in front of a horse: it pulls you forward by offering something you want.
nuance.etymology: From Latin incentivum, 'that which sets the tune or inspires', from incinere 'to strike up a song'.
common_mistakes: Using incentive as a verb ('to incentive people'); the verb is incentivize.
Pronouncing the ending as 'teev' instead of 'tiv'.
Mixing it up with 'insensitive' in fast speech.
patterns: [C, U] an incentive to do sth
an incentive for sb (to do sth)

incentive.etymology: From Medieval Latin *incentīvus* (“that strikes up or sets the tune”), from *incinō* (“to strike up”), from *in-* (“in, on”) + *canō* (“to sing”) + *-ive*.

senses.definition: To destroy by burning.
To annihilate (not necessarily by burning).
senses.example: The rebels threatened to incinerate the entire village, leaving nothing standing after the attack.

core.definition: To destroy something completely by burning it until only ash remains.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on SIN. The middle syllable is a reduced uh, not ee, and the r is an American r before the ay ending.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in technical use; often negative in news, describing destruction.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use incinerate for burning waste, documents, or medical materials in official or technical contexts: 'The records were incinerated.' In everyday talk they say burn up or burn. It can be used figuratively, as in 'the team's hopes were incinerated.'

distinctions.note: Burn is everyday and general; incinerate stresses complete destruction by fire.
Cremate means burning a body after death; incinerate is broader and covers waste or documents.

examples.everyday: The fire in the old shed was so hot it incinerated everything inside.
examples.professional: The hospital contracts with a facility that incinerates medical waste at very high temperatures.
examples.analytical: Some medieval accounts of hell describe the damned as burning without being incinerated, which preserves their suffering.

nuance.analogy: Like a log turned entirely to ash in a fireplace, incinerate means nothing is left behind.
nuance.etymology: From Latin incinerare 'to reduce to ashes', from in- 'into' and cinis 'ash'.
common_mistakes: Stressing the second syllable; the stress is on the first in IN-sin-uh-rayt.
Using incinerate for ordinary cooking; for food say burn or char.

incinerate.etymology: From Latin *incinerātus*, perfect participle of *incinerō* (“to burn into ashes”), from *cinis* (“ashes”).

senses.definition: Not computable; that cannot be computed, calculated or estimated.

core.definition: Impossible to compute, calculate or estimate, either because no procedure can do it or because it is too complex to do in practice.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on PYOO, the syllable of compute, with the ending -able pronounced 'uh-buhl'. The first syllable in- is light and the com- is reduced to 'kuhm'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and technical. It describes a limit on calculation, not a judgment of a person.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'uncomputable' more often than 'incomputable' in mathematics and computer science, especially for problems that no algorithm can solve. 'Incomputable' is less common and sometimes covers both cases: no procedure exists, or the calculation is too large to finish. In everyday talk, people say 'impossible to calculate' or 'too complicated to figure out'.

distinctions.note: Uncomputable is the usual term for problems no algorithm can solve, while incomputable is less common and can also mean too vast to calculate.
Intractable means a problem can be solved in principle but takes an impractical amount of time, while incomputable suggests no finite procedure can do it at all.
Unknowable means something cannot be known, while incomputable means it cannot be calculated, even if its value is in principle determined.

examples.everyday: With all those hidden fees, the real cost of that phone plan is practically incomputable.
examples.professional: The cross-product of those two tables is so large that the query is effectively incomputable on our current cluster.
examples.analytical: Turing showed that the halting problem is incomputable, so no algorithm can decide it correctly for every program.

nuance.analogy: Like trying to count every grain of sand on a beach before the tide comes in: in principle it has an answer, but no finite process gets there.
nuance.etymology: From in- 'not' plus computable, from Latin computare 'to reckon together'.
common_mistakes: Saying 'incomputable' when you mean 'uncomputable' in computer science; American texts usually use 'uncomputable' for undecidable problems.
Stressing the last syllable of 'computable' as in com-pyoo-TAH-buhl; the stress is on PYOO.

senses.definition: Not consolable; unable to be consoled or comforted, usually due to grief, disappointment, or other distress.
senses.example: The little girl was inconsolable after her favorite stuffed rabbit went missing at the airport.

core.definition: So sad, disappointed or grieving that nothing can comfort you.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on SOH, the third syllable. The 'able' ending is reduced to 'uh-buhl', and the prefix is 'in' followed by 'kuhn', not 'kon'.

nuance.connotation: Negative or sad. It describes deep grief or distress, and it is strong, so it should not be used lightly.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this word for deep grief, such as after a death, a breakup or a painful loss. It is more emotional than 'really upset' and is common in news stories and literature. In casual talk, a friend might say 'she's totally heartbroken' instead. A natural reply is 'That's so hard, I'm sorry.'

distinctions.note: Heartbroken is common and emotional, often about romance or loss; inconsolable stresses that no comfort works.
Unhappy is mild and everyday; inconsolable describes intense, prolonged distress.

examples.everyday: The little boy was inconsolable after he dropped his ice cream on the sidewalk.
examples.professional: Our client was inconsolable after the outage, so we called her personally to explain the fix.
examples.analytical: In the elegy, the speaker's grief is inconsolable, since no consolation the poem offers can restore the dead.

nuance.analogy: A broken vase that can never be glued back to its original shape: no repair seems to soothe the loss.
nuance.etymology: From in- (not) and consolable, from Latin consolari (to console).
common_mistakes: Mispronouncing the stress as 'in-kon-SOH-luh-bul' with a heavy final 'ble'.
Using it for mild disappointment, which is too strong for everyday situations.

senses.definition: In an incurable manner.

core.definition: In a way that cannot be cured or fixed; used to describe a permanent quality, especially a disease or a bad habit.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on KYOOR, the second syllable. The final -ably is reduced to 'uh-blee', so do not say it as a full word like 'able'. The vowel in 'in' is short, as in 'it'.

nuance.connotation: Negative in most uses. It can be used humorously to describe a habit or a personality trait, such as incurably optimistic.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use incurably mostly in medical, formal, or writing contexts, and in phrases like 'incurably romantic' or 'incurably optimistic' for humor. In ordinary speech, people often say 'hopelessly' or 'totally' in those cases. It is safe to use with describing a permanent condition, but it can sound stiff if used lightly.

distinctions.note: Terminally describes an illness that will lead to death, while incurably only says the illness cannot be cured, so a patient can be incurably ill but not terminal.
Hopelessly is more everyday and emotional, so it fits a person's behavior, while incurably often describes a permanent state.

examples.everyday: My grandpa is incurably optimistic, even when the Yankees are losing by ten runs.
examples.professional: The legacy billing system is incurably slow, so tuning queries will not fix it; we need to migrate.
examples.analytical: Her argument is incurably circular, because it assumes its conclusion in the first premise.

nuance.analogy: Something incurably broken is like a cracked foundation under a house: you can paint the walls, but the crack keeps spreading.
nuance.etymology: From incurable plus the adverbial suffix -ly.
common_mistakes: Stressing the final syllable (in-kyoor-uh-BLEE). The stress belongs on KYOOR.
Using incurably to mean 'carelessly' or 'in a way that cannot be seen'. It only means permanently, without cure.

senses.definition: The determination of the condition of the genital parts at the termination of the puerperium preliminary to the discharge of the patient.
senses.example: The obstetrician's indagation confirmed that the patient was ready for discharge after the puerperium.

core.definition: An obsolete medical term for examining the genital organs after childbirth, before a patient is discharged from care.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on GAY, the third syllable. The final -tion is pronounced 'shun'. The two middle syllables are unstressed and reduced to 'duh'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a clinical, historical term and carries no evaluative sense.
nuance.usage_note: Americans do not use indagation in modern speech or writing. It appears only in historical medical texts and dictionaries. If you encounter it in an older book, understand that it is obsolete and modern doctors would say 'postpartum examination' instead.

distinctions.note: Investigation is a modern word for any careful inquiry, while indagation is an obsolete medical term with a narrow clinical meaning.
Examination is the standard modern term for medical checks; indagation is historical and no longer used in practice.

examples.professional: The nineteenth-century obstetric manual lists indagation as a routine step before discharge.
examples.analytical: Indagation, as the older texts called it, shows how obstetric examination was once separated from general clinical care.

nuance.analogy: Indagation is like an old tool on a museum shelf: it explains how things used to be done, but no one uses it today.
nuance.etymology: From Latin indagatio, 'a tracking down', from indagare, 'to track down'.
common_mistakes: Using indagation as a modern term for an investigation. It is obsolete and medical.
Confusing it with indagator or indagate, which are related but also obsolete.

senses.definition: One who, or that which, is inducted.
senses.example: The newest inductee into the county baseball Hall of Fame gave a moving speech on Saturday.

senses.definition: A person who is inducted into an organization.
A person who is drafted or a volunteer that is activated into military service.

core.definition: A person who has been formally admitted into an organization, honor, or hall of fame, or into military service.

pronunciation.tip: The strongest stress falls on the last syllable, TEE, with a long e sound. The first syllable has a weaker secondary stress, so do not stress it as strongly as the last.

nuance.connotation: Positive in most uses, since being an inductee usually means an honor or achievement. In military contexts, it is neutral and describes a legal status.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use inductee most often for Hall of Fame members in sports, music, and other fields, and it appears in news about ceremonies. In the military, inductee can mean a draftee or someone who has just entered service, and it is a formal term. In everyday talk, people more often say new member or honoree for a Hall of Fame winner.

distinctions.note: A draftee is someone called into military service by law; an inductee can be a draftee or a volunteer who has been formally admitted.
A member is anyone in a group; an inductee has been formally brought in through a ceremony or process.
An honoree is someone being recognized for achievement; an inductee is specifically formally added to an organization or list.

examples.everyday: Did you see that the new Hall of Fame inductees will be announced next week?
examples.professional: The company honored its newest inductees into the leadership program at the annual meeting.
examples.analytical: The ceremony marks the transition of each inductee from outsider to member of the community's recognized tradition.

nuance.analogy: An inductee is like a new student who has just been officially welcomed into a school at an opening ceremony.
nuance.etymology: From induct, from Latin inducere, 'to lead in', plus the suffix -ee for a person who receives an action.
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable instead of the last syllable.
Using inductee for any new member of a club, when it usually implies a formal ceremony or selection.

senses.definition: In an industrious manner.

core.definition: In a hard-working, steady way, with real effort and persistence.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on DUS. The middle 'tree' and the 'us' are quick and short, and the -ly ending is a clear 'lee'.

nuance.connotation: Positive: it suggests steady, dedicated effort.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use industriously in writing about effort, such as in reviews, biographies, or reports: she worked industriously on the project. In conversation people usually say 'worked hard' or 'was hard at it'. The adverb sounds formal and somewhat literary.

distinctions.note: Diligently emphasizes careful attention; industriously emphasizes sustained, productive effort.
Hard is the everyday adverb; industriously is more formal and stresses diligence over time.

examples.everyday: My son practiced piano industriously all summer, which I did not expect at all.
examples.professional: The team worked industriously through the holidays to ship the model before the audit.
examples.analytical: Weber argued that Calvinist believers labored industriously in their vocations, partly as a response to uncertainty about salvation.

nuance.analogy: Like a bee moving from flower to flower all day without stopping.
nuance.etymology: Adverb from industrious, from Latin industria 'diligence'.
common_mistakes: Stressing it as in-dus-TREE-us-lee; the stress is on the first DUS.
Confusing industriously with industrially, which means in a manner related to industry.
Using it for a single quick action; it describes steady, ongoing effort.

senses.definition: A branch of statistics studying statistical inference—drawing conclusions about a population from a random sample drawn from it, or, more generally, about a random process from its observed behavior during a finite period of time.
senses.example: The analyst used inferential statistics to estimate voter support from a survey of two thousand people.

core.definition: The branch of statistics that uses a random sample to draw conclusions about a larger population, or about a random process, and measures how reliable those conclusions are.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on -REN- in inferential, not on the first syllable, and the -ial ending is a light 'shuhl'. In statistics the stress is on -TIS-, so the vowel in the first syllable is a weak 'uh'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral, a precise technical term with no emotional charge.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this term in university courses, research papers, data science interviews, and business analytics meetings. It is contrasted with descriptive statistics, which only summarizes the data you already have. In casual talk people just say 'stats' or 'statistics' without the adjective.

distinctions.note: Descriptive statistics summarizes the data at hand with means, medians and charts, while inferential statistics draws conclusions beyond that data.
Probability reasons from a known model to likely outcomes, while inferential statistics reasons from observed data back to the model or population.

examples.everyday: My sister is taking a class on inferential statistics, and she says it's harder than she expected.
examples.professional: Before we report the A/B test results, we need to run inferential statistics to see whether the difference is significant.
examples.analytical: Inferential statistics rests on the assumption that the sample is random, and without that assumption its conclusions about the population lose their justification.

nuance.analogy: Tasting one spoonful of soup to judge the whole pot: the spoonful is the sample, and inferential statistics tells you how confident you can be about the pot.
nuance.etymology: From Latin inferre, 'to bring in or conclude', with the -ential adjective ending.
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable (IN-fer-en-shul) instead of -REN-.
Using inferential to mean 'implied' in everyday speech; the word is technical.

senses.definition: The parts of a large city closer to its core, especially older, populous areas of low-income or immigrant families as opposed to centrally located commercial areas.

core.definition: The older, densely populated parts of a large city near its center, often home to low-income and immigrant families, as opposed to downtown business districts.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the second word, SIH, and the first word is a light 'IN-er' with an r-colored final vowel, not 'in-NER'. The final -y is a clear 'ee' sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to sensitive: the phrase is standard, but it often implies poverty, crime or racial segregation, so people may choose more specific terms in conversation.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this phrase in news, policy and everyday talk about cities like Chicago or Baltimore. It refers to neighborhoods, not the business center, so do not use it for downtown. Some people find it a polite euphemism, so 'urban neighborhoods' or the specific area's name is often more natural.

distinctions.note: Downtown is the commercial and office center of a city, while the inner city is the residential area around it.
Suburbs are outlying residential areas beyond city limits, usually newer and less dense than the inner city.

collocations: grew up in the inner city

examples.everyday: My cousin grew up in the inner city of Philadelphia, but he moved out to the suburbs when he got married.
examples.professional: Our nonprofit runs mentoring programs for students in inner-city schools across the metro area.
examples.analytical: Scholars debate whether the decline of the inner city reflects economic restructuring, deliberate policy choices or both.

nuance.analogy: Like the older, dense core of a tree trunk, the inner city is the original heart of the city that grew outward around it.
nuance.etymology: Inner comes from Old English innera, and city from Old French cite, from Latin civitas.
common_mistakes: Using inner city to mean downtown or the whole center of a city.
Stressing the second word equally with the first; the main stress belongs on SIH.

senses.definition: The state of being insane; madness.
senses.example: The defendant pleaded insanity in the hope of getting a reduced sentence.

core.definition: A serious mental illness, or behavior so foolish or reckless that it seems completely unreasonable. Also used loosely to mean a crazy, unwise plan.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the second syllable, SAN, not on the first. The final -ity is a weak, reduced syllable, and the t between vowels is usually a quick flap that sounds close to a d.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It describes something alarming or unreasonable. In casual talk it is hyperbole, as in 'That traffic is insanity,' and it is not meant literally.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'insanity' in two main ways: literally, in legal or historical contexts such as the 'insanity defense,' and figuratively, to call a plan or situation absurd. In medical settings, clinicians now prefer terms like 'psychosis' or 'mental illness,' and calling a person 'insane' can sound hurtful. In everyday speech, people often say 'That's crazy' or 'That's nuts' for the figurative sense, and 'insanity' sounds a bit more dramatic.

distinctions.note: 'Madness' is older, more literary, and broader; it can describe wild passion or folly as well as mental illness. 'Insanity' is more often used in legal or clinical language.
'Mental illness' is the modern, neutral medical term for any condition affecting thought, mood, or behavior. 'Insanity' is a legal or informal word, not a diagnosis.

examples.everyday: Driving to the coast in that storm was pure insanity, honestly.
examples.professional: Pushing the release to Friday without running the regression tests is sheer insanity.
examples.analytical: Foucault asked whether the boundary between reason and insanity is drawn by scientific knowledge or by institutional power.

nuance.analogy: Like a compass that has lost its needle's connection to north: the mind keeps moving, but it no longer points toward reality.
nuance.etymology: From Latin insanitas, from insanus 'unsound, mad,' from in- 'not' plus sanus 'healthy, sound.'
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable (IN-sanity); the stress belongs on SAN.
Using 'insanity' as a casual insult for people with mental illness, which Americans now see as hurtful; use 'crazy' only with care, and prefer 'that's nuts' for ideas.

senses.definition: Not secure.
senses.example: The old bridge was declared insecure after engineers found cracks in its supports.

senses.definition: Not comfortable or confident in oneself or in certain situations.
senses.example: He's a nice guy and all, but seems to be rather insecure around other people.

core.definition: Not feeling confident or sure of yourself, or feeling anxious about your worth, abilities, or relationships.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on the last syllable, -KYOOR, with a secondary stress on the first syllable. The middle vowel is reduced to a short 'ih' and the r is clearly pronounced.

nuance.connotation: Negative or mildly negative. It describes a lack of confidence, which people may find sympathetic but can sound critical if used about someone directly.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use insecure in everyday conversation about feelings, relationships, or appearance, often in phrases like 'I feel insecure about my work.' It is common in talk about relationships and social situations. Calling a specific person 'insecure' can sound judgmental, so it is kinder to say 'I think he's feeling a little insecure right now.' The word also means unsafe or unstable, as in 'an insecure building.'

distinctions.note: Anxious describes worry or nervousness about something specific or future events. Insecure describes a deeper, more ongoing doubt about one's own worth or position.
Nervous is a temporary feeling before an event, like a job interview. Insecure is a more lasting feeling about yourself.
Unstable refers to physical or emotional balance or reliability. Insecure, in its physical sense, refers to lack of safety or protection.

examples.everyday: I always feel a little insecure at parties where I don't know anyone.
examples.professional: A lot of new hires feel insecure at first, so it helps to give them clear feedback early on.
examples.analytical: Augustine suggests that a person who is insecure about their worth often seeks security in created things rather than in God.

nuance.analogy: Feeling insecure is like standing on a floor that might shift: you keep checking your footing because you do not trust it to hold you.
nuance.etymology: From Latin insecurus, from in- 'not' and securus 'free from care', from se- 'without' and cura 'care'.
common_mistakes: Using insecure as the noun (insecure instead of insecurity) when talking about the state of feeling insecure.
Pronouncing the stress on the first syllable (IN-suh-kyoor); the main stress is on the last syllable.

insecure.etymology: From *in* + *secure*, or from Medieval Latin *insēcūrus*, itself from *in-* (“in, un, non-”) + *sēcūrus* (“safe, certain”).

conversation.text: He's a little insecure about his height.
I felt insecure when everyone else seemed so confident.
She gets insecure when her boyfriend doesn't text back.

senses.definition: The condition of being insentient.

core.definition: The condition of lacking sentience, meaning the capacity to feel, perceive or have subjective experience.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable after "in," which is "SEN." The ending "-tience" sounds like "shuhns," the same as in "sentient," not "tee-ence."

nuance.connotation: Neutral and technical; it describes a philosophical or scientific condition without judgment.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this word mainly in philosophy of mind, animal ethics, artificial intelligence debates and scientific writing. In everyday speech people more often say "doesn't feel anything" or "not conscious." The word is useful in debate, but it can sound stiff in casual talk.

distinctions.note: Insentience is a technical term about lacking the capacity for experience, while insensibility describes a temporary or specific loss of feeling or awareness.
Unconsciousness describes a state a conscious being can enter, while insentience describes a permanent lack of the capacity for experience.

examples.everyday: My daughter asked whether plants can feel anything, and I said that their insentience is still an open question for scientists.
examples.professional: The ethics board asked us to justify treating the model's insentience as the threshold for excluding it from the study.
examples.analytical: Descartes argued that animals lack a thinking soul and so exhibit a kind of insentience, a view most modern philosophers reject.

nuance.analogy: Like a rock that sits in the sun but feels no warmth, the object is present in the world yet has no inner experience.
nuance.etymology: From in- (not) plus sentience, from Latin sentiens, the present participle of sentire, to feel.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it "in-SEN-tee-ence"; the ending is "shuhns," the same as "sentient."
Using "insentience" as a synonym for "stupidity" or lack of intelligence; the word means lack of feeling or experience.

senses.definition: Temporary inability to sleep.
senses.example: After the flight from Tokyo, she suffered insomnia for three nights and drank too much coffee.

senses.definition: A sleeping disorder that is known for its symptoms of unrest and the inability to sleep.
senses.example: My mother suffers from insomnia.

core.definition: Persistent difficulty falling asleep or staying asleep, or a sleep disorder marked by this problem.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on SAHM. The final -ia is a reduced uh, not a long ee-ah. The m is pronounced clearly before n-ee.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It describes a health problem, so it is used with sympathy or concern.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use insomnia both medically and casually, for example saying I have insomnia after a bad week. Doctors often distinguish short-term insomnia from chronic insomnia. In everyday talk, people more often say I can't sleep or I'm not sleeping well.

distinctions.note: Sleeplessness is a general, descriptive word for not sleeping; insomnia usually implies a repeated problem with sleep.
Sleep apnea is a breathing disorder during sleep; insomnia is difficulty falling or staying asleep.

examples.everyday: I've had insomnia all week, so I'm going to call the doctor about it.
examples.professional: The wellness program offers a session on managing insomnia for employees who work night shifts.
examples.analytical: The novel uses insomnia as a metaphor for a conscience that will not rest, which deepens the protagonist's guilt.

nuance.analogy: Like a phone that keeps ringing when you want it to stay quiet, so you can never really switch off.
nuance.etymology: From Latin insomnia, from insomnis 'sleepless', from in- 'not' plus somnus 'sleep'.
common_mistakes: Stressing the last syllable; the stress is on SAHM.
Saying in-so-MEE-nee-uh with the wrong vowel in the first syllable; the first vowel is short.

senses.definition: Containing insult, or having the intention of insulting.
senses.example: He received an insulting letter.

senses.definition: The act of giving insult.
senses.example: Her insulting of the guest at dinner made everyone at the table go silent.

core.definition: Offensive or rude, meant to hurt someone's pride or dignity, or likely to be seen that way.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on SULT, and the vowel is a short 'uh' sound. The ending -ing is a short 'ing', not 'eeng'.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It describes words, actions or offers that show disrespect toward someone.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use insulting for remarks, comments or offers: 'an insulting comment' or 'an insulting offer'. People often say 'That was insulting' right after a comment. It is a normal word in everyday talk and at work, but in a formal setting people may prefer 'offensive' or 'demeaning'.

distinctions.note: Offensive is broader and can describe language that is shocking or morally wrong; insulting focuses on a direct slight to a person.
Rude describes a lack of politeness in behavior; insulting describes words or actions that are meant to hurt or humiliate.
Demeaning is often used at work or in social settings to describe something that lowers a person's status or dignity over time.

examples.everyday: That comment about my cooking was pretty insulting, even if he was joking.
examples.professional: It was insulting to the team when management offered a bonus after ignoring our overtime requests.
examples.analytical: Dismissing a student's question as trivial is not merely rude; it is an insulting refusal to treat the student as a thinker.

nuance.analogy: Like a slap in the face with words instead of a hand.
nuance.etymology: From insult plus -ing; insult comes from Latin insultare, 'to jump on or trample'.
common_mistakes: Saying 'I am insulting' when you mean you are offended; the correct word for your feeling is 'insulted'.
Writing 'insulting to' with a noun that is a person, instead of a comment or action; the phrase 'insulting to me' is natural, but 'insulting of me' is not.

senses.definition: Executed directly, rather than via a compiled binary representation.

core.definition: In programming, executed line by line by an interpreter at runtime, rather than compiled ahead of time into machine code.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the TER. The middle syllables are quick and reduced, and the -ed ending after a t sounds like 'id'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a technical classification with no praise or blame.
nuance.usage_note: Common among developers, in job listings and in technical interviews. Outside software, 'interpreted' usually means translated or explained, which is a different everyday sense. A developer might say 'Python is an interpreted language' in an interview, but would not use the word in casual conversation.

distinctions.note: Compiled code is translated into machine code before it runs; interpreted code is translated and executed step by step at runtime.
Scripted is a looser term for code run by a script, often interpreted, but it does not name a precise execution method.

examples.everyday: My nephew wants to learn coding, and his teacher said Python is an interpreted language.
examples.professional: The build is slow because we're running the tests in interpreted mode instead of the compiled version.
examples.analytical: Whether a language is interpreted or compiled is a property of its implementations, not always of the language itself.

nuance.analogy: Like a live translator reading a speech sentence by sentence, rather than a finished written translation handed over in advance.
nuance.etymology: From interpret, from Latin interpretari 'to explain, translate'.
common_mistakes: Using 'interpreted' for the person who translates; that person is an interpreter.
Thinking an interpreted language is always slower or inferior; the distinction concerns how code runs, not its quality.

senses.definition: To know intuitively or by immediate perception.
senses.example: I could intuit from her silence that she had already decided to take the job.

core.definition: To understand or sense something directly, without relying on evidence or step-by-step reasoning.

pronunciation.tip: The stress is on the second syllable, TOO. The final syllable is a short, reduced 'it', not 'eet' or 'ate'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive; it suggests insight that feels immediate and reliable.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use intuit mostly in philosophy, psychology, or formal writing. In everyday talk they usually say 'I sensed,' 'I had a feeling,' or 'my gut told me.' Intuit sounds deliberate, so use it only when you want to emphasize direct, nonrational understanding.

distinctions.note: To infer is to reach a conclusion from evidence; to intuit is to know directly, without that evidence step.
Sense is broader and can describe physical perception; intuit refers specifically to direct mental understanding.

examples.everyday: I could intuit from her tone that the news wasn't good, so I didn't ask.
examples.professional: The team seems to intuit a pattern in the churn data, but we still need to test it before we act.
examples.analytical: Kant argues that we cannot intuit things in themselves, only the forms of our sensibility.

nuance.analogy: To intuit something is like finding your way home in the dark by feel, without a map or a flashlight.
nuance.etymology: From Latin intuēri, 'to look upon, contemplate'.
common_mistakes: Using intuit as a noun; the noun is intuition.
Confusing intuit with infer; intuiting is not reasoning from evidence.

intuit.etymology: A and *intuitive*; compare Latin *intuitus* (“observed; considered”), perfect participle of *intueor* (“to look at, upon or towards; to observe, regard; to consider, contemplate”), from *in-* (“in, inside”) (ultimately from Proto-Indo-European **h₁én*…

senses.definition: The act of investigating; the process of inquiring into or following up; research, especially patient or thorough inquiry or examination.
senses.example: The investigation into the crime has led to various leads as well as plenty of dead ends.

core.definition: A careful, often formal inquiry to find out the facts about a crime, accident, or problem.

pronunciation.tip: The primary stress falls on GAY, with a lighter secondary stress on the first syllable. The ending '-tion' is pronounced 'shun', not 'tee-on'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to serious. It implies official or systematic examination and can suggest suspicion when used about people.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'investigation' for police cases, government probes, internal company reviews, and scientific or medical inquiries. You can say 'under investigation' when something is being looked at officially. For a simple check of a broken item, 'look' or 'check' is more natural than 'investigation'.

distinctions.note: Inquiry is a broader word for any question or request for information, while investigation is more systematic and usually focused on a specific event.
A review re-examines work that is already done, while an investigation tries to establish what happened and why.
Search means looking for something physical or specific, while an investigation seeks facts, causes, or responsibility.

examples.everyday: The police are still doing an investigation into the car break-ins on our street, so they keep knocking on doors.
examples.professional: HR opened an investigation after the complaint, so please don't discuss it in the team channel.
examples.analytical: A serious historical investigation must weigh what the sources claim against what the physical evidence can actually show.

nuance.analogy: An investigation is like a detective's notebook: each clue is recorded, tested, and linked until the story becomes clear.
nuance.etymology: From investigate, from Latin investigare 'to track out, search into'.
common_mistakes: Using 'about' instead of 'into' after 'investigation'; the usual phrase is 'an investigation into'.
Confusing the noun 'investigation' with the verb 'investigate' in sentences, as in 'They did an investigate'.

investigation.etymology: From Middle English *investigacioun*, from Old French *investigacion*, from Latin *investigatio*.

senses.definition: A person who invests money in order to make a profit.

core.definition: A person or organization that puts money into stocks, property, or businesses to earn a profit.

pronunciation.tip: The stress is on VES, and the final '-or' is a reduced American 'er', not a full 'or' sound. Do not say 'in-vest-OR' with the stress on the last syllable.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive. It suggests financial planning and responsibility, though it can be neutral in tone.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'investor' for individuals, families, funds, and companies that buy stock, property, or business shares. 'Retail investor' refers to ordinary individuals, while 'institutional investor' refers to large organizations such as pension funds. In casual talk, you can say 'someone who invests' or 'a stock investor'.

distinctions.note: A shareholder owns shares of a company, while an investor may hold many different assets, including bonds, property, or private businesses.
A speculator bets on short-term price movements, while an investor usually seeks longer-term returns.
A donor gives money without expecting a return, while an investor expects financial benefit.

examples.everyday: My brother is a small investor, and he checks his account every morning with his coffee.
examples.professional: We need to update the board deck before the investors call on Thursday.
examples.analytical: A rational investor, as classical economics describes one, weighs expected return against risk and uncertainty.

nuance.analogy: An investor is like a gardener who plants seeds, waits, and accepts that some will not grow.
nuance.etymology: From invest, with the agent suffix -or, meaning 'one who does'.
common_mistakes: Confusing 'investor' with 'investment' when describing a person; say 'She is an investor', not 'She is an investment'.
Using 'investor' for someone who only spends time on a project; in that case, 'someone who is committed' is more natural.

senses.definition: Synonym of banker (“A type of envelope with a diamond shape or V-flap that opens on the long edge”).
senses.example: We picked out cream invitation envelopes with diamond flaps for the garden party.

core.definition: An envelope sized and shaped to hold a printed invitation card, usually with a sealed flap and a return address.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on TAY in invitation and on EN in envelope. The middle syllable of invitation is a reduced 'vih', and envelope is EN-vuh-lohp in American English, not the British ON-vuh-lohp.

nuance.connotation: Neutral: it is a practical, descriptive term used in everyday planning.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use invitation envelope when shopping for stationery or addressing wedding and party invitations, for example, 'Do you have matching invitation envelopes?' In casual speech people often just say 'envelope', and the context makes it clear. Note that banker envelope is a separate style name, not a general synonym.

distinctions.note: A banker envelope is named for its shape, a diamond or V-flap that opens on the long edge; an invitation envelope is named for its purpose.
A mailing envelope is any envelope used for posting letters; an invitation envelope is sized and styled for a formal card.

collocations: invitation envelope with a return address

examples.everyday: Can you grab an invitation envelope from the drawer so we can address the party cards?
examples.professional: The events team sent the invitation envelopes to the printer on Monday, so the mailing should go out this week.
examples.analytical: The invitation envelope, in its quiet way, signals the sender's taste before the reader ever opens the card.

nuance.analogy: Like gift wrap that signals the present is special before you unwrap it.
nuance.etymology: Invitation from Latin invitatio; envelope from French enveloppe, from envelopper, 'to wrap'.
common_mistakes: Using invitation envelope for any envelope that happens to hold an invitation; in casual talk 'envelope' is usually enough.
Stressing the last syllable of envelope (en-vuh-LOHP); American English stresses the first syllable: EN-vuh-lohp.

senses.definition: In an irenical manner.

core.definition: In a peaceful, conciliatory way that seeks to reduce conflict and find common ground between opposing positions.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on REE, the second syllable. The ending -ically is pronounced -ih-klee, with a short i and no extra al syllable.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It praises a calm, reconciling approach to disagreement.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use irenically mostly in theological, academic, and literary writing about debates and disputes. It is rare in everyday speech, so for casual talk you would say peacefully or diplomatically. When it is used, it implies a deliberate effort to reduce hostility, not just a quiet manner.

distinctions.note: Diplomatically emphasizes tact in handling people, while irenically emphasizes seeking reconciliation in the substance of a disagreement.
Peacefully describes the absence of violence or conflict, while irenically describes a conciliatory approach within an argument.

examples.professional: In the design review, she addressed the objection irenically, acknowledging the team's concerns before proposing a compromise.
examples.analytical: Several seventeenth-century divines wrote irenically about confessional disputes, seeking common ground rather than a decisive victory.

nuance.analogy: Writing irenically is like a mediator who lowers the temperature in a room, so that both sides can hear one another.
nuance.etymology: From Greek eirenikos, peaceful, from eirene, peace.
common_mistakes: Using irenically to mean quietly or calmly without any sense of reconciling a dispute.
Pronouncing the middle syllable as EYE-ren, when the stress belongs on REE.
nuance.biblical_note: The Greek word eirene, peace, lies behind irenic. Romans 14:19 urges believers to pursue what makes for peace and for mutual upbuilding, linking the search for peace with building up one another. Matthew 5:9 calls the peacemakers blessed, describing peace as an active work rather than passive calm. Ephesians 4:3 urges believers to maintain the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace, which describes peace as the setting in which disputes are handled.

senses.definition: Undecided or unsure how to act.
senses.example: He stood irresolute at the crossroads, unsure which road would lead him back home.

senses.definition: Indecisive or lacking in resolution.
senses.example: The irresolute senator delayed the vote again, unwilling to commit to either side.

core.definition: Unable to make a firm decision or stick to a course of action; hesitant and uncertain.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on 'REZ'. The final syllable rhymes with 'loot', not 'lyoot', in General American speech.

nuance.connotation: Negative, suggesting weakness or lack of nerve, though sometimes neutral when describing careful hesitation.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this word mostly in writing, history, politics, and literature to describe a leader or person who hesitates. In casual talk people usually say 'can't make up my mind' or 'wishy-washy'. Calling someone irresolute in conversation can sound harsh, so use it carefully.

distinctions.note: Indecisive is common and everyday, while irresolute is more formal and suggests a lack of firmness or will, not just a difficulty choosing.
Undecided describes a state of not yet having chosen, while irresolute describes a tendency to waver even after deciding.

examples.everyday: My brother is so irresolute about buying a car that he's been looking for two years.
examples.professional: The manager seemed irresolute about the timeline, so the team asked for a clear decision by Friday.
examples.analytical: Hamlet is often read as an irresolute figure whose hesitation exposes the gap between thought and action.

nuance.analogy: An irresolute person is like a compass needle that keeps swinging back and forth without settling on a direction.
nuance.etymology: From Latin irresolutus, from in- ('not') and resolutus, the past participle of resolvere ('to loosen, resolve').
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the ending as 'lyoot', saying 'ih-REZ-uh-lyoot'.
Using it for a single moment of hesitation, when 'hesitant' is more natural for brief uncertainty.

senses.definition: Saying you will pay for everyone; also "My treat."

core.definition: Said when you will pay for everyone's food or drinks; it means the same as my treat.

pronunciation.tip: In natural speech, ON carries the stress, so say its AHN mee with a quick, light its. The t of it's often blends into the s sound, and me is weak.

nuance.connotation: Positive; it sounds generous and friendly.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say this in restaurants, bars and coffee shops, often before the bill arrives. The phrase can also mean taking responsibility for a mistake, as in It's on me, I forgot to book. A natural reply is Thanks, that's really generous.

distinctions.note: Let's split it means everyone shares the cost equally, while it's on me means you are paying for the group.
It's on you means it is your responsibility, which can refer to paying or to blame, so it can sound pointed.

collocations: I'll get it, it's on me

examples.everyday: Dinner's on me tonight, so you can order dessert too.
examples.professional: Lunch is on me for the team, since we shipped the model early.
examples.analytical: The phrase it's on me turns a bill into a gift, which shows how American etiquette treats paying as a social signal.

nuance.analogy: Like a host who opens the door and takes care of the evening's cost and welcome.
nuance.etymology: On here means at the expense of, and the sense of who pays draws on that meaning.
common_mistakes: Saying it's on my instead of it's on me.
Saying I'll pay for the treat as a way to offer to cover the bill; the natural phrase is it's on me or my treat.

conversation.text: Don't worry about the check; it's on me.
Put your card away; it's on me since you helped me move.
I forgot to make the reservation. Sorry, guys, it's on me.

core.definition: A bronze pillar standing at the entrance of Solomon's Temple, and also a personal name and a clan name in the Old Testament.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, JAY, and end with a short 'in'. The 'ch' is a 'k' sound, not the 'ch' of 'church'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral
nuance.usage_note: Jachin is used in Bible study and church discussion, especially for the temple pillar. Americans often mention it together with Boaz, the other pillar, and it also appears in Masonic symbolism.

examples.everyday: At church, the pastor pointed to the picture of the pillars Jachin and Boaz.
examples.professional: The slide shows Jachin and Boaz at the temple porch, with a short note on their architectural symbolism.
examples.analytical: The naming of the pillar Jachin, meaning 'he establishes', suggests the temple as a place where God's promise is made firm.

nuance.analogy: Jachin is like a pillar holding up a porch: it stands at the entrance and signals what the building rests on.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the 'ch' as in 'chin' or 'church'.
Confusing the pillar Jachin with Boaz, the other pillar.
nuance.biblical_note: Jachin is the name of one of two bronze pillars at the porch of Solomon's Temple, the other being Boaz (1 Kings 7:21; 2 Chronicles 3:17). The name is often understood to mean 'he establishes', suggesting firmness and stability. Genesis 46:10 lists Jachin as a son of Simeon, and 1 Chronicles 9:10 names a priestly family or figure called Jachin.

senses.definition: A ladder leading to heaven.
A flowering plant of the genus Polemonium.
senses.example: The garden center sold Jacob's ladder, a blue-flowered plant with feathery leaves, for shady beds.

senses.definition: A toy consisting of blocks of wood, held together by strings or ribbons, that appear to cascade downward as they flip over.
senses.example: My daughter spent an hour watching the wooden blocks of Jacob's ladder tumble down.

senses.definition: A pocketknife consisting of two handle segments joined by a pivot, with a blade connected by a second pivot to the end of one handle segment.
senses.example: Grandpa carried a worn Jacob's ladder knife, its two handles joined by a pivot.

senses.definition: A noncompact surface resembling a ladder made of handlebodies.
senses.example: In topology class, we learned that Jacob's ladder is a noncompact surface built from handlebodies.

senses.definition: A high-voltage electrical device, often used as a visual effect in old movies, which has a pair of vertical electrodes that form an arc between them starting at the bottom, rising to the top, then repeating.
senses.example: The vintage horror film featured a Jacob's ladder crackling between two metal rods.

senses.definition: A rope ladder from the ratline to the upper mast.
senses.example: The sailor climbed the Jacob's ladder to the topmast to fix the rigging.

senses.definition: (rare) A ladder or run in an item of hosiery.
senses.example: Mom noticed a Jacob's ladder running down my nylon stocking before the wedding.
senses.label: rare

core.definition: The ladder in Genesis that Jacob dreamed of, reaching from earth to heaven, with angels moving up and down it.

pronunciation.tip: Stress LAD, with a secondary stress on JAY. The possessive ending is pronounced /z/ after the voiced b, and the final -er is a reduced American r-colored vowel.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive. In religious settings it suggests a link between heaven and earth or a sign of God's presence.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'Jacob's ladder' mainly in church, Bible study, or sermons, and it sounds natural in those settings. Outside religious talk, it usually refers to the wooden toy, and people may say 'the Jacob's ladder toy' to be clear.

distinctions.note: A stairway is a generic staircase, while Jacob's ladder refers to the specific dream image in Genesis 28.
The flowering plant Polemonium shares the name, but its leaves are arranged like ladder rungs, so the name is not about the dream.

examples.everyday: Our pastor's sermon on Jacob's ladder made me think of prayer as a two-way road.
examples.professional: For the church newsletter, I wrote a short piece on Jacob's ladder for the youth group.
examples.analytical: The ladder in Genesis 28 is read as a sign of communication between heaven and the earthly place of promise.

nuance.analogy: Jacob's ladder is like a phone line between earth and heaven, with messages going both up and down.
nuance.etymology: Named for Jacob, the patriarch in Genesis 28; 'ladder' comes from Old English 'hlæder'.
common_mistakes: Writing 'Jacobs ladder' without an apostrophe, or saying 'Jacob ladder' without the possessive.
Stressing 'Jacob' too strongly, when the main stress falls on 'ladder'.
nuance.biblical_note: The Hebrew word for ladder in Genesis 28 is sullam, a stairway or ramp. Genesis 28:12 describes Jacob dreaming of a ladder set on the earth with its top reaching to heaven, with angels going up and down it. Genesis 28:17 has Jacob say that this place is the gate of heaven, and John 1:51 applies the image to Jesus, who tells Nathanael that the angels ascend and descend on the Son of man.

senses.definition: A dessert made by boiling gelatine, sugar and some flavoring (often derived from fruit) and allowing it to set.

core.definition: A sweet, wobbly dessert made from gelatin, sugar and flavoring, usually fruit-flavored and set in a mold or cup.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable and end with a long o, not 'ay' or 'uh.' The brand is spelled Jell-O, but most people write jello for the generic dessert.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to slightly nostalgic: it suggests kids' party food, school lunches or home cooking, and it can sound childish in formal settings.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use jello as a generic word for fruit gelatin desserts, especially in cafeterias, hospitals and at family events. Jell-O is the brand name, owned by Kraft Heinz, so the capitalized, hyphenated form is correct when you mean the brand. On formal menus or in recipes, people usually say gelatin or gelatin dessert.

distinctions.note: Gelatin is the ingredient or the general category; jello is the sweet, colored, commercial dessert, usually fruit-flavored.
Pudding is creamy and spoonable, while jello is clear and wobbly and holds its shape.

examples.everyday: The hospital gave me lime jello after my surgery, and honestly it was the best part of the day.
examples.professional: For the team potluck, Dana brought a retro jello salad, and everyone took a photo of it before eating.
examples.analytical: Jello illustrates a sol-gel transition: dissolved gelatin forms a network as it cools, which is why the set dessert wobbles.

nuance.analogy: Like a cushion made of colored water, it holds its shape but jiggles at a touch.
nuance.etymology: From the brand name Jell-O, a variant of jelly; it became a generic word in American English.
common_mistakes: Capitalizing and hyphenating the generic word, which is only correct for the brand.
Using jello for savory meat aspic; Americans call that gelatin or aspic.

senses.definition: A part of a building that jets or projects beyond the rest; specifically, an upper story which overhangs the part of the building below.
senses.example: The old house had a jetty on the upper floor, overhanging the narrow street below.

senses.definition: A structure of stone or wood which extends into a river or sea to protect a bank, beach, harbor, etc. from currents or tides; a breakwater.
A dock or wharf extending into a river from a bank, or into a sea from a shore, for boats to land or moor at; a pier.
senses.example: Fishermen tied their small boats up at the wooden jetty near the harbor entrance.

senses.definition: A natural piece of land projecting into a body of water; a peninsula, a promontory.
senses.example: The rocky jetty stretched far into the lake, sheltering the cove from the wind.
