senses.definition: The stalk that connects the stigma(s) to the ovary in a pistil of a flower.
A small, thin, pointed body part.
senses.example: the anal styles of insects

senses.definition: A long, slender, bristle-like process near the anal region.
senses.example: the anal styles of insects

senses.definition: A set of rules regarding the presentation of text (spelling, typography, the citation of references, etc.) and illustrations that is applied by a publisher to the works it produces.
senses.example: the house style of the journal

senses.definition: To design, fashion, make, or arrange in a certain way or form (style).
To call or give a name or title to.
senses.example: The pope is styled His or Your Holiness.

senses.definition: To create for, or give to, someone a style, fashion, or image, particularly one which is regarded as attractive, tasteful, or trendy.
To act in a way which seeks to show that one possesses style.

core.definition: No longer fashionable or popular; no longer in the current style of clothes, design, or behavior.

pronunciation.tip: Keep the diphthong clear and avoid a short i.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to mildly negative, implying something has become dated; sometimes said with humor about clothes or décor.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this for clothing, hairstyles, furniture, and even slang or ways of speaking, and it is casual in tone. Saying something is out of style is a light criticism, and people often respond with 'Yeah, I know, I still like it, though.' Do not confuse it with 'out of stock' or 'out of date' for food.

distinctions.note: Old-fashioned can be a warm compliment for something charming, while out of style suggests it is no longer current or desirable.
Dated emphasizes that something visibly belongs to a past era, while out of style focuses on current fashion.

examples.everyday: Those wide ties are so out of style now, but my dad still wears them to church.
examples.professional: Our slide template looks out of style, so let's update the colors and fonts before the client meeting.
examples.analytical: A theory can go out of style when its assumptions stop matching the evidence, not merely when it stops being fashionable.

nuance.analogy: Like a radio station that plays songs nobody requests anymore: the music is still there, but the audience has moved on.
nuance.etymology: 'Style' comes from Latin stilus, a writing instrument, which came to mean a manner of writing and then a manner or fashion generally.
common_mistakes: Using 'out of style' for food being old, when 'stale' or 'expired' is more accurate.
Saying 'out of the style' with an unnecessary 'the'.

out-of-style.etymology: The noun is derived from Middle English *stile* (“writing tool; piece of written work; characteristic mode of expression; demeanour; person's designation or title; stem of a plant; period of time”) (compare semantic development to *по́черк* (“handwriting,…

senses.definition: The part of something that faces out; the outer surface.
senses.example: He's repainting the outside of his house.

senses.definition: The external appearance of someone or something.
senses.example: Her outside was stern, but inside was a heart of gold.

senses.definition: The space beyond some limit or boundary.
senses.example: Viewed from the outside, the building seemed unremarkable.

senses.definition: The furthest limit, as to number, quantity, extent, etc.
senses.example: It may last a week at the outside.

senses.definition: The part of a road towards the central division: towards the right if one drives on the left, or towards the left if one drives on the right.
senses.example: On a motorway, you should always overtake other vehicles on the outside.

senses.definition: The side of a curved road, racetrack etc. that has the longer arc length; the side of a racetrack furthest from the interior of the course or some other point of reference.
senses.example: On the final bend, the second-place car tried to go around the outside of the leader but spun off into the barrier.

senses.definition: The outer part of the sea, away from the peak of a wave.
senses.example: Surfers paddled past the breakers into the outside, where the swells were gentler.

senses.definition: Of or pertaining to the outer surface, limit or boundary.
senses.example: The outside surface looks good.

senses.definition: Of, pertaining to or originating from beyond the outer surface, limit or boundary.
senses.example: The company hired an outside consultant to review our data pipeline.

senses.definition: Away from the interior or center of something.
senses.example: The outside walls of the church were painted white last summer.

senses.definition: Originating from, arranged by, or being someone outside an organization, group, etc.
senses.example: The Board did not trust outside information about their rivals.

senses.definition: Extending or going beyond the borders or scope of an organization, group, etc.
senses.example: Our project needs help from outside groups, not just people in this department.

senses.definition: Away (far) from the batter as it crosses home plate.
senses.example: The first pitch is ... just a bit outside.

senses.definition: Reaching the extreme or farthest limit, as to extent, quantity, etc; maximum.
senses.example: an outside estimate

senses.definition: Positioned towards the shoulder of a road: towards the left-hand side if one drives on the left, or right-hand side if one drives on the right.
senses.example: the outside lane of the highway

senses.definition: Not legally married to or related to (e.g. not born in wedlock to), and/or not residing with, a specified other person (parent, child, or partner); existing between two such people.
senses.example: Their outside child was raised by his mother, and the father rarely visited.

senses.definition: To or in the outdoors or outside; to or in an area that is beyond the scope, limits, or borders of a given place.
senses.example: I am going outside.

senses.definition: Not in prison.
senses.example: After three years inside, he was finally outside and looking for work.

senses.definition: Beyond the breaking waves.
senses.example: We anchored outside, past the breaking waves, and waited for the tide.

senses.definition: Outdoors.
senses.example: I slept outside last night.

senses.definition: On the outside of, not inside (something, such as a building).
senses.example: Please leave your muddy boots outside the front door before coming in.

senses.definition: Beyond the scope, limits, or borders of.
senses.example: tourists from outside the country

senses.definition: Near, but not in.
senses.example: Our new apartment is just outside the city, near the highway.

senses.definition: Except, apart from.
senses.example: Outside of winning the lottery, the only way to succeed is through many years of hard work.

senses.definition: To ostracize or exclude.
senses.example: Her coworkers began to outside her after she reported the safety violations.

core.definition: In or to the open air, not inside a building or shelter; outdoors.

pronunciation.tip: As an adverb or preposition, stress falls on the second syllable (owt-SIDE). The noun and adjective move the stress to the first syllable (OWT-side). The ou is the ow diphthong, not oo.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. The word describes location and is used constantly in everyday speech.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say outside for outdoors all the time: 'It's nice outside' or 'Let's eat outside.' For a more specific open area, people may say out back or in the yard. The word is friendly and everyday, not formal. Notice that the adverb takes no preposition.

distinctions.note: Outdoors refers to open-air space in general, often in nature; outside is the broader word and can also mean the exterior of a building.
In casual speech outside of is common, but in careful writing use outside with its object directly, as in outside the house.

examples.everyday: It's freezing outside, so grab a jacket before you go.
examples.professional: The team will meet outside by the loading dock at noon.
examples.analytical: The argument stays inside the framework of the theory and never looks outside, to the evidence that could refute it.

nuance.analogy: Like a window: the view is everything beyond the glass, not the room where you are standing.
nuance.etymology: Compound of out and side, meaning the side or surface facing away from the inside.
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable in the adverb (OWT-side) instead of owt-SIDE.
Saying I'm going to outside instead of I'm going outside; the adverb takes no preposition in this sense.

senses.definition: Prominent or noticeable; sovereign.
senses.example: The outstanding peak rose above the valley, impossible to miss from any road.

senses.definition: Exceptionally good; distinguished from others by its superiority.
Projecting outwards.
senses.example: The outstanding balcony projected over the street, shading the shop below.

senses.definition: Unresolved; not settled or finished.
senses.example: I have several outstanding tasks on my to-do list.

senses.definition: Owed as a debt.
senses.example: You must pay any outstanding corporate card balance immediately.

core.definition: Excellent and clearly better than others of its kind; exceptionally good and worth noticing.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on STAND, with a lighter stress on OUT. Non-native speakers often stress the first syllable too heavily, and the ending is a short 'ing' sound, not 'eeng'.

nuance.connotation: Strongly positive, used for praise in work, school and service settings.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say 'outstanding work', 'outstanding job' or 'outstanding service' to praise. As a one-word exclamation it sounds a bit formal or like a teacher. In finance, 'outstanding' means unpaid, so context matters, as in 'an outstanding balance'.

distinctions.note: Excellent describes high quality, while outstanding means it stands clearly above other excellent things.
Remarkable stresses that something is worth noticing, sometimes surprisingly; outstanding stresses clear superiority.
In finance, outstanding means unpaid or still owed, which is a different meaning from praise.

examples.everyday: Your pad thai was outstanding, honestly the best I've had in this town.
examples.professional: The team did outstanding work on the migration, and the rollout went live without a single outage.
examples.analytical: Among the outstanding theologians of the twentieth century, Barth stands out for insisting that God's self-revelation shapes all human knowledge.

nuance.analogy: Like a player who not only scores but scores more than anyone else on the team.
nuance.etymology: From out plus standing, the present participle of stand, literally standing out from the rest.
common_mistakes: Using 'outstanding' to mean unpaid in a praise context, or praise in a billing context, which confuses listeners.
Stressing OUT too heavily instead of the second syllable.

senses.definition: To do too much; to exceed what is proper or true in doing; to carry too far.
senses.example: I overdid the sweets during the holidays and put on some weight.

senses.definition: To cook for too long.
senses.example: to overdo the meat

senses.definition: To give (someone or something) too much work; to require too much effort or strength of (someone); to use up too much of (something).
senses.example: to overdo one’s strength

core.definition: To do something to excess, such as exaggerating, working too hard, or using too much of something.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on DOO, rhyming with 'do' and 'two'. The first syllable has secondary stress, and the middle 'ver' is a reduced rhotic vowel.

nuance.connotation: Mostly negative: it suggests excess that causes harm or annoyance. It is often said kindly, as in 'Don't overdo it.'
nuance.usage_note: Americans say 'Don't overdo it' constantly, especially after an illness, an injury, or a hard workout, and also when someone is spending or eating too much. The idiom overdo it means to exert yourself too much. A natural reply is 'Yeah, I know, I'll take it easy.'

distinctions.note: Overcook is specific to cooking food for too long; overdo applies to effort, behavior, exaggeration, and many other things.
Exaggerate means describing something as bigger or worse than it is; overdo can mean doing an action to excess, including exaggerating.
Overwork means making someone, or yourself, work too hard; overdo is broader and can refer to any excess, including a joke or a diet.

examples.everyday: You just had surgery, so don't overdo it and carry all the groceries yourself.
examples.professional: We shouldn't overdo the dashboard; five key metrics are enough for the executive summary.
examples.analytical: Some preachers overdo the warnings of judgment, so that the gospel sounds like a threat rather than good news.

nuance.analogy: Like adding salt to soup: a pinch helps, but a handful ruins it.
nuance.etymology: From over- plus do, from Old English don 'to do'.
common_mistakes: Using overdone as the simple past; the past tense is overdid, and overdone is the past participle.
Confusing overdo with overdue, which means late, as in 'The bill is overdue.'

overdo.etymology: From Middle English *overdon*, from Old English *oferdōn*, equivalent to *over-* + *do*.

senses.definition: To supply more than is needed.
An excessive supply.
senses.example: The market suffered from an oversupply of cheap apartments after the building boom.

core.definition: To provide more of something than people need or want, so that the supply is larger than demand.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on PLY, and the middle syllables are weak, so say 'suh' quickly. The word is usually heard as four syllables with the strongest sound at the end.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in business and economics, but negative when describing a market problem such as lower prices or waste.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this in economics, agriculture, energy, and business news, such as 'The market is oversupplied with housing.' In everyday talk people often say 'too much' or 'a glut.' The verb sounds technical, so use it when discussing supply and demand rather than ordinary abundance.

distinctions.note: Glut is an everyday noun meaning too much of something, while oversupply is a technical term about supply and demand.
Surplus is a neutral economic term for extra supply left over, while oversupply suggests the excess is a problem for the market.

examples.everyday: The grocery store has an oversupply of bananas, so they're practically giving them away.
examples.professional: The product team noticed an oversupply of inventory in the warehouse, so they paused new orders.
examples.analytical: Economists debate whether a temporary oversupply of housing reflects weak demand or excessive construction during an unusual period.

nuance.analogy: Like a restaurant that cooks far more food than customers order, the extra portions go to waste and drive prices down.
nuance.etymology: From over- (more than enough) plus supply, from Latin supplere, 'to fill up'.
common_mistakes: Writing 'oversupply' when you only mean 'a lot of', since it implies a problem or imbalance.
Pronouncing the middle as a full vowel; say the 'suh' quickly.

senses.definition: In an overwhelming manner; very greatly or intensely.
senses.example: Voters overwhelmingly rejected the measure, with nearly eighty percent voting no.

senses.definition: Mostly; predominantly; almost completely.

core.definition: By a very large margin, or to a very great extent; almost completely.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress is on WEL, and the -ly ending is pronounced as a clear ee sound, not a separate lee syllable. Do not stress the final syllables.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It emphasizes a strong or large result, often in polls, votes or evidence.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use overwhelmingly often in news, politics and everyday conversation about votes, opinions or preferences, such as overwhelmingly positive reviews. It is a strong, emphatic word, so use it when the margin is clearly large. For a softer everyday tone, people say mostly or by a wide margin.

distinctions.note: Mostly is softer and simply means more than half; overwhelmingly means by a very large margin.
Very intensifies an adjective or adverb generally; overwhelmingly stresses a large majority or a dominant effect.

examples.everyday: Everyone at the table voted for the pizza place, so we went there overwhelmingly.
examples.professional: Our survey shows that users overwhelmingly prefer the simpler dashboard to the older version.
examples.analytical: The data points overwhelmingly to one conclusion, though the sample excludes the groups most affected by the policy.

nuance.analogy: Overwhelmingly is like a tide that covers almost the whole beach, leaving only a few stones above the water.
nuance.etymology: From overwhelming plus the adverbial suffix -ly.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the -ly ending as a separate syllable; it is usually said as a short ee sound.
Using overwhelmingly with a small or neutral result; it implies a large margin.

senses.definition: An ache or bodily suffering, or an instance of this; an unpleasant sensation, resulting from a derangement of functions, disease, or injury by violence; hurt.
senses.example: The greatest difficulty lies in treating patients with chronic pain.

senses.definition: The pangs or sufferings of childbirth, caused by contractions of the uterus.
The condition or fact of suffering or anguish especially mental, as opposed to pleasure; torment; distress.
senses.example: In the final analysis, pain is a fact of life.

senses.definition: An annoying person or thing.
senses.example: Your mother is a right pain.

senses.definition: Labor; effort; great care or trouble taken in doing something.
(dated) Suffering inflicted as punishment or penalty.
senses.example: You may not leave this room on pain of death.
senses.label: dated

senses.definition: To hurt; to put to bodily uneasiness or anguish; to afflict with uneasy sensations of any degree of intensity; to torment; to torture.
senses.example: The wound pained him.

senses.definition: To render uneasy in mind; to disquiet; to distress; to grieve.
senses.example: It pains me to say that I must let you go.

senses.definition: (dated) To hurt; to feel painful.
senses.label: dated

core.definition: An unpleasant physical sensation caused by injury or illness, or a feeling of emotional suffering, sadness or distress.

pronunciation.tip: This is one syllable with a long a and a clear final n. Don't drop the n or say 'pay', and don't add a vowel after it.

nuance.connotation: Negative; pain is unwelcome, though it can be used lightly, as in 'what a pain' for annoyance.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use pain for physical hurt and for emotional distress, as in 'I have a pain in my lower back' or 'It was a real pain to fix.' At a doctor's office, 'I'm in pain' is a common and natural way to describe it. Calling a person a pain means they are annoying, which is informal, as in 'My neighbor is such a pain.'

distinctions.note: An ache is a dull, lasting pain, while pain can be sharp, sudden or dull.
Suffering is a broader word for prolonged hardship, often emotional or moral, while pain is usually a single sensation or feeling.
Hurt is the everyday word for injury or emotional wounding, and pain is slightly more neutral and formal.

examples.everyday: I've had this back pain since I moved the couch last week.
examples.professional: Our biggest pain point is that deployments take three hours, so the team wants to automate them.
examples.analytical: Philosophers have long asked whether pain is a sensation, a judgment or a state of the mind.

nuance.analogy: Pain works like a smoke alarm: it is unpleasant, but it signals that something in the body or in life needs attention.
nuance.etymology: From Old French peine, from Latin poena, meaning punishment or penalty.
common_mistakes: Saying 'I'm in a pain' instead of 'I'm in pain', since pain is uncountable in this sense.
Adding an extra syllable (pay-in) instead of saying one clean syllable.
nuance.biblical_note: In Scripture, pain is tied to the consequences of the Fall. Genesis 3:16 describes the pain of childbearing after the disobedience of Adam and Eve, and the Hebrew word ʿiṣṣāvôn, meaning toil or pain, also appears in Genesis 3:17 for the hardship of work. Revelation 21:4 describes a new creation in which God wipes away tears and there is no more death, mourning, crying or pain.

pain.etymology: From Middle English *peyne*, *payne*, from Old French and Anglo-Norman *peine*, from Latin *poena* (“punishment, pain”), from Ancient Greek *ποινή* (“bloodmoney, weregild, fine, price paid, penalty”), from **kʷoinā́*, from Proto-Indo-European **kʷoynéh₂*…

senses.definition: To avoid, deflect, or ward off (an attack, a blow, an argument, etc.).
A defensive or deflective action; an act of parrying.
senses.example: His quick parry saved him from the blow, and the crowd cheered loudly.

senses.definition: A simple defensive action designed to deflect an attack, performed with the forte of the blade.
senses.example: The fencing coach drilled a simple parry, using the strong part of the blade.

senses.definition: A defensive move intended to change the direction of an incoming strike to make it miss its intended target, rather than block and absorb it; and typically performed with an open hand in a downward or sideways slapping motion.
senses.example: In the kung fu class, she learned a sweeping parry to deflect punches with an open palm.

core.definition: To deflect or ward off an attack, blow, or question, often by turning it aside rather than blocking it head-on.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable. The vowel is the short a of 'cat' followed by r, not the long 'air' sound of 'pair'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It describes skillful avoidance, and can be admiring when someone deflects a hard question gracefully.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'parry' most often for fencing, boxing, or a person dodging a tough question, as in 'She parried every question about the budget.' In casual speech, 'deflect' or 'dodge' is more common for dodging questions, while 'parry' sounds slightly more polished or dramatic.

distinctions.note: Deflect is the everyday general word for turning something aside; parry usually implies a deliberate, skillful response to an attack or challenge.
Block means stopping something directly; parry means turning it aside so it misses, which is a more active redirection.
Evade means avoiding something entirely by moving away; parry means responding to it while keeping it from landing.

examples.everyday: My sister always parries my questions about her dating life with a joke.
examples.professional: During the meeting, the director parried the questions about the delayed launch by pointing to next quarter's plan.
examples.analytical: The author parries the objection by reframing the question as one about intention rather than outcome.

nuance.analogy: Like a boxer turning a punch aside with the glove so it slides past the head.
nuance.etymology: From French 'parer', to ward off, from Italian 'parare', from Latin 'parare', to prepare.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it like 'pair-ee' with the diphthong of 'pair'.
Using 'parry' for simply blocking or stopping something, when it implies turning it aside.

parry.etymology: From earlier *parree*, from Middle English **parree*, **paree*, from Old French *paree* (“preparation, ceremony, parade”), from Medieval Latin *parāta* (“preparation, parade”), from *paro* (“to ward off, guard, defend, prepare, get ready”).

senses.definition: To a partial degree or extent, incompletely.
senses.example: The bridge was partially damaged, so the city closed one lane for repairs.

core.definition: To a limited extent; not completely or entirely.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, and the -tial is a reduced shuh. Do not stress the second syllable or stretch the middle vowel into a long ah sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It can signal hedging or a precise, measured statement.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use it in writing and in formal speech, such as on weather forecasts ('partially cloudy') or in official notices ('partially refunded'). In casual talk people more often say 'kind of,' 'a little' or 'partly.' A natural reply to 'Did you finish?' is 'Mostly,' though 'partially' is also understood.

distinctions.note: Partly is more common and more neutral in everyday speech; partially sounds more official or technical and often describes something not yet complete.
Incompletely stresses that something lacks an ending or a full set of parts; partially stresses that some part is present.

examples.everyday: The forecast says it'll be partially cloudy, so you probably don't need a jacket for the game.
examples.professional: The vendor only partially fixed the bug, so the dashboard still shows stale numbers for March.
examples.analytical: The argument is only partially persuasive: it explains the correlation but does not establish causation.

nuance.analogy: Like a glass that is half full: some of it is there, but it is not full.
nuance.etymology: From partial (Late Latin partialis, 'of a part') plus the adverbial suffix -ly.
common_mistakes: Overusing partially in casual speech, where partly or a little sounds more natural
Stressing the second syllable: PAHR-shuh-lee, not pahr-SHAH-lee

senses.definition: Relating to participation.
senses.example: participatory behavior

senses.definition: Open to participation.

core.definition: Involving people actively in making decisions or taking part, rather than only receiving or watching something.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on TISS, the second syllable, and -ory is pronounced 'or-ee' with a secondary stress on -tor-. Many learners stress the final syllable or drop the r in -tory.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It implies inclusion, democracy, and shared responsibility.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use participatory in discussions of government, education, design, and research: 'participatory budgeting' or 'a participatory design process.' In casual talk, 'hands-on' or 'interactive' is more common. It sounds professional and somewhat academic.

distinctions.note: Participative is a close synonym, especially in management writing; participatory is more common in civic, social, and research contexts.
Interactive means responding to user actions; participatory emphasizes people taking real part in decisions or creation.

examples.everyday: The city is doing participatory budgeting this year, so residents can vote on which park projects get funded.
examples.professional: We're using a participatory design process, so the nurses will help decide the new workflow before we build anything.
examples.analytical: A participatory model of democracy holds that legitimacy depends not only on elections but on citizens' continuous involvement in public deliberation.

nuance.analogy: A participatory process is like a potluck dinner: everyone brings a dish, rather than one chef cooking for passive guests.
nuance.etymology: From participate plus the suffix -ory, meaning 'pertaining to participation'.
common_mistakes: Stressing the last syllable: pahr-tiss-ih-puh-TOR-ee.
Using participatory where the meaning is simply 'participating' as a verb or noun, such as 'a participatory student.'
Confusing it with participant.

senses.definition: The flesh or meat of this bird eaten as food.
Any bird of a number of genera in the family Phasianidae, notably in the genera Perdix and Alectoris.
senses.example: On the first day of Christmas, my true love sent to me a partridge in a pear tree.

core.definition: A small, plump game bird of the pheasant family, hunted for sport and sometimes eaten as food.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable and make the r sounds clearly, since American English is rhotic. The d is silent in speech, so the word sounds like 'PAR-trij'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. In everyday talk it refers to the bird, often as a hunting or cooking subject; in Scripture it appears as a symbol of unjust gain or of a fleeting hiding place.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use partridge mostly for the bird in hunting, cooking and country contexts, and in the phrase 'partridge in a pear tree' from the Christmas carol. Most Americans see the word in the carol or in Bible reading rather than in daily talk. For ordinary meat dishes, Americans often just say game or quail.

distinctions.note: Quail is a smaller bird that Americans more often see on restaurant menus and in grocery stores; partridge is more often associated with hunting or the carol.
Pheasant is larger and has a long tail; partridge is a plumper, shorter-tailed bird.

examples.everyday: My uncle went out hunting for partridge in Wyoming last fall.
examples.professional: The restaurant's new menu features roast partridge with figs, so we need to confirm the supplier's delivery date.
examples.analytical: In 1 Samuel 26:20 David compares himself to a partridge hunted in the mountains, which stresses how vulnerable he feels to Saul.

nuance.analogy: Like a bird that is hunted in the open, a partridge stands for something that is easily caught.
nuance.etymology: From Old French perdriz, from Late Latin perdix, from Greek perdix, meaning partridge.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the d, as in 'PAR-trij-d'.
Saying 'partridge' for any small game bird, when Americans usually say quail for the common restaurant bird.
nuance.biblical_note: In Hebrew the bird is most likely qore (קֹרֵא), possibly linked to a root meaning 'to call', which fits its loud calls. In 1 Samuel 26:20 (RSV), David says the king of Israel pursues him as one hunts a partridge in the mountains, showing his danger. In Jeremiah 17:11 (RSV), the partridge that gathers a brood it did not hatch is used as an image of someone who gets riches unjustly, and it will not last.

partridge.etymology: From Middle English *partrich*, *partriche*, *pertriche*, *perdriz*, from Old French *perdriz*, *partriz*, from Latin *perdīx* (“partridge”), from Ancient Greek *πέρδιξ* (“partridge”), probably from *πέρδομαι* (“to fart”).

senses.definition: Land, specifically, an open field, on which livestock is kept for feeding.
senses.example: The farmer moved the herd to the north pasture before the afternoon heat set in.

senses.definition: Ground covered with grass or herbage, used or suitable for the grazing of livestock.
senses.example: The rain has made the pasture lush, so the cattle will graze happily this summer.

senses.definition: To move animals into a pasture.
senses.example: Each spring the rancher pastures the cows on the hillside until the first frost.

senses.definition: To graze.
senses.example: The horses pasture quietly along the creek while the sun sets over the hills.

senses.definition: To feed, especially on growing grass; to supply grass as food for.
senses.example: The farmer pastures fifty oxen.

core.definition: A field of grass or other plants where cattle, sheep, or horses graze.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, PASS, and pronounce the middle sound as 'ch' followed by a reduced, r-colored final syllable. Do not say a separate 'sh' sound, and do not add a t before ch.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It describes land used for animals, and it can suggest a peaceful rural scene.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use pasture for grassy land where farm animals graze, such as a cow pasture or horse pasture. Farmers and ranchers say put the cows out to pasture or go out to pasture. Outside rural settings, people more often say field or grassland.

distinctions.note: A meadow is a natural field of grass and flowers, often unused by livestock, while a pasture is grazed land.
Field is a general word for open land, while pasture specifically means land for grazing animals.

examples.everyday: The cows are out in the pasture behind the barn this afternoon.
examples.professional: The ranch rotates the herd between three pastures to let the grass recover.
examples.analytical: In Psalm 23 the image of green pasture evokes provision and rest under the shepherd's care.

nuance.analogy: A pasture is like a buffet table for animals, set with grass and refilled as the seasons change.
nuance.etymology: From Old French pasture, from Latin pastura, grazing.
common_mistakes: Saying pasture with a full ch-sh-er sound, as PASS-shur.
Using pasture for a lawn or a park, since pasture implies grazing animals.
nuance.biblical_note: In Hebrew and Greek the idea of pasture is tied to shepherding and care for the flock. Psalm 23:2 says the LORD makes the psalmist lie down in green pastures. In John 10:9 Jesus says the one who enters through him will go in and out and find pasture. Ezekiel 34:14 promises that God will feed his people in good pasture.

senses.definition: In a paternalistic manner.

core.definition: In a controlling way that claims to serve someone's own good, treating them as if they cannot decide for themselves.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on LIS, and the ending -ically is pronounced 'ik-lee', with the 'al' dropped in speech. Keep the middle 'er' r-colored and reduced.

nuance.connotation: Negative; it suggests unwelcome control framed as kindness.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this adverb in formal criticism, such as articles, meetings, or policy debates, to describe how a person or government acted. In casual speech, people say treated me like a kid instead. Because it is critical, avoid it when you only mean someone was kind.

distinctions.note: Paternally describes warm, fatherly care; paternalistically adds the sense of unwanted control, even when well-meant.
Protectively describes guarding someone without implying that their choices are being overridden.

examples.everyday: He talked to me paternalistically, as if I couldn't understand my own phone bill.
examples.professional: The policy was written paternalistically, limiting which employees could see their own compensation data.
examples.analytical: A state that restricts adults' choices about their own health acts paternalistically, even when the aim is their wellbeing.

nuance.analogy: Like a coach who calls every play for a skilled player: the help is real, but the player never gets to decide.
nuance.etymology: From paternalistic with the adverb suffix -ally, from Latin pater, 'father'.
common_mistakes: Confusing it with paternally, which is warm and fatherly rather than controlling.
Writing paternalisticly; the adverb keeps the -ally ending, as in paternalistically.

senses.definition: A supporter of patriarchalism.

core.definition: A person who supports patriarchalism, the view that men or fathers should hold authority in family, church, or state.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on AHR, the third syllable. The final -ist is a short ist that rhymes with list, and the syllable kuhl is short with no separate vowel after the l.

nuance.connotation: Often negative, because critics use it as a label; supporters may describe themselves as traditionalists instead.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use patriarchalist in daily life; it appears mostly in political theory, history, and debates about gender and religion. Because it works as a label, it can sound like an accusation, so people usually describe what someone believes rather than calling them a patriarchalist. In religious debates, people often say traditionalist or complementarian instead, though those words are not exact equivalents.

distinctions.note: A traditionalist values established customs in general, while a patriarchalist specifically supports male authority over family and society.
A feminist advocates for equality between women and men, while a patriarchalist supports the view that men should lead.
A patriarch is a male family head or church leader, while a patriarchalist is someone who holds a political or social belief.

examples.everyday: My cousin once called himself a patriarchalist, and it made the dinner conversation tense.
examples.professional: The panel included a patriarchalist commentator, so the moderator asked both guests to define their terms before debating.
examples.analytical: Early patriarchalists such as Robert Filmer grounded monarchy in fatherly authority, and critics such as John Locke answered that political power rests with the people.

nuance.analogy: A patriarchalist is like someone who believes a ship must have one captain, with that authority passed down through the male line.
nuance.etymology: From patriarchal plus the suffix -ist, meaning a person who believes in or supports a doctrine.
common_mistakes: Confusing patriarchalist with patriarch: a patriarchalist holds a belief, while a patriarch is a male family or church leader.
Using it as a neutral self-description; most people use it as a label, so be careful when describing others.

senses.definition: To become worthwhile; to produce a net benefit.
senses.example: Her years of Spanish classes finally paid off when she found herself in Mexico and realized she could communicate with people.

senses.definition: To bribe, especially to deter oversight.
senses.example: I thought the guards would give us trouble, but apparently he had paid them off.

senses.definition: To pay back; to repay.
senses.example: He paid off the loan three months early.

senses.definition: To pay back (repay) the entirety of a loan, thereby effecting the release of a lien on (the thing that was financed).
senses.example: This contract requires you to pay off the car by 2025.

senses.definition: To pay and discharge (an employee).
senses.example: The company paid off the remaining staff early when the contract ended.

senses.definition: To fall to leeward, as the head of a vessel under sail.
senses.example: The skipper ordered the crew to pay off the bow before the squall hit.

core.definition: To finish paying a debt completely, or to turn out to be worthwhile in the end.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the particle 'off' most strongly, with 'pay' secondary. The 'o' in 'off' is the American cot-caught vowel, like 'aw'.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It suggests success, reward or a long effort finally being worth it.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say 'Hard work pays off' or 'It finally paid off' when an effort brings results. For finishing a debt they say 'paid off the car' or 'paid off the loan'. The bribery sense is serious and negative, and it is usually used in news or legal contexts.

distinctions.note: Pay off means finish paying a debt or be worth it; pay back means return money to someone.
Succeed is general and emphasizes achieving a goal; pay off emphasizes a reward for patience or effort.

examples.everyday: We finally paid off the car last month, so now we have a little extra every week.
examples.professional: Our investment in better testing tools is starting to pay off, since bugs are being caught earlier.
examples.analytical: Patience in building trust eventually pays off, although the process often looks like it is producing nothing at all.

nuance.analogy: Paying off is like finishing a long hike and finding that the view was worth every step.
common_mistakes: Confusing pay off with pay back when speaking about a loan you repay.
Using pay off with the object before off in the wrong order, such as pay it off or off it pay, which is unnatural.

conversation.text: We finally paid off our mortgage!
I'm paying the car off a little at a time.
All that studying really paid off.

senses.definition: To be very parsimonious or stingy.
senses.example: Ever since losing his job, my uncle has had to penny-pinch to cover the mortgage.

core.definition: To spend as little money as possible, often to the point of being stingy or depriving yourself.

pronunciation.tip: Stress PINCH, the stronger word; penny keeps a lighter first stress. In speech the words link smoothly as pen-ee-PINCH.

nuance.connotation: Negative; it suggests stinginess, though friends may say it teasingly.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this informally to describe someone who counts every dollar, often in a teasing way. The phrase 'pinch pennies' is at least as common ('She's always pinching pennies'). Applied to a person's generosity, the verb sounds judgmental; a neutral alternative is 'to be careful with money'.

distinctions.note: Save is neutral and positive; penny-pinch suggests excessive stinginess that can hurt comfort or generosity.
Frugal is a respectful word for careful spending; penny-pinch can imply the person is mean.

collocations: penny-pinch to save for a house

examples.everyday: My roommate penny-pinches on everything, so we always buy the cheapest toilet paper.
examples.professional: Finance keeps trying to penny-pinch the travel budget, but our team still needs to attend the conference.
examples.analytical: Economists debate whether a government that penny-pinches on public health actually saves money over time.

nuance.etymology: From penny and pinch, with pinch meaning to economize closely.
common_mistakes: Writing penny pinch without a hyphen in formal writing; the hyphen is standard.
Using with after the verb; American speakers normally say penny-pinch on groceries, not with groceries.

senses.definition: Persons forming or belonging to a particular group, such as a nation, class, ethnic group, country, family, etc.
senses.example: a people apart

senses.definition: A group of persons regarded as being servants, followers, companions or subjects of a ruler or leader.
senses.example: Moses said, "Let my people go."

senses.definition: One's colleagues or employees.
senses.example: I'll have my people call your people.

senses.definition: A person's ancestors, relatives or family.
senses.example: My people lived through the Black Plague and the Thirty Years War.

senses.definition: The mass of a community as distinguished from a special class (elite); the commonalty; the populace; the vulgar; the common crowd; the citizens.
senses.example: The people have successfully stood up against tyranny and totalitarianism.

senses.definition: People in general, humans, by extension sentient beings real or fictional.
senses.example: People don't like it when you tweak their noses.

senses.definition: To stock with people or inhabitants; to fill as with people; to populate.
senses.example: The government planned to people the empty frontier with settlers from the east.

senses.definition: To become populous or populated.
senses.example: The coastal towns began to people rapidly once the railroad arrived.

senses.definition: To inhabit; to occupy; to populate.
senses.example: Mountain goats and eagles people these remote cliffs above the river.

senses.definition: (rare) To interact with people; to socialize.
senses.example: She hated crowds and rarely wanted to people, preferring quiet evenings with her books.
senses.label: rare

core.definition: Human beings in general, or the men, women and children who make up a group, community or nation.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, PEE, and make the second syllable a reduced schwa, so it sounds like PEE-puhl with a soft final l. Do not separate it into two strong syllables.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It refers to human beings and can carry warmth when used for communities, families or ordinary folks.
nuance.usage_note: In everyday American English 'people' is the plural of 'person' and is used with 'some,' 'a lot of' and 'most' (for example, 'a lot of people'). The plural 'persons' is formal and is used in legal or official text, such as 'three persons were injured.' As a verb, 'people' means to fill with inhabitants, and it is literary.

distinctions.note: 'Persons' is a formal or legal plural and is countable. 'People' is the everyday plural.
'Population' is a statistical or demographic term for the total number of inhabitants. 'People' is general and everyday.
'Folks' is informal and friendly, often used for family or acquaintances. 'People' is neutral.

examples.everyday: There were so many people at the farmers market that we couldn't find parking.
examples.professional: We need to hire two more people on the data team before the launch next quarter.
examples.analytical: The prophet's concern is not the abstract idea of humanity but the actual people who suffer injustice in the city.

nuance.analogy: Like water in a river: one word for the whole flow, even though it is made of countless separate drops.
nuance.etymology: From Old French peuple, from Latin populus, meaning the people or a community.
common_mistakes: Using 'peoples' to mean a crowd; 'peoples' is used for distinct ethnic or national groups.
Saying 'a people' to mean an individual; 'people' is used for many individuals, while 'a person' is singular.
nuance.biblical_note: In the Hebrew Bible the word usually translates 'am, a people or nation, often a people chosen by God. In the Greek New Testament it usually translates laos, a people or congregation, and sometimes ethnos, a nation or Gentile group. Exodus 19:5 describes Israel as God's own possession among all peoples. Matthew 1:21 says the child will save his people from their sins. Psalm 100:3 declares that God's people are the sheep of his pasture.

people.etymology: From Middle English *puple*, *peple*, *peeple*, from Anglo-Norman *people*, from Old French *pueple*, *peuple*, *pople*, from Latin *populus* (“a people, nation”), from *populus*, from earlier *poplus*, from even earlier *poplos*, from Proto-Italic…

senses.definition: The foot of a human.
The hoof of a quadruped.
senses.example: The farrier trimmed the pes of the mare and checked the hoof wall for cracks.

senses.definition: Clubfoot or talipes.
senses.example: Doctors began casting the newborn's pes right after birth, hoping to correct the clubfoot early.

senses.definition: A neume representing two notes ascending.
senses.example: The chant manuscript marked a pes above the syllable, signaling two ascending notes to the singers.

core.definition: Anatomy: the foot of a human or the hind limb of an animal, used mainly in medical and scientific terms.

pronunciation.tip: Pronounce it as one syllable, 'peez,' with a long e and a clear z at the end. Do not say 'pess' or add an extra vowel.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and clinical, used in medical or scientific language.
nuance.usage_note: Americans almost never use 'pes' in everyday speech, where they say 'foot' or 'feet.' You will mainly see it in medical records and anatomy textbooks, in phrases such as 'pes planus' for flat feet. In casual conversation, use 'foot' to be understood.

distinctions.note: 'Foot' is the everyday American word, while 'pes' is a technical Latin term used in anatomy and medicine.
'Hoof' refers to the hard covering on the foot of an animal such as a horse, while 'pes' refers to the foot itself in an anatomical sense.
'Pedal' is an adjective meaning 'relating to the foot,' used for things such as pedal muscles or foot-operated controls.

examples.everyday: My podiatrist said I have pes planus, but I just call it having flat feet.
examples.professional: The orthopedic note lists bilateral pes planus with mild overpronation, so we should check the arch support.
examples.analytical: Anatomists describe the pes as the distal segment of the hind limb, which is adapted for bearing weight and balance.

nuance.analogy: Like a legal term in a contract: correct in the document, but people usually say the everyday word out loud.
nuance.etymology: From Latin pes, pedis, 'foot'.
common_mistakes: Using 'pes' as an everyday word for foot, which sounds odd and overly technical in ordinary conversation.
Pronouncing it as 'pess' with a short e and a hard s, rather than the standard American 'peez'.

senses.definition: Something that is personally annoying; a personal dislike.
senses.example: Forgetting to finish a sentence with a period is one of my pet peeves.

core.definition: Something that particularly annoys you; a small habit or behavior you dislike more than most others.

pronunciation.tip: Put the main stress on PET and say peev as one long, clear vowel, not 'pee-vee'. The two words are said quickly, so the phrase sounds almost like PET-peev.

nuance.connotation: Mildly negative but light and often humorous. People say it playfully, so it rarely sounds hostile.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this phrase constantly in casual talk to introduce a small annoyance, such as 'My pet peeve is people who chew loudly.' It is lighthearted, so it works with friends, coworkers and family, but for serious wrongs use stronger words like outrage or grievance. A natural reply is 'Oh, I know what you mean' or 'Mine too.'

distinctions.note: An annoyance is any general irritation, while a pet peeve is one specific thing you find especially irritating.
A grievance is a serious or formal complaint about unfair treatment, whereas a pet peeve is a small, personal irritation.
A bugbear is a persistent problem that bothers you repeatedly; it sounds more literary and less casual than pet peeve.

examples.everyday: Honestly, people who chew with their mouths open are my biggest pet peeve.
examples.professional: My pet peeve in meetings is when someone brings up a topic we already settled last week.
examples.analytical: Pet peeves are revealing because they expose the unspoken norms we hold so firmly that a violation feels personal rather than merely inconvenient.

nuance.analogy: A pet peeve is like a pebble in your shoe: small, specific and hard to ignore.
nuance.etymology: Pet (a favorite or darling, of uncertain origin) plus peeve, probably back-formed from peevish in the 1800s.
common_mistakes: Misspelling it as 'pet peave', which looks like a different phrase.
Saying 'pee-vee' with two syllables; peeve is one syllable, /piv/.

senses.definition: A heavy iron tool with a wooden handle; one end of the head is pointed, the other has a chisel edge.
senses.example: He was mining stone using a pickaxe.

senses.definition: To use a pickaxe.
senses.example: The miners spent all morning pickaxing through frozen clay to reach the vein.

core.definition: A heavy tool with a curved steel head, a wooden handle and a pointed or chisel end, used to break up hard ground or rock.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, and pronounce the x as a ks sound. Say PIK-aks, not 'pick-AX' or 'pick-ex'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a practical tool word.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this word in construction, mining, landscaping and in stories about the Gold Rush or video games. The standard American spelling is one word, pickaxe, not 'pick-axe' or 'pickax'. Pick alone can also mean this tool in mining talk.

distinctions.note: Pick is a shorter name for the same tool, used mainly in mining and construction, while pickaxe is the full standard name.
A mattock has a flat blade across the head, like a hoe, while a pickaxe has a pointed or chisel end.

collocations: the wooden handle of a pickaxe

examples.everyday: We used a pickaxe to break up the old concrete in the backyard.
examples.professional: The crew needs a pickaxe and a shovel for trenching before the pipe goes in.
examples.analytical: The pickaxe, like the plow, marks a technology that shaped human labor and settlement.

nuance.analogy: A pickaxe is like a fork for stone, prying and breaking apart hard ground.
nuance.etymology: From pick (a pointed tool) and axe, both from Middle English.
common_mistakes: Writing 'pick-axe' or 'pickax'; the standard American spelling is pickaxe.
Pronouncing the x as 'ex' or stressing the second syllable.

pickaxe.etymology: Middle English *pykeaxe*, *pecaxe*, *pyke exe* (“pickaxe”), an alteration (due to folk etymology association with *pick* and *axe*) of *pikeyse*, *pikeys*, *pykois*, from Anglo-Norman **pikeis*, Old French *picois*, *pecois*, from Latin *picōsa*…

senses.definition: A plausible statement, argument etc.
senses.example: The detective dismissed the suspect's excuse as a plausibility designed to buy time.

senses.definition: The fact of being believable; believability, credibility.
senses.example: The plausibility of the hypothesis depends on whether the sample data is representative.

senses.definition: (rare) The appearance of truth, especially when deceptive; speciousness.
senses.example: The con artist's plausibility lay in his warm smile and his perfectly rehearsed sincerity.
senses.label: rare

core.definition: The quality of seeming believable or reasonable, even if the claim is not proven.

pronunciation.tip: The primary stress is on BIL, the third syllable. The final -ity is pronounced ih-tee, with the last vowel reduced and the t flapped toward a soft d sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to negative. It usually means 'seems true,' but it can imply that something only appears credible and may be false.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use plausibility in debates, analysis, news and academic writing when judging a claim or story. In everyday conversation people usually say 'that makes sense' or 'that sounds believable.' Be careful, because the word can suggest that something only looks true, as in questioning a story's plausibility.

distinctions.note: Probability is a measured likelihood, often numerical, while plausibility is a judgment about whether something seems believable.
Credibility refers to trust in a person or source, while plausibility refers to whether a claim or story seems true.

examples.everyday: I doubt the plausibility of his story about the missing car keys.
examples.professional: Before we ship the model, we need to test the plausibility of its forecasts against last quarter's numbers.
examples.analytical: The argument's plausibility depends on premises we have no independent reason to accept.

nuance.analogy: Plausibility is how well a story fits the furniture of what you already know about the world.
nuance.etymology: From Latin plausibilis (worthy of applause, acceptable), from plaudere (to applaud).
common_mistakes: Confusing plausibility with probability; plausibility is a judgment, not a calculated number.
Stressing the wrong syllable; the stress is on BIL, not on PLAW.

senses.definition: To pull something sharply; to pull something out.
senses.example: She plucked the phone from her bag and dialed.

senses.definition: To take or remove (someone) quickly from a particular place or situation.
senses.example: The rescue helicopter plucked the hikers off the ledge before the storm arrived.

senses.definition: To remove feathers from (a bird).
To play a string instrument pizzicato.
senses.example: Plucking a bow instrument may cause a string to break.

senses.definition: To pull or twitch sharply.
senses.example: to pluck at somebody's sleeve

senses.definition: Of a glacier: to transport individual pieces of bedrock by means of gradual erosion through freezing and thawing.
senses.example: Over thousands of years, the advancing glacier plucked huge boulders from the valley floor.

senses.definition: To play (a single string on a musical instrument) by pulling and then releasing it, such as on a guitar.
senses.example: Whereas a piano strikes the string, a harpsichord plucks it.

senses.definition: (rare) To rob, steal from; to cheat or swindle (someone).
senses.example: The dealer plucked the naive tourists of every dollar they had brought to the fair.
senses.label: rare

senses.definition: An instance of plucking or pulling sharply.
senses.example: Those tiny birds are hardly worth the tedious pluck.

senses.definition: The lungs, heart with trachea and often esophagus removed from slaughtered animals.
senses.example: The butcher sold the pluck from the lamb, including its heart, liver, and lungs.

senses.definition: Guts, nerve, fortitude or persistence.
senses.example: He didn't get far with the attempt, but you have to admire his pluck.

senses.definition: Cheap wine.
senses.example: Pour me another glass of that pluck, Harry, and quit your complaining.

core.definition: To pull something quickly and sharply, especially to remove it, such as a hair, feather, or flower.

pronunciation.tip: Use a short 'uh' vowel, as in 'luck,' and end with a clear, unvoiced 'k.' Do not stretch the vowel into 'plook.'

nuance.connotation: Neutral; the word is literal and physical in most uses, though it can be figurative, as in 'pluck up courage.'
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'pluck' mostly for picking fruit or flowers, plucking eyebrows, or plucking a guitar string. For removing feathers from a chicken, cooks may say 'pluck' or 'dress,' but in everyday talk 'pluck' is common in rural and cooking contexts. The noun 'pluck' meaning courage is more formal and somewhat old-fashioned.

distinctions.note: Pick is the everyday word for gathering fruit or flowers; pluck often suggests a quicker, sharper pull.
Pull is the general word for any force; pluck specifies a short, quick motion, often with the fingers.

examples.everyday: Can you pluck a few basil leaves from the garden for the pasta?
examples.professional: The technician will pluck the damaged cable out of the housing before replacing it.
examples.analytical: Her argument plucks a single phrase from the text and builds an entire theory on it, which weakens her reading.

nuance.analogy: Pluck is like a quick tug on a loose thread, removing it with one motion.
nuance.etymology: From Old English pluccian, meaning to pull or tear off.
common_mistakes: Using 'pluck' for slow, gentle picking; in everyday English 'pick' is more common.
Confusing the verb meaning 'pull out' with the noun meaning 'courage' in a sentence about feeling brave.

pluck.etymology: From Middle English *plucken*, *plukken*, *plockien*, from Old English *pluccian*, *ploccian* (“to pluck, pull away, tear”), also "to pluck, pull, snatch; pluck with desire", from **plukkōn*, from Proto-Germanic **plukkōną*, **plukkijaną* (“to pluck”), of…

senses.definition: One who, or that which, plugs.
A dental instrument used to insert fillings.

core.definition: A person or tool that plugs or packs material into a hole, especially a dental tool used to press filling into a tooth.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable with a short 'u' as in 'bus'. The final '-er' is a reduced American r-colored vowel, not a full 'ur' sound, and the 'g' is voiced.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and technical. It is a specialist word with no emotional tone.
nuance.usage_note: Most Americans will never use this word outside dentistry or a repair setting. Dentists and dental students know it as an instrument for packing filling material. In everyday life you would simply say 'the dentist's tool' or describe what it does. Do not confuse it with 'plunger', which is the toilet tool.

distinctions.note: A plunger is the rubber-cup tool for clearing drains, while a plugger is a dental or repair instrument for packing material into a hole.
A packer is a dental instrument for pressing filling material into a cavity, which is similar but has a different shape and use than a plugger.

collocations: use a plugger to pack filling

examples.everyday: My dentist said she still uses an old-style hand plugger for some fillings.
examples.professional: The dental assistant handed me the plugger to pack the composite into the cavity.
examples.analytical: The history of the plugger shows how dentists learned to condense gold foil, linking technique to the physical properties of the material.

nuance.analogy: A plugger is like a tamper pressing coffee grounds into a filter basket, packing the material firmly so there are no gaps.
nuance.etymology: From plug (verb) with the agent suffix -er.
common_mistakes: Confusing 'plugger' with 'plunger', which is the rubber tool for toilets and drains.
Using 'plugger' to mean a power plug; Americans call that a plug.

senses.definition: Synonym of plutocratic.

core.definition: Meaning the same as 'plutocratic': relating to a society or government controlled by the wealthy.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on 'KRAT', and the final '-ical' is pronounced 'ih-kul', with a weak middle vowel. Keep the 'k' clear.

nuance.connotation: Negative, like 'plutocratic'. It is now rare and can sound dated or overly learned.
nuance.usage_note: Americans almost always say 'plutocratic' rather than 'plutocratical', which is an older and less common form. You may see 'plutocratical' in older books or in writing that wants a more elaborate style. For everyday or professional writing, use 'plutocratic'.

distinctions.note: The two words mean the same thing, but 'plutocratic' is the standard modern form and 'plutocratical' is a longer, rarer variant.

examples.everyday: My grandfather still calls the whole arrangement plutocratical, which always makes me smile.
examples.professional: The memo describes a plutocratical funding structure in which a few donors control the agenda.
examples.analytical: Nineteenth-century reformers often described the political order as plutocratical, a term that sounded more learned to them than plutocratic.

nuance.analogy: 'Plutocratical' is like an old coat that still fits the same person: the meaning is the same, but the style has changed.
nuance.etymology: Formed from 'plutocratic' with the adjective suffix '-al'; from Greek ploutos, 'wealth', and kratos, 'rule'.
common_mistakes: Choosing 'plutocratical' in modern writing, where 'plutocratic' is more natural.
Confusing the word with 'bureaucratic', which describes rule by officials and rules.

senses.definition: Containing plutonium in a higher oxidation state.
senses.example: The chemist reported that the sample contained plutonic compounds in a higher oxidation state.

core.definition: Describing igneous rock that cooled slowly deep underground, forming large crystals, such as granite.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on 'TAH', the second syllable. Do not confuse it with 'plutonium', which is pronounced 'ploo-TOH-nee-um'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a precise scientific term with no emotional tone.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'plutonic' in geology and earth science, usually in phrases like 'plutonic rock'. Most people outside geology would simply say 'granite' or 'deep igneous rock'. The word is not related to the element plutonium, though the spelling looks similar.

distinctions.note: Volcanic rock cools quickly at or near the surface, forming small crystals, while plutonic rock cools slowly deep underground, forming larger crystals.
'Plutonium' is a radioactive chemical element, while 'plutonic' describes a type of rock formed underground.

examples.everyday: The guide said these gray granite hills are plutonic, formed from magma that cooled underground.
examples.professional: The core samples show a coarse plutonic granite beneath the volcanic layers.
examples.analytical: Plutonic rocks crystallize slowly at depth, which allows large, interlocking mineral grains to form.

nuance.analogy: Plutonic rock is like honey that cools slowly in a jar: it hardens with large, visible crystals, while a fast-cooling surface forms small, sharp ones.
nuance.etymology: Named for Pluto, Greek Plouton, the god of the underworld, with the suffix '-ic'.
common_mistakes: Confusing 'plutonic' with 'plutonium' because the words look alike.
Stressing the first syllable, as in 'PLOO-tonic', instead of the second.

senses.definition: To prod or jab with an object such as a finger or a stick.
To stir up a fire to remove ash or promote burning.
senses.example: Dad knelt by the stove to poke the coals before adding more wood.

senses.definition: To rummage; to feel or grope around.
senses.example: I poked about in the rubble, trying to find my lost keys.

senses.definition: To put a poke (device to prevent leaping or breaking fences) on (an animal).
senses.example: to poke an ox

senses.definition: To thrust at with the horns; to gore.
senses.example: The angry bull lowered its head and tried to poke the farmhand with its horns.

senses.definition: To notify (another user) of activity on social media or an instant messenger.
senses.example: Can you poke me when the team finishes the report?

senses.definition: To thrust (something) in a particular direction such as the tongue.
senses.example: The toddler would poke his tongue out whenever someone took his photo.

senses.definition: To penetrate in sexual intercourse.
(dated) To modify the value stored in (a memory address).
senses.example: The exploit could poke a new value into the target memory address.
senses.label: dated

senses.definition: A prod, jab, or thrust.
senses.example: He gave his brother a poke in the ribs to wake him up.

senses.definition: A lazy person; a dawdler.
senses.example: My brother is a poke who never gets off the couch before noon.

senses.definition: A stupid or uninteresting person.
senses.example: Don't be such a poke; read the instructions again.

senses.definition: An old, worn-out horse.
senses.example: That old poke of a horse hardly made it up the hill.

senses.definition: A device to prevent an animal from leaping or breaking through fences, consisting of a yoke with a pole inserted, pointed forward.
senses.example: The farmer fitted each pig with a poke to keep it from breaking through the fence.

senses.definition: A notification sent to get another user's attention on social media or an instant messenger.
senses.example: I sent her a poke on the app, but she never answered.

senses.definition: A poke bonnet.
senses.example: She tied her poke bonnet beneath her chin before stepping out into the sun.

senses.definition: A long, wide sleeve.
senses.example: The 1890s gown had enormous poke sleeves that barely fit through the doorway.

senses.definition: Slices or cubes of raw fish or other raw seafood, mixed with sesame oil, seaweed, sea salt, herbs, spices, or other flavorful ingredients.
senses.example: For dinner we ordered a bowl of ahi poke with seaweed and sesame oil.

senses.definition: A hit, especially an extra base hit.
senses.example: The shortstop's poke into the gap drove in two runs.

senses.definition: (dated) The storage of a value in a memory address, typically to modify the behavior of a program or to cheat at a video game.
senses.label: dated

core.definition: To push or jab something quickly with a finger, stick, or other object.

pronunciation.tip: It is one syllable with a long oh sound and a clear k at the end. Do not add a vowel; say POHK, not POH-uk.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in physical use, but it can be playful or annoying depending on context. Poke fun at is mildly negative.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use poke in casual speech for a light, quick push, often with a finger, and in idioms such as poke fun at, poke around, and poke your head in. Poking a coworker in a meeting may seem rude, so use it mainly with friends, family, or children.

distinctions.note: Prod suggests a more deliberate and sometimes firmer push to get someone's attention or to move them along.
A jab is a quick, sharp thrust, often with a stick or fist, while poke is usually softer and less forceful.
A nudge is a gentle push with the elbow or hand, usually to get attention without disturbing someone.

examples.everyday: Stop poking your brother with that pencil.
examples.professional: Can you poke your head into the room and see if the client is ready?
examples.analytical: The reviewer poked a hole in the argument by testing its weakest assumption.

nuance.analogy: Like tapping a sleeping friend's shoulder to see if they are awake.
nuance.etymology: From Middle English poken, probably from a Low German or Dutch source.
common_mistakes: Confusing poke with poker, which is a card game or a fireplace tool.
Saying POH-kuh with an extra syllable; the word has one syllable, POHK.

poke.etymology: From Middle English *poken*, perhaps from Middle Dutch *poken* or *poken*, both from **pukōn* or similar, which is itself of uncertain origin, but may be from an Proto-Germanic root.

senses.definition: A peace officer who is a member of a police force.

core.definition: A member of a police force whose job is to enforce the law, keep public order and respond to crimes.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the second syllable of police, 'lees', and the first syllable of officer. Do not say 'PO-lice', and the final -er in officer is a rhotic, reduced vowel.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. Tone depends on context, and it can sound respectful or critical depending on the speaker and the situation.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say 'police officer' in formal or neutral contexts, and 'officer' when speaking to someone directly. Informally they say 'cop'. 'Policeman' is now dated and gendered, so use 'police officer' for any gender. If a police officer stops you, say 'Yes, officer' politely.

distinctions.note: A detective investigates crimes, often in plain clothes, while a police officer is usually in uniform and handles patrol and emergencies.
'Cop' is informal slang, while 'police officer' is the standard neutral term.
A sheriff is an elected county official, while a police officer works for a city or state police department.

collocations: a police officer pulled me over

examples.everyday: Two police officers came to the door to ask whether we had seen a gray car on the street.
examples.professional: The police officer on scene asked for a supervisor before she filed the incident report.
examples.analytical: A police officer's discretion in deciding whether to arrest raises questions about how the law is actually applied.

nuance.etymology: Police from French police, from Latin politia, from Greek politeia, civil administration; officer from Latin officium, duty.
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable of police, as in 'PO-lice'.
Using 'the police' with a singular verb; in American English it takes plural verbs, as in 'The police are here'.

senses.definition: An ignoble or total coward; a dastard; a mean-spirited wretch.
senses.example: The senator called his rival a poltroon for skipping the debate to avoid questions.

senses.definition: Cowardly.
senses.example: The poltroon general fled the battlefield while his soldiers held the line.

core.definition: A contemptible coward; a person who lacks courage and is despised for it.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the second syllable, which rhymes with 'room'. Americans say the first syllable as 'pahl', not 'pole', and the r is pronounced clearly.

nuance.connotation: Strongly negative. It is an insult that suggests shameful cowardice.
nuance.usage_note: Poltroon is rare in American speech and sounds bookish or old-fashioned in conversation. Writers use it for dramatic effect, as in a novel or an editorial. The everyday American word is coward, and a person might say 'he is a total coward' in ordinary talk.

distinctions.note: Coward is common and neutral to strong, while poltroon is literary and more emphatically contemptuous.
Dastard is also literary, but it emphasizes a treacherous or sneaky wrongdoer, while poltroon focuses on cowardice.

examples.professional: A manager who blames his team to protect his own job is acting like a poltroon, and everyone notices.
examples.analytical: The novelist portrays the narrator as a poltroon whose fear of consequences betrays his own conscience.

nuance.analogy: A poltroon is like a dog that runs at the first bark, showing fear where others stand firm.
nuance.etymology: From Italian poltrone, lazy or idle person, from poltro, bed or lazy.
common_mistakes: Using poltroon for mild shyness, when it is a strong insult
Pronouncing the final syllable as 'tron' rather than 'troon'

senses.definition: Someone proficient in the art of mimicking various sounds, like a ventriloquist.
senses.example: William Edward Love was a 19th century polyphonist.

senses.definition: A musician skilled at of polyphony.

core.definition: A musician who is skilled at writing or performing polyphony, music with several independent voices.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on LIF, the second syllable; the first and third syllables are reduced to a quick 'uh' sound. Don't pronounce the 'o' in poly as a long vowel.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and rare, with a learned, slightly literary tone. It is a positive term when applied to a composer.
nuance.usage_note: This is a rare word that Americans seldom use. In music, people more often say 'composer', 'choral arranger' or 'contrapuntist'. The dictionary's older sense, a person who imitates many voices like a ventriloquist, is almost never used today.

distinctions.note: A contrapuntist is a musician skilled in counterpoint; a polyphonist is a rarer and broader term for anyone skilled in multi-voiced music.
A ventriloquist throws his or her voice to make it seem to come from elsewhere; the older sense of polyphonist refers to imitating many different voices.

examples.everyday: Our choir director is a real polyphonist; she can split any hymn into four parts on the spot.
examples.professional: The concert program describes her as a polyphonist known for her Renaissance motet arrangements.
examples.analytical: Tallis was a master polyphonist whose English church music balances independent voices with clear, intelligible text.

nuance.analogy: A polyphonist is like a juggler keeping several balls in the air, each moving on its own path without colliding.
nuance.etymology: From polyphony, from Greek polyphōnia 'many sounds', from polyphōnos 'many-voiced'.
common_mistakes: Stressing the wrong syllable, such as POL-ih-FO-nist; the stress is on LIF, the second syllable.
Assuming it means a polyglot or a speaker of many languages; in music it refers to skill with multi-voiced writing.

senses.definition: In a poor manner or condition; without plenty, or sufficiency, or suitable provision for comfort.
senses.example: to live poorly

senses.definition: With little or no success; indifferently; with little profit or advantage.
senses.example: to do poorly in business

senses.definition: Meanly; without spirit.
senses.example: The crowd applauded poorly, their enthusiasm drained after the long, dull speech.

senses.definition: Without skill or merit.
senses.example: He plays tennis poorly.

senses.definition: In a negative manner; with disapproval; unfavorably.
senses.example: I think poorly of them.

senses.definition: Ill, unwell, sick.
senses.example: to report one's child poorly

core.definition: In a bad or unsuccessful way; not well, or without enough skill, care or success.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, POOR, and the final -ly is a light lee sound, not lie. Pronounce the r clearly, and do not make the vowel of poor sound like pool.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It describes poor results, skill or condition, and it can be neutral when used in a technical or factual report.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use poorly in both speech and writing to describe results, performance or quality, such as slept poorly or performed poorly. The sense meaning unwell or sick is mainly British, and in the United States people say sick, not well, or not feeling good instead. In everyday talk, badly is often more common, while poorly sounds slightly more formal.

distinctions.note: Badly is more common in everyday speech and can be more emotional, while poorly sounds more neutral and formal.
Poor is an adjective, so you write the team performed poorly, not the team performed poor.

examples.everyday: I slept poorly last night, so I'm running on coffee today.
examples.professional: The vendor documented the API poorly, so we spent two days reverse-engineering the endpoints.
examples.analytical: The argument is poorly structured, since its central premise is assumed rather than tested.

nuance.analogy: Working poorly is like a car that runs but stalls on every hill; it still moves, but not in the way it should.
nuance.etymology: From poor and the suffix -ly, from Old English adverbial formation.
common_mistakes: Using poor as an adverb: say performed poorly, not performed poor.
Using poorly to mean sick in American English; say I'm sick or I don't feel well.
Confusing poorly with poverty-related meanings; poorly describes manner or quality, not money.

senses.definition: An allocated amount.
That which is divided off or separated, as a part from a whole; a separated part of anything.
senses.example: She cut the cake and gave each guest a generous portion.

senses.definition: One's fate; lot.
senses.example: Scripture teaches that each of us must accept the portion life assigns us.

senses.definition: The part of an estate given or falling to a child or heir; an inheritance.
senses.example: The farm was left to the eldest son, while each daughter received a smaller portion.

senses.definition: A wife's fortune; a dowry.
senses.example: The bride's family offered a sizable portion, which the groom's parents accepted gladly.

senses.definition: To divide into amounts, as for allocation to specific purposes.
senses.example: We portioned the grant money across three research projects this year.

senses.definition: To endow with a portion or inheritance.
senses.example: The old merchant portioned his daughters so each could marry well.

core.definition: A part or share of something, especially an amount of food served to one person.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The final syllable is a weak "shun," with the sh sound followed by a reduced vowel.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; in food contexts it is factual, and in financial or legal contexts it is formal.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use portion for the amount of food served to one person, such as a large portion or a small portion, often on menus. In everyday talk, they also say piece, share or part. Portion is also common in formal writing about shares of money, time or responsibility.

distinctions.note: A serving is the standard amount recommended or served; a portion is the amount actually given to one person, which may be bigger or smaller.
Part is a general word for any piece of a whole; portion often refers to a share that is allocated or served.

examples.everyday: Those fries are a huge portion, so you can share them with me.
examples.professional: We allocated a portion of the quarterly budget to the data quality project.
examples.analytical: Each portion of the argument depends on the one before it, so a flaw in the first step undermines the whole structure.

nuance.analogy: A portion is like a slice of pie: it is one part cut from a larger whole, meant for one person.
nuance.etymology: From Latin portio, share or part, from pars, part.
common_mistakes: Using portion for a small piece of a large item where part is more natural; portion often implies a share or serving.
Pronouncing it POR-tee-on, adding an extra syllable.

portion.etymology: From Middle English *porcioun*, borrowed from Old French *porcion*, accusative of Latin *portiō* (“a share, part, portion, relation, proportion”), from *portiō*, akin to *pars* (“part”); see *part*.

conversation.text: The portions here are huge; we should share.
Can I get a half portion of the pasta?
You get a decent portion for the price here.
Smaller portions help me eat less.
She gave me a huge portion of pasta.
Restaurant portions in the US are really big.

senses.definition: The study of the cultural legacies of colonialism and imperialism; postcolonialism.

core.definition: An academic field examining the cultural, political and psychological legacies of colonialism and imperialism.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on LO in 'colonial', not on the first syllable. The s in 'studies' is pronounced as a 'z' sound.
