senses.example: The second watch of the night began at midnight.

senses.definition: A period of wakefulness between the two sleeps of a biphasic sleep pattern (the dead sleep or first sleep and morning sleep or second sleep): the first waking.
senses.example: During the long night, she woke for a quiet watch between her first and second sleep.

senses.definition: A person or group of people who guard.
senses.example: The watch stopped the travelers at the city gates.

senses.definition: The post or office of a watchman; also, the place where a watchman is posted, or where a guard is kept.
senses.example: The old guard had kept the night watch at the gate for thirty years.

senses.definition: The act of seeing, or viewing, for a period of time.
senses.example: A brief watch of the meteor shower left the kids speechless.

senses.definition: A group of sailors and officers aboard a ship or shore station with a common period of duty: starboard watch, port watch.
senses.example: He served in the port watch on a destroyer during the Korean War.

senses.definition: A period of time on duty, usually four hours in length; the officers and crew who tend the working of a vessel during the same watch. (FM 55–501).
senses.example: The second mate took the midnight watch and kept the ship on course.

senses.definition: (rare) A group of nightingales.
senses.example: Poets once described a watch of nightingales singing in the hedgerows at dusk.
senses.label: rare

senses.definition: To look at, see, or view for a period of time.
senses.example: Watching the clock will not make time go faster.

senses.definition: To observe over a period of time; to notice or pay attention.
senses.example: Watch this!

senses.definition: To mind, attend, or guard.
senses.example: Please watch my suitcase for a minute.

senses.definition: To be wary or cautious of.
senses.example: You should watch that guy. He has a reputation for lying.

senses.definition: To attend to dangers to or regarding.
senses.example: watch your head; watch your step

senses.definition: To remain awake with a sick or dying person; to maintain a vigil.
senses.example: My sister stayed to watch with our dying father through the final night.

senses.definition: To be vigilant or on one's guard.
senses.example: For some must watch, while some must sleep: So runs the world away.

senses.definition: To act as a lookout.
senses.example: Two scouts were posted to watch from the ridge while the patrol rested.

senses.definition: To serve the purpose of a watchman by floating properly in its place.
senses.example: The anchored buoy continues to watch over the channel even in heavy seas.

core.definition: To look at something, such as a show, game or event, for a period of time.

pronunciation.tip: Use the short American 'ah' vowel, as in 'father', and do not round your lips into 'wotch'. The ch is one sound, not a t followed by sh.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It can be relaxed (watch a movie) or careful (watch the children), depending on context.
nuance.usage_note: This is one of the most common verbs in American English. People say 'watch TV', 'watch a movie' or 'watch the game' every day, and never 'see TV' for that. As a noun, 'watch' also means a timepiece worn on the wrist. Context decides whether it means enjoying a show or guarding someone.

distinctions.note: Look means direct your eyes toward something; watch means look at something for a period, often with attention.
See is the basic act of perceiving; watch implies deliberate attention over time.
Observe is more formal and is used in scientific or careful study; watch is everyday.

examples.everyday: Do you want to watch a movie tonight, or are you too tired?
examples.professional: I'd like to watch the migration closely for the first two weeks after the rollout.
examples.analytical: Historians watch how ideas migrate across traditions, noting where they change shape along the way.

nuance.analogy: Like a lifeguard watching the water: attention kept up over time, not just a quick glance.
nuance.etymology: From Old English wæcce, related to wake; the root sense is staying awake.
common_mistakes: Saying 'see TV' or 'look TV' instead of 'watch TV'.
Adding a preposition where none is needed, as in 'watch to the movie'; say 'watch the movie'.
Confusing the verb with the noun: 'I bought a new watch' is the timepiece, while 'I watch a new show' is the action.
nuance.biblical_note: In Scripture, watching means staying alert and awake, especially in view of the coming of the Lord. The Greek word is grēgoreō, 'to be awake, keep watch'. Matthew 24:42 tells disciples to watch because they do not know the day of the Lord's coming. Matthew 26:41 has Jesus tell the disciples to watch and pray so they do not enter into temptation. Mark 13:33 repeats the call to take heed and watch because the time is unknown.

watch.etymology: As a noun, from Middle English *wacche*, from Old English *wæċċe*.

senses.definition: Able to be worn.
senses.example: a wearable device

senses.definition: Suitable for wear by ordinary people, or in ordinary circumstances, as opposed to being unusual, uncomfortable, or otherwise difficult to wear.
senses.example: Engineers designed the new headset to be comfortable and wearable for all-day use.

senses.definition: Something that can be worn; an item of clothing.
senses.example: The startup's latest wearable tracks sleep and heart rate through a soft fabric band.

senses.definition: Ellipsis of wearable computer (“small computer which can be worn on the body”).

core.definition: Adjective: able to be worn comfortably. Noun: a device or garment worn on the body, such as a smartwatch or fitness tracker.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the first syllable, and the second and third syllables are weak and reduced to a schwa. Many learners say WEER-uh-bul with a long e, but the vowel is the one in 'air' because the word comes from 'wear'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive. The adjective praises comfort or practicality, and the noun is a neutral technology term.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'wearable' most often for smartwatches, fitness trackers and similar devices, and in fashion for clothing that is easy to wear every day. Saying a garment is 'wearable' suggests it is practical or presentable, which can be a mild compliment or a slightly lukewarm one depending on tone. The short form 'wearables' is a common shopping and tech-news term.

distinctions.note: Portable means able to be carried or moved from place to place, while wearable means able to be put on the body.
Comfortable describes how a thing feels to wear, while wearable only says that it can be worn at all or is suitable for everyday wear.

examples.everyday: My dad got a fitness wearable for his birthday, and now he checks his heart rate every hour.
examples.professional: The product team is prioritizing wearable integrations so users can see notifications on their watches.
examples.analytical: A wearable is defined less by its form than by its position on the body, which changes how we study human and machine interaction.

nuance.analogy: A wearable is like a tool you put on as easily as a jacket.
nuance.etymology: From wear (Old English werian, 'to clothe, wear') plus the suffix -able.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the first syllable as a long e (WEER) instead of the vowel in 'air'.
Using 'wearable' to mean only 'comfortable' when it does not describe comfort.

senses.definition: Asking what will happen after the meeting and who will do it.

core.definition: A question asking what actions will happen after a meeting or decision, and who is responsible for each one.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on STEPS, the last content word, as in most American phrases. Link the words smoothly: wuh-TAR-thuh-NEKST-STEPS, with the t in next often dropped to nekst and the r in ahr lightly pronounced.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive; it shows you are organized and ready to act, and it is a normal way to close a meeting.
nuance.usage_note: Americans ask this at the end of meetings, in calls, or in work chats to clarify who does what next. A natural reply is a short list, such as 'I'll send the draft Friday, and Maria will book the room.' You can also ask 'So what's the plan from here?' in a more casual team setting.

distinctions.note: Asks for the overall strategy, while next steps asks for the immediate actions.
A formal noun phrase for the written list of tasks that comes out of a meeting; next steps is the spoken question that leads to it.

examples.everyday: Thanks for dinner, Sam. So what are the next steps for getting the kitchen remodeled?
examples.professional: Thanks, everyone. What are the next steps, and who owns each one before Thursday's review?
examples.analytical: A decision without defined next steps remains an opinion, because it assigns no responsibility for turning intention into action.

nuance.analogy: Next steps are like the first few turns on a trail map: they tell you where to walk now, even if the destination is far away.
nuance.etymology: Next comes from Old English nēahst, superlative of nēah, meaning nearest; step comes from Old English stæpe.
common_mistakes: Saying 'next steps' with stress on NEXT, which makes it sound like a list of numbered items; the usual stress is on STEPS.
Using 'What are the next steps' for the past; for past actions, say 'What did we decide?'

conversation.text: Okay, so what are the next steps?

senses.definition: Any of the several cereal grains, of the genus Triticum, that yields flour as used in bakery.
senses.example: They bought a sack of wheat and a sack of rye with the intent to try their hand at milling and baking.

senses.definition: A light brown color, like that of wheat.
senses.example: wheat:

senses.definition: Ellipsis of wheat bread.
senses.example: Customer: A tuna sandwich, please. Waiter: Sure, hon. You want that on white, wheat, or rye?

senses.definition: Wheaten, of a light brown color, like that of wheat.
senses.example: She wore a wheat-colored sweater that matched the late summer fields.

core.definition: A cereal grass grown for its grains, which are ground into flour for bread, pasta and other foods.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the single syllable and make the final t a clear, released sound, not a flap, since it ends the word. Keep the vowel long and sweet, like the word 'sweet'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a basic food and farming word, though 'whole wheat' is often seen as healthier in American food marketing.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'wheat' constantly in grocery shopping, bread ordering and farming news, so it is an everyday word. At a deli or cafe, you can ask for a sandwich 'on wheat' to mean wheat bread, which is a common ellipsis. In the US, 'wheat' is also used as a light brown color name, as in 'a wheat-colored jacket'.

distinctions.note: Whole wheat keeps the bran and germ of the grain, so it has more fiber, while plain wheat products are often refined and whiter.
Barley is a different cereal grain used for soups, beer and some breads, and it is not a type of wheat.

examples.everyday: Can I get the sandwich on wheat instead of white bread?
examples.professional: The grain buyer said the wheat harvest came in lower than forecast this year.
examples.analytical: Jesus's parable of the wheat and the tares asks how a community can tell true believers from false ones before the harvest.

nuance.analogy: Wheat is like the base ingredient in a kitchen, used so often that it fades into the background of daily food.
nuance.etymology: From Old English hwæte, related to words for white, perhaps from the pale color of the grain.
common_mistakes: Saying an extra vowel, such as 'WEE-uht', which makes the word sound like two syllables.
Using 'wheat' as a countable noun, when Americans usually say 'some wheat' or 'wheat products' rather than 'wheats'.
nuance.biblical_note: In Scripture, wheat is the staple grain of Israel and a symbol of God's provision and the harvest of the final judgment. The Greek word is sitos (σῖτος), meaning grain or wheat. Matthew 13:24-30 describes the parable of the wheat and the tares, in which the wheat is left to grow alongside weeds until the harvest. John 12:24 says that a grain of wheat must fall into the earth and die to bear much fruit, a saying Jesus applies to his own death. Matthew 3:12 pictures the Messiah gathering his wheat into the granary, separating the righteous from the chaff.

wheat.etymology: From Middle English *whete*, from Old English *hwǣte*, from **hwaitī*, from Proto-Germanic **hwaitijaz*, from **hwītaz* (“white”).

senses.definition: Asking where it's allowed or best to leave your car.

core.definition: Asking where it is allowed, safe, or most convenient to leave your car while you are somewhere.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on PARK, and 'should' is often reduced to 'shud' in speech. The r in 'park' is pronounced clearly in American English; do not drop it or add a British-style long vowel.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a practical, everyday question.
nuance.usage_note: Americans ask this of friends, hosts, or parking staff, and it is common when visiting a new city or a crowded venue. Typical replies are 'Right out front is fine,' or 'Park in the garage across the street, because street spots fill up fast.' In cities, people may also say 'Where can I park?' with the same meaning.

distinctions.note: 'Can' asks what is permitted; 'should' asks for the best or wisest choice.
This asks for the location of a lot, not the spot where you should leave the car on the street.

examples.everyday: We're almost there, but where should I park? The lot looks full.
examples.professional: Where should I park for the client meeting? I want to make sure I'm not blocking the loading dock.
examples.analytical: The question 'Where should I park?' reveals how urban space rewards local knowledge, since the best spot depends on signage, time of day, and the unwritten norms of the block.

nuance.analogy: Like asking where to sit at a dinner party: the rules are there, but a good answer also depends on the situation.
nuance.etymology: 'Park' comes from Old French 'parc' (enclosed area), via Medieval Latin 'parricus'.
common_mistakes: Saying 'Where I should park?' with no inversion; in a question, use 'Where should I park?'
Pronouncing 'park' with a British-style vowel, as in 'pahk'; American English keeps a clear 'ar' sound.

conversation.text: I'm almost at your place. Where should I park?
"Where should I park?" "In the driveway, behind my car."
Where should I park for the concert? The lot looks full.

senses.definition: Of an animal such as a boar: to sharpen (its horns, teeth, tusks, etc.) by rubbing on a stone, etc. in preparation for an attack.
senses.example: The wild boar began to whet its tusks against a rock before charging the hunters.

senses.definition: To make more keen or to stimulate (someone's appetite, interest, etc.); to hone, to sharpen.
senses.example: to whet one's appetite or one's courage

senses.definition: To make more keen; to stimulate.
senses.example: The documentary's bold opening scene was meant to whet our appetite for the series.

senses.definition: To prepare for an attack.
senses.example: The rebel army began whetting for a dawn assault on the walled city.

senses.definition: An act of sharpening something by rubbing on an object, especially a whetstone.
senses.example: Give your kitchen knife a quick whet on the stone before you carve the roast.

senses.definition: An occasion to do something; a go, a turn.
senses.example: Let me have a whet at that stubborn jar lid before you give up.

senses.definition: A period of time between two sharpenings of a scythe.
senses.example: The farmer timed each whet of the scythe to finish the meadow before the rain.

senses.definition: An item of drink or food consumed as an appetizer or to ward off hunger until a meal; specifically, a small amount of liquor drunk as an appetizer; a dram, a nip.
senses.example: Before dinner, my grandfather always poured a small whet of bourbon for himself.

senses.definition: A thing which makes one's desire, interest, etc. more keen; an incitement, an inducement.
senses.example: The promise of a bonus was a whet for the team to push harder on the launch.

core.definition: To stimulate or increase a desire, appetite, or interest, such as making someone hungry or curious.

pronunciation.tip: It rhymes with 'bet' and 'set'; don't add a glide like 'wait.' The 'wh' is pronounced as a plain 'w' in most American speech.

nuance.connotation: Positive or neutral. It usually describes something pleasant that builds anticipation, such as a smell that whets your appetite.
nuance.usage_note: Americans mostly use 'whet' in the fixed phrase 'whet someone's appetite' or 'whet your appetite for,' often about food, travel, or a new show. The older sense of sharpening a blade is mostly literary or in outdoor and craft talk. In casual speech, 'get someone excited' is the everyday alternative.

distinctions.note: 'Whet' is narrower and always implies building a desire or appetite, while 'stimulate' can refer to any kind of activity or growth.
'Sharpen' is the everyday word for making a blade or skill better, while 'whet' is mostly used figuratively for appetite or interest.

examples.everyday: That smell from the bakery really whetted my appetite for breakfast.
examples.professional: The preview of the new dashboard whetted the sales team's interest in the upcoming launch.
examples.analytical: The early chapters whet the reader's appetite for a theological argument that the final pages never fully deliver.

nuance.analogy: Like a sharpening stone that makes a dull knife cutting again, a good preview makes your interest sharp and ready.
nuance.etymology: From Old English hwettan, 'to sharpen,' related to 'keen' and 'quick.'
common_mistakes: Saying 'whet the hunger' instead of 'whet the appetite,' which is the standard phrase.
Confusing 'whet' with 'wet,' which sounds the same in some speakers but means something completely different.

whet.etymology: The is derived from Middle English *whetten* (“to make the edge of sharp; to grunt, snort; to scrape the ground with; to make a chattering or grinding sound; of a person: to prepare for battle; to make alert or keen; to strengthen; to incite, provoke”),…

senses.definition: US standard spelling of wilfully.

core.definition: Deliberately or on purpose, often in a way that one knows is wrong.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on WIL, and the final syllable is a long E, as in 'lee'. Do not pronounce the middle syllable as 'ful' with a strong vowel.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It implies intentional wrongdoing or deliberate disobedience.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use willfully in legal and official contexts, such as 'he willfully ignored the warning', and in news reports about deliberate misconduct. It is less common in casual talk, where people say 'on purpose' or 'deliberately'. A natural reply might be 'Are you sure he did it on purpose?'

distinctions.note: Deliberately is neutral and everyday, while willfully adds a sense of defiance or intentional wrongdoing.

examples.everyday: Mom says I willfully ignored her, but I honestly did not hear her call me.
examples.professional: The contractor willfully violated the safety code, so the company may be held liable.
examples.analytical: The author argues that a person who willfully acts against known moral truths bears a greater share of responsibility than one who acts in error.

nuance.analogy: Like a driver who sees a stop sign and goes through anyway: the act is deliberate, not a mistake.
nuance.etymology: From 'willful' plus '-ly', formed in English from 'will' and '-ful'.
common_mistakes: Writing 'wilfully', the British spelling; Americans write 'willfully'.
Using willfully for accidental actions; it always implies intent.

senses.definition: Having never won; without a win; unsuccessful.

core.definition: Having never won any game, contest or election; without a single win, especially over a season.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, and the final -less is a reduced 'lus', not a full 'less' with a long e. Don't pronounce the i as in 'wine'.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It signals failure or a losing streak, usually said with sympathy or teasing, depending on context.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use winless mostly for sports teams, but also for candidates, startups or anyone with no successes yet. Phrases like 'still winless this season' are common in sports news and casual talk. For a single lost game, people usually say 'lost' or 'losing'. Winless suggests a longer run without any victories.

distinctions.note: Losing describes a single game or a current state; winless means no wins at all across a whole season or run.
Unsuccessful is broader and can apply to any attempt; winless is specific to contests and records.

examples.everyday: Our kids' soccer team is still winless this season, so they're getting a little discouraged.
examples.professional: The migration team has been winless on its last five deadlines, so we need to rethink the schedule.
examples.analytical: A winless season can conceal real progress, because a team's record captures outcomes but not the quality of its play.

nuance.analogy: Like a scoreboard that still shows a zero in the win column after every game.
nuance.etymology: From win plus the suffix -less, meaning 'lacking'.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the first vowel like 'wine' (WYNE-less) instead of the short i in 'win'.
Using winless for a single defeat, when losing is more natural.

senses.definition: Yarn made from long strands of wool.
The fine, smooth fabric made from such wool yarn.
Defeated, overcome.
senses.example: The worsted army fled in disarray.

core.definition: A smooth, firm yarn spun from long wool fibers, or the fabric woven or knit from it.

pronunciation.tip: The r in the spelling is silent, so the vowel is the short oo of 'wood' and the ending is -id. Say WOOS-tid, not worst-ed with an r sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it is a textile term used in fashion and manufacturing.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use worsted mainly in fashion, tailoring, textile and knitting contexts, as in 'a navy worsted suit' or 'worsted wool.' Most people outside those fields will not use the word. The adjective sense meaning defeated is archaic and should not be used in modern American English.

distinctions.note: Worsted yarn is smooth and tightly twisted from long fibers combed parallel; woolen yarn is softer, fuzzier and made from shorter fibers.
Wool is the general fiber from sheep; worsted is a specific smooth yarn or fabric made from it.

examples.everyday: This navy worsted suit doesn't wrinkle much, so it's great for travel.
examples.professional: Our buyer wants a worsted fabric with a smoother finish for the new winter line.
examples.analytical: Historians of the wool trade distinguish worsted from woolen cloth by how the fibers are combed and spun.

nuance.analogy: Like a neatly combed strand of hair compared with a tangled one, worsted yarn has its fibers aligned and smooth.
nuance.etymology: Named after the village of Worstead in Norfolk, England, where the yarn was historically made.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it with a clear r, as worst-ed; the r is silent.
Confusing the noun with the archaic adjective meaning defeated, which modern speakers rarely use.

worsted.etymology: Middle English *worstede*, *worsted*, from *Worstede* (now *Worstead*; **Wurϸestede*), a town in Norfolk, England.

senses.definition: The state or quality of being wrongful.

core.definition: The quality of being unjust, unlawful or morally wrong, especially in an act or conduct.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, and keep the 'ful' syllable very short and unstressed. The final 'ness' is a reduced 'nuhs,' so the word has four quick syllables.

nuance.connotation: Negative in most uses, referring to the moral or legal character of an act. In philosophy and law it is used neutrally to analyze whether something is wrong.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use 'wrongfulness' in casual conversation; they say 'it's wrong' or 'it's not right' instead. It appears mostly in legal briefs, court opinions, philosophy and ethics writing. In everyday speech, 'the wrongness of it' is more natural than 'the wrongfulness.'

distinctions.note: 'Wrongfulness' is the quality of an act being wrong, while 'wrongdoing' is the act itself or a case of doing wrong.
'Illegality' refers strictly to violating a law, while 'wrongfulness' can refer to moral or civil wrongs too.
'Injustice' describes an unfair condition or outcome, while 'wrongfulness' describes the defect in the act or conduct that caused it.

examples.everyday: Nobody in the family disputes the wrongfulness of lying to a friend about where you were.
examples.professional: The lawyer argued that the wrongfulness of the company's conduct was clear from the internal emails.
examples.analytical: Some ethicists locate the wrongfulness of deception in its violation of trust rather than in its consequences.

nuance.analogy: Wrongfulness is the stain on the act itself, not the spill that followed from it.
nuance.etymology: From 'wrongful' plus the noun suffix '-ness,' from Old English wrang and the suffix -ful.
common_mistakes: Using 'wrongfulness' in casual speech, where 'wrongness' or 'it's wrong' is more natural.
Confusing 'wrongfulness' with 'wrongdoing,' which refers to the act rather than its quality.

core.definition: The personal name of God in the Hebrew Bible, written YHWH; many English Bibles render it as 'the LORD' in capitals.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable and pronounce the W as a consonant before 'ay'. Do not say 'Yah-HWAY-hay' or drop the final vowel.

nuance.connotation: Neutral
nuance.usage_note: Americans use Yahweh mainly in academic study, theology and some Catholic liturgical settings. In church and everyday speech, people say 'the LORD' or 'God'. Note that the exact original pronunciation is uncertain, so 'Yahweh' is a scholarly reconstruction, not a certainty.

distinctions.note: Yahweh is the fuller traditional reconstruction of the divine name, while Yah is a shorter poetic form.
Lord translates Adonai or Kyrios in English Bibles and is a title of respect; Yahweh is the personal name.

examples.everyday: My Hebrew teacher said the name Yahweh is a scholarly guess, since Jews have not spoken the divine name aloud for centuries.
examples.professional: In the seminar paper, I used Yahweh for the personal name of God, but in the sermon I said 'the LORD' as the congregation expects.
examples.analytical: The reconstruction Yahweh rests on vocalization evidence from transliterations in Greek and Latin sources, and its use in scholarship reflects a deliberate effort to recover the name's original form.

nuance.analogy: Like the difference between a person's real name and the title everyone uses in public: the name is personal and specific, the title is the one people say aloud.
nuance.etymology: From the Hebrew divine name YHWH, whose vocalization as Yahweh is a modern scholarly reconstruction.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it as 'Yah-WHAY' with an extra syllable
Assuming Yahweh is a certain historical pronunciation, when it is a reconstruction
nuance.biblical_note: Yahweh is the scholarly reconstruction of the Hebrew divine name YHWH (יהוה), the personal name of God. The RSV prints it as 'the LORD' in capitals. Exodus 3:14 records God's answer to Moses, 'I AM WHO I AM', a wordplay connected to the verb hayah (to be). Exodus 3:15 identifies God as 'the LORD, the God of your fathers', linking the name to the covenant with Israel. Exodus 20:7 forbids taking the name of the LORD in vain, which is the basis for the Jewish practice of not pronouncing the name aloud.

traditions.view: The Orthodox generally avoid pronouncing the Hebrew divine name and use 'Lord' (Kyrios) in liturgy, following the Septuagint's tradition of substituting Kyrios for YHWH.
Catholic translations, such as the Jerusalem Bible, have used 'Yahweh' in the text, while the Latin liturgy and many vernacular translations use 'Dominus' or 'Lord' in worship.

Protestant English Bibles such as the RSV use 'LORD' in capitals, though scholarly Protestant writers commonly discuss Yahweh; Lutheran and Reformed scholars differ on how much to emphasize the Hebrew name in preaching.

senses.definition: To decrease the focal length of a zoom lens in order to obtain a reduced magnification of the image, or a wider-angle view.
senses.example: The director asked to zoom out for a wider shot of the landscape.

senses.definition: To manipulate a display (such as a computer screen) so as to make the image smaller and possibly less detailed.
senses.example: You can zoom out on the screen to see the entire document.

core.definition: To change a view, such as a map, photo, or screen, so you can see more of it and things look smaller.

pronunciation.tip: The particle 'out' gets the main stress, so say 'zoom OUT.' The 'ou' is the diphthong in 'house,' not the vowel in 'hot.'

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It describes a practical action and carries no judgment.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'zoom out' for maps, photos, spreadsheets, and video calls, often to see the bigger picture. It is casual and everyday. A natural reply is 'Good idea, let me see the whole thing' or 'Yes, that helps.' In meetings, 'let's zoom out' often means stepping back from details to a broader issue.

distinctions.note: Reduce makes a file or image physically smaller, while zoom out changes only the view and leaves the content unchanged.
Step back is a figurative phrase for considering a problem more broadly, while zoom out can be literal or figurative in meetings.

collocations: zoom out to see the whole map
zoom out for the big picture

examples.everyday: Zoom out a little so I can see the whole map, please.
examples.professional: Let's zoom out to the quarterly view before we decide whether the dip is real.
examples.analytical: Zooming out from the anecdote to the population data changes what the story can legitimately claim.

nuance.analogy: Zooming out is like backing up from a painting to see the whole composition instead of one brushstroke.
nuance.etymology: Phrasal verb from 'zoom,' an imitative word for a buzzing or humming sound, combined with 'out.'
common_mistakes: Saying 'zoom out the screen' instead of 'zoom out' or 'zoom out on the screen.'
Confusing 'zoom out' (change the view) with 'shrink' (make the object smaller).
